[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether a contract's failure semantics are legible from its signatures, and this interface is the clearest example in the module because it deliberately carries two. Four methods return a Result, the ordinary shape for this module: a refusal is a typed failure the page renders. Two methods return SelfCheckInOutcome<TResult> instead, because those two are the endpoints an attendee reaches by scanning a printed code, and every refusal there has to be told apart by a stable error CODE and rendered as a calm sentence. The type doc states exactly that split (ICheckInUIService.cs:13-18). The same two methods are also the only ones whose idempotency key is the caller's to supply, because the page reuses it across its own Retry; the two organizer writes carry a key too, but CheckInService mints it internally per check-in (CheckInService.cs:140-145). The class doc on CheckInService (CheckInService.cs:16-19) states the other axis: every call is authenticated, the badge read is caller-scoped ("my badge"), and the three organizer calls are role-gated server-side, so [Rubric §11, Security] lives on the server, not in this contract.
    • Walkthrough (ICheckInUIService.cs:20-85):
      • GetMyBadgeAsync(ct) (:27) fetches the signed-in attendee's own badge credential; an attendee with no badge answers ErrorType.NotFound, which the badge page renders as its empty state (:22-26).
      • CheckInByCredentialAsync(request, ct) (:34-36) checks an attendee in from a scanned or typed badge payload; organizer only (:30).
      • ManualCheckInAsync(request, ct) (:44-46) is the fallback used when a badge cannot be scanned; organizer only (:40). Both post through the shared PostCheckInAsync (CheckInService.cs:131), whose doc (:126-130) records that a repeat check-in is reported through AlreadyCheckedIn rather than as a failure, so there is no conflict branch to interpret.
      • RecordSponsorVisitAsync(sponsorId, idempotencyKey, ct) (:58-61) records the caller's visit to one sponsor booth; the doc states a repeat visit is a success carrying AlreadyVisited, not a failure (:50).
      • RecordRoomCheckInAsync(roomId, checkInCode, idempotencyKey, ct) (:71-75) checks the caller into whatever session the scanned room is hosting right now. The doc sentence at :64-65 is the whole design of that surface: the session is never sent, the server resolves it from the room and the configured grace window, which is why a printed room code never expires when the schedule moves. The nullable checkInCode (:68) is the room's check-in code the scanned QR carried, if any, and travels in the request body.
      • The idempotencyKey on both self-service writes (param docs at :53-56 and :69) is one key per attendee attempt, reused by every retry of it, the page's Retry included, so the server's idempotency filter replays the first answer instead of reporting a second visit. The pages mint it with Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N") (SponsorVisit.razor.cs:77, RoomCheckIn.razor.cs:87), and both server endpoints carry [Idempotent] (CheckInsController.cs:159, :194).
      • GetAttendanceStatsAsync(eventId, ct) (:82-84) fetches the attendance rollup for one event; organizer only (:78, enforced by [HasPermission] at CheckInsController.cs:213).
    • Why it's built this way: one interface rather than one per surface keeps the whole check-in vocabulary, and the single checkins resource it maps to (CheckInService.cs:31), in one reviewable place; the six methods correspond one-for-one to the six endpoints on CheckInsController (ADR-071 for the scan surfaces, ADR-072 for the check-in and points model).
    • Where it's used: implemented by CheckInService (CheckInService.cs:26), registered scoped (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:57), and injected into five pages: CheckInScan (CheckInScan.razor.cs:26), MyBadge (MyBadge.razor.cs:17), OrganizerAttendance (OrganizerAttendance.razor.cs:19), RoomCheckIn (RoomCheckIn.razor.cs:35, passing the code it was opened with at :112) and SponsorVisit (SponsorVisit.razor.cs:31). Server-side the whole controller sits behind [FeatureGate(EngagementFeatures.CheckIn)] (CheckInsController.cs:39) with the two self-service writes gated again individually (:160, :195), see EngagementFeatures and ADR-031.

    BookmarkApiClient

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Bookmarks · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/BookmarkApiClient.cs:21 · Level 4 · sealed class (internal)

    • What it is: the three bookmark HTTP calls (read the session-id map, create, delete), shared by SessionBookmarkUIService and the two offline replay handlers.
    • Depends on: AuthenticatedServiceBase, ITokenStorageService, HttpResultExecutor, ProblemDetailsResultReader, IdempotencyHeaders, CreateBookmarkRequest, UserSessionBookmarkDTO, Result. Externals: IHttpClientFactory, System.Net.Http.Json, System.Globalization.
    • Concept introduced, constructed rather than resolved to break a DI cycle. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses, among other things, whether dependencies point the right way and stay intentional. The type doc (BookmarkApiClient.cs:11-14) states the constraint: the offline write queue takes the replay handlers in its constructor and the toggle service takes the queue, so a shared registered client would close that circle. Each consumer therefore news its own instance from the factory and token storage it already holds (SessionBookmarkUIService.cs:43, BookmarkCreateReplayHandler.cs:29, BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler.cs:24). The class is internal, so the choice stays invisible outside the assembly.
    • Walkthrough (BookmarkApiClient.cs:21-100):
      • Endpoint = "bookmarks" (:24); NewCreateKey() (:28) exposes the base class's NewIdempotencyKey() so the caller can pick a create's key before the first attempt.
      • GetSessionIdsAsync(userId, ct) (:34-52) GETs bookmarks/session-ids?userId= (invariant formatting) under the shared RetryPolicy and reads a Dictionary<SessionIdentifierType, UserSessionBookmarkIdentifierType>, so a caller learns both "is it starred" and "which id deletes it".
      • CreateAsync(request, idempotencyKey, ct) (:63-78) stamps the given key on the per-operation client (:69) before the retried POST; the doc (:54-58) records the two effects: a retried or replayed create is answered from the server's replay cache (ADR-017), and the key lets the shared retry policy treat the POST as replay-safe.
      • DeleteAsync(bookmarkId, ct) (:84-99) DELETEs bookmarks/{id}; a bookmark that is not there is a NotFound failure (:80).
    • Why it's built this way: nothing here throws for a server answer (:16-18): responses come through ProblemDetailsResultReader with the API's ErrorType intact, and transport faults become Http.TransportFailure failures through HttpResultExecutor, which is the code SessionBookmarkUIService keys its queue fallback on (ADR-144).
    • Where it's used: SessionBookmarkUIService, BookmarkCreateReplayHandler, BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler.

    CheckInService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.CheckIns · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/CheckIns/CheckInService.cs:26 · Level 4 · sealed class

    • What it is: the single HTTP client for every badge and scan surface in the module, implementing ICheckInUIService against the checkins resource (CheckInService.cs:31). It carries six calls with three different audiences: the attendee reading their own badge, the organizer scanning or manually checking someone in, and the attendee self-recording a sponsor booth or room visit. The two self-service writes also carry their own bounded retry, token-refresh replay and caller-supplied idempotency key, because the attendee is standing at the booth or the door when they fire; the two organizer writes carry an internally minted key so a retried scan is replayed rather than counted twice.
    • Depends on: ICheckInUIService, AuthenticatedServiceBase, ITokenStorageService, ITokenRefresher (optional, CheckInService.cs:29), HttpResultExecutor, ProblemDetailsResultReader, IdempotencyHeaders, MyBadgeDTO, CheckInAttendeeRequest, ManualCheckInRequest, CheckInResultDTO, SponsorVisitRequest, SponsorVisitResultDTO, RoomCheckInRequest, RoomCheckInResultDTO, AttendanceStatsDTO, SelfCheckInOutcome<TResult>. Externals: IHttpClientFactory, System.Net (HttpStatusCode), System.Text.Json (JsonDocument), System.Net.Http.Json (JsonContent, ReadFromJsonAsync), System.Globalization, and the System.Threading.Lock behind the single-flight refresh.
    • Concept introduced, two failure dialects in one client. The authenticated-HTTP shape is taught at BookmarkApiClient; what is new here is that this class deliberately reports failure two different ways depending on who is looking at the screen. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether a client contract preserves the distinctions the server actually makes. The four organizer and badge calls answer with a Result, carrying the server's own error code and type. The two attendee self-service calls do not: they return a SelfCheckInOutcome<TResult> carrying only a raw error-code string, because the QR landing pages have to tell "no session is running in this room" from "the owning event is not published" and both arrive as HTTP 404 (CheckInService.cs:155-171, and the outcome record's own doc at SelfCheckInOutcome.cs:3-13). A status code alone cannot pick the state, so the code is read out of the problem body and handed to the page. The same doc adds a third answer (:162-170): an attempt that got no definitive answer is not a refusal. A 408, 409 (the same key still in flight), 429 or 5xx is retried in place, a 401 is refreshed and replayed once, and whatever is still unanswered comes back as IsTransient, which the page offers a Retry for; only the caller's own cancellation propagates. [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] is the reason the pages then collapse several of the refusal codes into one message: see CheckInState and VisitState.
    • Walkthrough (public calls first, then the self-service send pipeline)
      • The primary constructor (:26-29) takes the factory, the token storage and an optional ITokenRefresher defaulting to null; the param doc (:22-25) records that a host registering no refresher reports a 401 on a self check-in as transient instead of replaying it. SelfCheckInMaxAttempts = 3 (:37, the first send plus two retries, kept small because the page's Retry covers anything longer) and MaxRetryAfter of 5 seconds (:43) bound the in-place retries. _refreshSync and _refreshInFlight (:45-46) hold the shared refresh, and the internal settable Delay delegate (:52) lets a test run the retries without waiting out the real delays.
      • GetMyBadgeAsync (:55-70) GETs checkins/my-badge. The comment (:65-67) records the contract precisely: a 404 arrives as a NotFound failure rather than the old null, so "this attendee has no badge" stays a distinguishable state while the badge page renders exactly the empty surface it rendered for null. The server action is CheckInsController.GetMyBadgeAsync (CheckInsController.cs:64).
      • CheckInByCredentialAsync (:73-76) and ManualCheckInAsync (:79-82) are one-line delegations to PostCheckInAsync, differing only in the relative URL: the root checkins and checkins/manual. Both server endpoints are permission-gated on EngagementPermissions.CheckInManage and marked [Idempotent] (CheckInsController.cs:104-105, :128-129), so the client does no role check of its own.
      • RecordSponsorVisitAsync (:85-93) and RecordRoomCheckInAsync (:96-105) build their requests inline (SponsorVisitRequest with the sponsor id; RoomCheckInRequest with the room id and the scanned CheckInCode, :103) and delegate to PostSelfCheckInAsync together with the caller's idempotencyKey. Neither call passes an attendee identity: the server takes it from the token, so a scanned code can only ever check in the person holding the phone. Each also has its own feature gate on the server (CheckInsController.cs:160, :195).
      • GetAttendanceStatsAsync (:108-124) GETs checkins/stats?eventId= with invariant formatting (:116) and returns the AttendanceStatsDTO rollup; the endpoint is permission-gated the same way as the writes (CheckInsController.cs:213).
      • PostCheckInAsync<TRequest> (:131-153) is the Result-returning poster shared by the two organizer writes. Its doc comment (:126-130) records why there is no conflict branch: a repeat check-in comes back with AlreadyCheckedIn set rather than as a 409, so the caller has one success shape to interpret. It stamps one freshly minted IdempotencyHeaders.IdempotencyKey on the per-operation client (:145) before the retried POST; the comment (:140-144) gives the reason: a scan whose response is lost on the venue network is retried and the server replays the first answer instead of "already checked in", and without a key the retry policy would resend a POST only when it failed before being sent. The key is minted once, outside the retried delegate.
      • PostSelfCheckInAsync<TRequest, TResult> (:172-208) is the outcome-returning poster, and notably the one path in the class that does not go through HttpResultExecutor or the reader. It rejects a blank key up front (:179), sends through SendSelfCheckInAsync, and on success reads the payload with ReadFromJsonAsync and wraps it (:185-189). A 401 or a retryable status that is still standing becomes IsTransient: true (:191-194); any other non-success becomes new SelfCheckInOutcome<TResult>(null, await ReadErrorCodeAsync(...)) (:196), so a refusal is data, not an exception. An HttpRequestException (:198-201) and an OperationCanceledException the caller did not ask for, which is how HttpClient.Timeout surfaces (:202-207), are both transient too.
      • SendSelfCheckInAsync (:216-243) runs the retrying send on an authenticated client (:223-226) and returns that response unless it is a 401 with a refresher available (:228-231). Then it acquires a refreshed token (:233-237), disposes the rejected response and replays the write once on a client built with the new token (:239-242). The doc (:210-215) explains why storage is not simply re-read: the stored token can still look fresh by the client clock after the server rejected it.
      • SendWithRetriesAsync (:250-278) loops until it gets a definitive answer or runs out of attempts, with the backoff starting at one second (:258) and doubling after each wait (:276). Only the last attempt lets a transport failure propagate (throwOnTransportFailure: retriesLeft == 0, :263); earlier ones come back as a null response and wait the current backoff (:267).
      • TrySendOnceAsync (:283-308) builds a fresh HttpRequestMessage per attempt, since a sent message cannot be sent again (:291-297), and stamps every one with the same IdempotencyHeaders.IdempotencyKey header (:298).
      • RetryWait (:315-324) answers null, meaning final, on the last attempt or a non-retryable status, and otherwise prefers the server's Retry-After over the backoff; a requested wait past MaxRetryAfter also ends the attempt (:323) rather than holding the page on its loading state. IsRetryableStatus (:331-334) is 408, 409, 429, or any 5xx except 501 and 505, and RetryAfter (:337-352) reads either header form, clamped at zero.
      • TryAcquireRefreshedTokenAsync (:360-374) is single-flight under _refreshSync: two check-ins landing on one rejected token share one rotation, because on MAUI a second rotation presenting the same refresh token is read as reuse and revokes the session (BR-206, per the doc at :354-359). Each caller waits on the shared task with its own token (:373), while AcquireRefreshedTokenAsync (:376-393) runs under CancellationToken.None (:380), so one caller giving up never cancels the refresh for another. A blank token, an InvalidOperationException (no JS interop during SSR prerender) or an HttpRequestException yields null (:381-392), which leaves the 401 standing and the outcome transient.
      • ReadErrorCodeAsync (:400-435) walks the problem body's errors array and returns the first element's code string (:417-425). Everything else yields null: an empty body (:407-408), a body with no errors array (:411-415), a non-string code, or a JsonException from an HTML error page or a bare challenge (:429-434, with the comment naming that case). null is a meaningful value here, it is what the pages render as the generic "unavailable" state.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc (:16-19) sets the rule that every call is authenticated, including the badge read, because the badge is caller-scoped rather than public (CheckInsController.cs:64). The split between the two posters is the client-side consequence of a server design decision recorded in ADR-072: organizer scanning and attendee self-service produce the same domain writes but face very different humans, so the refusal vocabulary is stable (CheckInErrorCodes) and the client passes it through untranslated. Retrying any of the four writes is only safe because every attempt of one operation carries the same key and all four server endpoints are [Idempotent] (CheckInsController.cs:104, :128, :159, :194): a replayed first answer can never be counted as a second check-in or visit.
    • Where it's used: registered scoped as ICheckInUIService (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:57) and injected by five surfaces: MyBadge (MyBadge.razor.cs:17, called at :63), CheckInScan (CheckInScan.razor.cs:26, called at :265, :288), OrganizerAttendance (OrganizerAttendance.razor.cs:19, called at :160), RoomCheckIn (RoomCheckIn.razor.cs:35, called at :112) and SponsorVisit (SponsorVisit.razor.cs:31, called at :98). The whole controller sits behind the EngagementFeatures.CheckIn gate (CheckInsController.cs:39), so a deployment with the feature off answers 404 to every one of these calls.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: CheckInServiceTests covers mostly the self-service path: response disposal on success and failure (:39, :67), the idempotency key on both writes (:88, :100), a 429 honoring Retry-After under the same key (:119), the bounded retry ending transient (:139), a Retry-After past the cap (:154), the 401 refresh-and-replay and its unrefreshable case (:167, :185), repeated transport failure and an HttpClient timeout (:200, :212), and caller cancellation propagating (:223). Two tests cover the organizer key: a retried organizer check-in resends the same non-empty key (:241) and each manual check-in mints a fresh one (:265). The badge read and the stats read are exercised indirectly through the bUnit page tests (MyBadgeTests, CheckInScanTests, OrganizerAttendanceTests, RoomCheckInTests, SponsorVisitTests), which mock the interface rather than the transport. Which error codes a given server build emits is the API's contract, not this file's.

ReplayAsync (:35-53) reads the payload as a CreateBookmarkRequest (:39), answering a validation failure Bookmarks.Replay.InvalidPayload when it cannot (:41-42); posts it with write.IdempotencyKey (:45), the same key the online attempt used; returns any failure other than UserSessionBookmarkErrorCodes.Duplicate (:46-49); and then notifies the reminder layer of the add (:51) before succeeding (:52).

    • What it is: the offline write handler that replays a queued bookmark removal (kind BookmarkOfflineWrites.DeleteKind), resolving the bookmark id by session when the queued write did not know it.
    • Depends on: IOfflineWriteHandler, PendingWrite, BookmarkApiClient, BookmarkOfflineWrites, BookmarkDeletePayload, SessionReminderCoordinator, Result, Error. Externals: IHttpClientFactory.
    • Concept introduced: none new beyond BookmarkCreateReplayHandler; the difference is that a delete is idempotent by outcome rather than by key, so it carries no idempotency key and instead treats "not there" as removed.
    • Walkthrough (BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler.cs:19-67): own BookmarkApiClient (:24), Kind => BookmarkOfflineWrites.DeleteKind (:27). ReplayAsync (:30-66) reads a BookmarkDeletePayload (:34, invalid payload at :36-37). With no BookmarkId (:40-53) it reads the session-id map, returns a failed read as a failure (:44-47), and takes the id for the session if present (:49-52). With an id (:55-62) it deletes, returning any failure except NotFound (:58). Either way it then notifies the reminder layer of the removal (:64) and succeeds (:65): a session that is not in the map, or a 404, means the bookmark is already gone.
    • Why it's built this way: a star set by a queued add has no id on the device, and an add then remove while offline coalesces to a single delete; resolving by session on replay is what lets that delete be a clean no-op when the add never reached the server (ADR-144; tested by Offline_AddThenRemove_LeavesExactlyOneQueuedDelete_ThatReplaysAsANoOpWithoutTheBookmark, SessionBookmarkSetBookmarkedTests.cs:232).

    SessionBookmarkUIService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Bookmarks · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/SessionBookmarkUIService.cs:36 · Level 9 · sealed class

    • What it is: a cross-module service implementing ISessionBookmarkUIService, used by the Conference UI to read bookmark state and toggle bookmarks inline. Every successful read or mutation also feeds the session-reminder layer, and a toggle that cannot reach the server is kept on the device's offline write queue and replayed later.
    • Depends on: ISessionBookmarkUIService, BookmarkApiClient (constructed, :43), ITokenStorageService, SessionReminderCoordinator (injected as a concrete class, :39), IOfflineWriteQueue and OfflineWriteOptions, IConnectivityStatusService, BookmarkOfflineWrites, BookmarkDeletePayload, BookmarkWriteOutcome, CreateBookmarkRequest, UserSessionBookmarkDTO, UserSessionBookmarkErrorCodes, HttpResultExecutor (for TransportErrorCode). Externals: IHttpClientFactory.
    • Concept introduced, the side effect on the write path, and the offline fallback. [Rubric §19, State Management] assesses where derived client state is kept in step with the server. Local session reminders are exactly that kind of derived state: they are only correct if they track the bookmark set, and the bookmark set can change from any page or any device. Putting the reminder calls inside this one service, rather than in each component that toggles a bookmark, is what makes that hold regardless of entry point. The ordering is the load-bearing part: HTTP first, reminder only after a confirmed success. The class doc adds the guarantee that makes this safe to read (:19-24): nothing here throws for a server answer, the response is read through ProblemDetailsResultReader with the API's own ErrorType intact and transport faults become failures through HttpResultExecutor, so the reminder layer is driven only by outcomes the server actually confirmed. [Rubric §29, Resilience]: reminder failures are swallowed inside the coordinator, so they never surface to the bookmark caller; and a toggle that never got an answer is not lost, it goes on the Common offline write queue and is replayed by BookmarkCreateReplayHandler and BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler (:25-29). The rule that picks the queue is narrow on purpose: only a request that never got an answer falls back to the queue, a refusal is an answer (IsTransportFailure, :215-217).
    • Walkthrough
      • GetBookmarkedSessionIdsAsync (:46-60) reads the map through BookmarkApiClient.GetSessionIdsAsync (:49), a Dictionary<SessionIdentifierType, UserSessionBookmarkIdentifierType>, which is why a page can render a bookmark toggle and know the id needed to delete it from one call. A failure is re-wrapped with its original errors and returns early (:51-54), so the reminder call is unreachable on that path. On success it calls reminderCoordinator.ResyncAsync([.. bookmarks.Keys], cancellationToken) (:57) with the comment naming the intent: this response is the authoritative set, so it is the right moment to heal drift caused by another device.
      • DeleteBookmarkAsync (:63-76) DELETEs by bookmark id and calls NotifyBookmarkRemovedAsync(sessionId, ...) only on a confirmed delete (:70-73). A 404 is a NotFound failure and therefore does not notify here.
      • SetBookmarkedAsync(userId, sessionId, bookmarked, knownBookmarkId, ct) (:79-135) is the toggle, answering a BookmarkWriteOutcome. First it cancels any write still queued for the same user and session (:91, the newest intent wins and is always issued in full, comment at :86-90: a create queued after a transport failure may already have reached the server, so the opposite toggle must still reach it as a remove). It picks the create's idempotency key before any attempt (:96, comment at :93-95) so a queued retry carries the same key. A device that already knows it is offline queues at once (:100-103). Online, an add that succeeds returns Queued: false with the new id (:108-111); an add that meets UserSessionBookmarkErrorCodes.Duplicate notifies the reminder layer and counts as done with no id (:113-119); a transport failure queues, any other failure is returned (:121-123). A remove that succeeds returns Queued: false (:126-130); its transport failure queues likewise (:132-134).
      • CreateOnlineAsync (:137-150) posts the CreateBookmarkRequest with the chosen key and notifies the add only on success (:144-147).
      • RemoveOnlineAsync (:157-182) resolves a missing id through the session-id read (:166); a session not in the map is already removed and succeeds (:172-175), and a 404 from the delete also counts as success (:180-181).
      • EnqueueAsync (:189-213) queues one complete write under BookmarkOfflineWrites.CoalesceKey(userId, sessionId) (:197): a create of kind CreateKind carrying the chosen key (:199-203), or a delete of kind DeleteKind carrying a BookmarkDeletePayload (:204-208). A write the queue refuses comes back as a failure, never as queued (:210-212).
      • IsTransportFailure (:215-217) matches HttpResultExecutor.TransportErrorCode; IsDuplicate (:219-221) matches UserSessionBookmarkErrorCodes.Duplicate.
      • The coordinator members these calls use are ResyncAsync (SessionReminderCoordinator.cs:71), NotifyBookmarkAddedAsync (:60) and NotifyBookmarkRemovedAsync (:64).
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc (:13-18) records both reminder halves: the wiring lives here so reminders track bookmarks no matter which page toggled them (ADR-042 Wave 2), and reminder failures never reach the bookmark caller. The offline half follows ADR-144; the registration comment (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:37-41) notes that on a Blazor Server circuit the queued writes live in the browser's storage through JS interop, so the queue works only while the circuit is up. The coordinator is registered scoped alongside this service (DependencyInjection.cs:48) and is a no-op on hosts whose local-notification capability is unsupported, which is why a web-only host pays nothing for the reminder coupling.
    • Where it's used: registered scoped as ISessionBookmarkUIService (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:35); resolved optionally by the Conference public pages, which call ServiceProvider.GetService<ISessionBookmarkUIService>() and null-check the result (PublicSessionList at PublicSessionList.razor.cs:38, :141; SessionBookmarkButton, the toggle the detail page renders, at SessionBookmarkButton.razor.cs:33, :56, calling SetBookmarkedAsync at :122), passed down as a nullable parameter to PublicSessionListView (PublicSessionListView.razor.cs:71, toggling at :164, :186), and taken by PublicSessionBookmarkState (PublicSessionBookmarkState.cs:15). That optional resolution is the extraction story in practice: Conference renders correctly in a host where the Engagement UI module is not registered at all. Covered by SessionBookmarkUIServiceTests (the HTTP contract) and SessionBookmarkSetBookmarkedTests (the online and offline toggle paths, SessionBookmarkSetBookmarkedTests.cs:47-313).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the dependency is on the concrete SessionReminderCoordinator, not an interface, so a test of this service has to construct a real coordinator; the test suite does exactly that, assembling an inert one from mocks (SessionBookmarkUIServiceTests.cs:180-193). Whether a reminder is actually scheduled is decided inside the coordinator and SessionReminderPlanner, not here.

    NowNextSessionInfo

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.HappeningNow · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/HappeningNow/INowNextService.cs:26 · Level 0 · sealed record

    • What it is: one row of the now-and-next snapshot, a session's identifier, title, room name, and its wall-clock start and end in the event's own time zone.
    • Depends on: the SessionIdentifierType alias (solution-wide global using, see primer §2). Externals: BCL DateTime, plus System.Text.Json name-based binding at the call site.
    • Concept, the locally mirrored wire shape. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether a module can be lifted out without dragging a neighbor's assembly along, and [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] how a payload contract is expressed to its consumers. The bytes on the wire are produced by Conference's NowNextSessionDTO; Engagement redeclares only the fields it renders instead of referencing MMCA.ADC.Conference.Shared for one payload, and JSON binds them by property name. The type doc on the enclosing snapshot records that this is a deliberate mirror and that the Android home-screen widget makes the same call with a mirror of its own (INowNextService.cs:6-9; the widget's private copy is at MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/Platforms/Android/NowNextWidgetProvider.cs:128-132). The same tolerant-reader trade-off taught on AttendeeRow applies: nothing at compile time keeps the mirror aligned with the DTO, only the round-trip tests do.
    • Walkthrough (INowNextService.cs:26-31): five positional members, SessionId (line 28, the deep-link target), Title (29), RoomName (30, nullable), StartsAtLocal (31), and EndsAtLocal (32). Two details are load-bearing. RoomName is null whenever the session carries no room id, or carries one the event's room map does not contain, a decision the server makes in a single expression (GetNowNextHandler.cs:78). And the two times are plain DateTime wall clock in the event's zone, not UTC and not DateTimeOffset: the server passes the stored wall-clock values straight through (GetNowNextHandler.cs:79-80) while keeping the UTC instants it computed for its own filtering on its side of the row (:81-82), so no client ever converts a zone.
    • Why it's built this way: glanceable surfaces (a page card, a home-screen widget) should print exactly what the printed schedule says, so the wall-clock value travels as data. The UTC instants stay on the server's side of the contract for callers that do their own math; this mirror deliberately drops them, along with EventId. The slice arrives with ADR-042 Wave 8 (GetNowNextHandler.cs:13).
    • Where it's used: only inside NowNextSnapshot's Now and Next lists; the HappeningNow page holds them in _sessionsNow / _sessionsNext (HappeningNow.razor.cs:55-56) and renders one card per row.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the mirror is checked by NowNextServiceTests round-tripping a JSON body, not by the compiler, so a renamed server property would deserialize to a default value rather than break the build.

    SessionReminder

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.HappeningNow · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/HappeningNow/SessionReminderPlanner.cs:15 · Level 0 · sealed record

    • What it is: an immutable value describing one planned on-device reminder for a bookmarked session, a stable notification id, when it should fire, and where a tap takes the user.
    • Depends on: the SessionIdentifierType alias (solution-wide global using, see primer §2). Externals: BCL DateTimeOffset. No first-party types beyond the alias.
    • Concept, the immutable planning DTO. [Rubric §19, State Management] assesses whether client-side state is modeled as explicit, predictable values rather than mutable ad-hoc fields. A sealed record gives value equality and init-only positional members for free (see primer §4), so a planned reminder is a snapshot that cannot drift after SessionReminderPlanner computes it. The type carries no behavior: it is pure data handed from the pure planner to the stateful coordinator.
    • Walkthrough (SessionReminderPlanner.cs:15-29): six positional members, NotificationId (int, line 16), SessionId (17), SessionTitle (18), StartsAtUtc (19), DeliverAt (20), and DeepLinkRoute (21), plus one init-only body property, IsImmediate (:28). The doc comment (:5-14) is load-bearing intent: NotificationId is derived deterministically from the session id so rescheduling replaces an existing OS notification instead of stacking a duplicate, DeliverAt is the fire instant (start minus lead, clamped to now), and DeepLinkRoute is the app-relative route published on tap. IsImmediate (doc at :23-27) marks a reminder whose session was already inside the lead window at planning time, so its DeliverAt was clamped to fire almost at once; the doc states the contract the coordinator enforces, such a reminder fires once, when the session becomes tracked, not again on every replan. It is a body property rather than a seventh positional member, so existing positional construction stays valid and the planner sets it with an object initializer.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the planned reminder as a value lets the planner stay a pure function and the coordinator diff plans by id (ADR-042 Wave 2, the local-notification dispatcher). Carrying IsImmediate on the value, rather than having the coordinator recompute "was this clamped", keeps the window decision in the one place that did the date math.
    • Where it's used: produced by SessionReminderPlanner.Plan (SessionReminderPlanner.cs:90-99); consumed by SessionReminderCoordinator, which calls Plan at SessionReminderCoordinator.cs:175, reads IsImmediate to skip an already-issued immediate reminder (:215), and turns each remaining value into a LocalNotificationRequest (:223).

    NowNextSnapshot

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.HappeningNow · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/HappeningNow/INowNextService.cs:14 · Level 1 · sealed record

    • What it is: the whole "happening now / up next" payload for one event as the Engagement UI consumes it, the event's display name, whether the event is live at the query instant, and two lists of NowNextSessionInfo rows.
    • Depends on: NowNextSessionInfo. Externals: BCL IReadOnlyList<T>.
    • Concept, the two-bucket time projection, computed once on the server. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether work sits where it is cheapest, and [Rubric §18, UI Architecture] whether a page renders a prepared view model rather than deriving one. Both buckets are decided by GetNowNextHandler against a single instant taken from an injected TimeProvider (GetNowNextHandler.cs:29), never from the browser clock. Now is every eligible session whose window is half-open around that instant, StartsAtUtc <= utcNow && utcNow < EndsAtUtc (GetNowNextHandler.cs:53), so a session that ends exactly now is already out and the one starting exactly now is already in. Next is not "the next session": it is the batch that shares the earliest future start (:58-66), which is what makes parallel tracks appear together instead of one arbitrary room winning. The empty cases are ordinary, not error states: between sessions Now is empty, after the last session Next is empty (nextStart is null and the list is [], :60-62), and before the first session Now is empty while Next carries the opening batch.
    • Walkthrough (INowNextService.cs:14-18): four positional members, EventName (line 16), IsLive (17), Now (18), and Next (19). IsLive is independent of the two lists: the server compares the same instant against the event's live window from CurrentEventSelector.GetLiveWindowUtc(StartDate, EndDate, TimeZone) (GetNowNextHandler.cs:68-69), so a live event during a coffee break reports IsLive: true with an empty Now. Ordering is fixed server-side too: Now sorts by start then by room name ordinal-ignore-case (:54-55), Next by room name alone (:65) since every row in it shares one start.
    • Why it's built this way: no client can compute either bucket correctly on its own, because eligibility depends on data a public catalog read does not expose (see INowNextService), so the snapshot is shipped precomputed and every surface (page and widget) shows the same answer. The one snapshot type also keeps IsLive next to the lists, which is what lets a caller distinguish "the conference is not running" from "nothing is on right now".
    • Where it's used: carried by the Result that INowNextService.GetAsync returns; the HappeningNow page projects it with result.Value?.Now ?? [] and result.Value?.Next ?? [] (HappeningNow.razor.cs:197-199), so a failed read renders the same empty state as an empty list. Conference's own wire type is NowNextDTO (GetNowNextHandler.cs:71), and the Android widget deserializes a third copy of the shape (NowNextWidgetProvider.cs:127, :132).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: nothing on the record marks how fresh it is. Staleness is bounded by one cache only, the endpoint's 60-second NowNextCache output-cache policy (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:293, applied at MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventsController.cs:178 and :193); GetNowNextQuery deliberately has no query-level cache under it (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Sessions/UseCases/NowNext/GetNowNextQuery.cs:10-12). The page fetches the snapshot from its own load path (HappeningNow.razor.cs:197) and has no timer of its own for it, so a long-open tab keeps its first now-and-next lists until something refreshes it.

    SessionReminderPlanner

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.HappeningNow · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/HappeningNow/SessionReminderPlanner.cs:39 · Level 1 · static class

    • What it is: a pure, side-effect-free planner that turns a set of bookmarked sessions plus an event time zone and a lead time into a list of SessionReminder values. All the date math (wall-clock to UTC, DST edge cases, lead-window clamping) lives here.
    • Depends on: SessionReminder, SessionInfo (the input session shape), EngagementRoutePaths (the tap route), and the SessionIdentifierType alias. Externals: BCL TimeZoneInfo, DateTimeOffset.
    • Concept, the deterministic pure function. [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether logic can be exercised without infrastructure. Every input the planner needs is a parameter, including now (SessionReminderPlanner.cs:61), the current instant, which the caller supplies rather than the planner reading DateTimeOffset.UtcNow itself. That single choice makes DST behavior, lead-window clamping and skip rules unit-testable with fixed clocks and no OS notification stack. [Rubric §27, Internationalization] also applies: session times are wall-clock local to the event's IANA time zone, never UTC in the DTOs (SessionInfo.StartsAt is a bare DateTime?, ISessionLookupService.cs:13), so correct conversion is a first-class concern here rather than an afterthought.
    • Walkthrough:
      • NotificationIdSeed (:44) is a private constant offset that keeps reminder ids clear of any other local-notification ids the app might use. The comment above it (:41-43) states the assumption the whole replace-by-id contract rests on: SessionIdentifierType hash codes are stable for value types.
      • GetNotificationId(sessionId) (:47-48) shifts the seed 16 bits and XORs the session id's hash unchecked, producing that stable id.
      • Plan(bookmarkedSessions, timeZoneId, leadTime, now) (:57-103) guards its arguments (:63-64), resolves the TimeZoneInfo (:66), then per session skips those with no start time (:71-74) or already started (:77-80), computes deliverAt = startsAtUtc - leadTime (:82) and captures isImmediate = deliverAt <= now (:83); when that holds it fires the reminder 30 seconds out rather than dropping it (:84-88). Finally it emits a SessionReminder whose tap route comes from EngagementRoutePaths.SessionDetails (:90-96, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/EngagementRoutePaths.cs:12), with IsImmediate = isImmediate set by object initializer (:97-99). The planner only records the clamp; deciding whether a clamped reminder should actually be scheduled again is the coordinator's job.
      • ToUtc(localWallClock, timeZone) (:105-118) is the DST-correct converter: it marks the wall time Unspecified (:107), shifts a spring-forward invalid time forward one hour (:110-113), and lets GetUtcOffset resolve ambiguous fall-back times to the standard offset (:115-117).
    • Why it's built this way: separating planning (pure, here) from scheduling (I/O, in the coordinator) means the tricky calendar logic is provable in isolation and the coordinator stays a thin best-effort orchestrator (ADR-042 Wave 2, named in the type doc at :32).
    • Where it's used: called by SessionReminderCoordinator.ReplanAsync (SessionReminderCoordinator.cs:175); GetNotificationId is also called there to cancel reminders for sessions that left the tracked set (:109), to cancel everything when reminders are switched off (:138), and to sweep the ids that dropped out of the plan (:190). Covered by SessionReminderPlannerTests.

    INowNextService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.HappeningNow · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/HappeningNow/INowNextService.cs:39 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the UI-side contract for reading one event's now-and-next snapshot, a single method returning a Result over a NowNextSnapshot.
    • Depends on: NowNextSnapshot, Result, and the EventIdentifierType alias. Externals: BCL Task, CancellationToken.
    • Concept, a port over a server-owned computation. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture] assesses whether components depend on typed contracts rather than transport, and [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] whether cross-module reads travel through an explicit boundary. The interface doc (INowNextService.cs:33-38) is the contract worth memorizing, because it enumerates what the server owns and the client therefore must not re-derive: session eligibility (scheduled, non-service, not declined or cancelled), the event-local wall-clock conversion, and the "next = the batch sharing the earliest future start" rule. Concretely, eligibility is CalendarExportMapper.IsExportable (GetNowNextHandler.cs:48). None of that is visible in a public catalog listing, which is precisely why the page cannot compute now-and-next itself; the implementation's doc records that this endpoint replaces the old whole-catalog fetch on Happening Now (NowNextService.cs:8-12).
    • Walkthrough (INowNextService.cs:48-50): one method, GetAsync(eventId, cancellationToken = default), returning Task<Result<NowNextSnapshot>>. The failure contract is the doc at :42-46: an event that is not found or not published answers an ErrorType.NotFound failure, which the page renders as "nothing scheduled". The server produces it as Result.Failure carrying Error.NotFound when the event is missing or IsPublished is false (GetNowNextHandler.cs:32-36), the API surfaces it as a 404, and ProblemDetailsResultReader turns it back into a typed failure in the client (NowNextService.cs:31-33). Answering with a failure rather than throwing is what lets a caller degrade to an empty schedule with no try/catch of its own.
    • Why it's built this way: the one-method port is the DI swap point (services.AddScoped<INowNextService, NowNextService>(), MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:74) and the test extension point, so the page can be exercised against a fake snapshot with no HTTP stack; it also keeps Engagement free of any compile-time reference to Conference for this read (ADR-007 and ADR-008 put the module in its own process, so this crosses a real service boundary over public HTTP; the implementation uses the plain "APIClient" factory client with no token, NowNextService.cs:23, because the endpoint is anonymous).
    • Where it's used: injected into the HappeningNow page (HappeningNow.razor.cs:28) and called from its load path (:156). Implemented by NowNextService (NowNextService.cs:14); covered by NowNextServiceTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the contract exposes only the per-event form. The endpoint also serves an id-less form where the server auto-selects the current-or-next published event, but no first-party C# client for it exists in this UI; the Android widget calls Events/now-next with a bare HttpClient instead (NowNextWidgetProvider.cs:119-120). Note also a wording gap: the doc comment says "not declined or cancelled" while the code's actual gate is the calendar-export allow-list above.

    NowNextService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.HappeningNow · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/HappeningNow/NowNextService.cs:14 · Level 4 · sealed class

    • What it is: the HTTP implementation of INowNextService, one GET against the Conference API's anonymous Events/{id}/now-next endpoint, read into a NowNextSnapshot and handed back untouched.
    • Depends on: INowNextService, NowNextSnapshot, HttpResultExecutor, IdempotentReadRetry, ProblemDetailsResultReader. Externals: IHttpClientFactory, HttpClient, CultureInfo.
    • Concept introduced, the thin lookup service (the contrast with the authenticated services above). [Rubric §18, UI Architecture] and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]. Unlike BookmarkApiClient (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/BookmarkApiClient.cs:21-22), the module's bookmark HTTP client, this class does not derive from AuthenticatedServiceBase: it takes the named "APIClient" from the factory directly (NowNextService.cs:23), the same shape as the module's other read-only lookups (SessionLookupService). That named client is registered once in the framework (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:146) with the gateway base address plus the auth and culture delegating handlers, so a bearer token still rides along when the user has one, but the endpoint is [AllowAnonymous] (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventsController.cs:140) and an anonymous visitor gets the same payload. The consequence to notice: no token fetch wraps this call, because there is nothing user-specific to authorize. Retry still applies, without the base class: the GET goes through IdempotentReadRetry.GetAsync (:26-29), whose policy is the same object AuthenticatedServiceBase uses (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Api/IdempotentReadRetry.cs:24), so a transient failure (an HttpRequestException, a 5xx other than 501/505, 408 or 429) is re-sent up to three times with exponential backoff plus jitter (IdempotentReadRetry.cs:10-12). The inline comment names why that is safe here (NowNextService.cs:25): the read is idempotent and anonymous, like the other lookups.
    • Walkthrough (NowNextService.cs:17-35), which is mostly guards
      • The whole body runs inside HttpResultExecutor.ExecuteAsync (:20), so a refused connection or a broken socket becomes a Http.TransportFailure failure rather than an exception the page has to catch.
      • Both disposables are scoped with using, the client (:23) and the final response (:26), so a per-call fetch leaks neither; any response a retry discards is disposed by the policy itself (IdempotentReadRetry.cs:27-28).
      • The relative URI is built with string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, $"Events/{eventId}/now-next") (:28). Invariant formatting is not decoration: the id is interpolated into a path, and a culture-sensitive numeric format would produce a path the API cannot route.
      • The response goes through ProblemDetailsResultReader.ReadAsync<NowNextSnapshot> (:33), so 404 becomes a NotFound failure, with the comment naming the case it covers (an unpublished or deleted event) and the consequence: the page shows nothing scheduled, exactly as it did for the old null (:31-32). A 5xx becomes a failure carrying the server's status code instead, so the page can tell "no such event" from "the service is broken" by reading the error rather than by catching an exception.
      • The CancellationToken is threaded through the retried GET (:29, honoured between attempts as well as by each send), the read (:33) and the executor (:35), so page disposal cancels an in-flight fetch or a pending backoff and the cancellation propagates rather than being reported as an error.
      • There is no client-side filtering, sorting or time math anywhere in the method: the lists arrive ordered and filtered and are passed straight to the page.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc (:8-13) states the rationale directly, the endpoint already excludes service, declined and cancelled sessions and does the event-local time math, so nothing is recomputed here. A whole-catalog fetch plus client-side time comparison could not tell an ineligible session apart, since eligibility is not part of a public catalog listing. The call is also cheap to repeat: the server output-caches it under the NowNextCache policy (EventsController.cs:178) and the payload is identical for every role, so no per-user cache key is needed.
    • Where it's used: registered scoped as INowNextService in the module's UI wiring (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:74); consumed only by the HappeningNow page today (HappeningNow.razor.cs:28, called at :156). [Rubric §14, Testability]: covered by three facts in NowNextServiceTests, the exact request path (:20), the unchanged projection of the server snapshot (:33), and the 404-to-NotFound-failure degradation (:50).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the retry lives in the call, not on the named client: no timeout or circuit breaker is configured on this path in the framework registration of "APIClient". A failure that survives the three retries is one transport failure and one localized error message, with a page reload as the next attempt. Note also that the Conference API exposes a second, id-less form of the same snapshot for the home-screen widget (EventsController.cs:154); this service does not call it.

    SessionReminderCoordinator

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.HappeningNow · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/HappeningNow/SessionReminderCoordinator.cs:30 · Level 8 · sealed partial class

    • What it is: the piece that keeps on-device session reminders in step with the user's bookmarks (ADR-042 Wave 2). It owns a tracked session set and two settings in device preferences, and on every change it replans the whole schedule and cancel-then-reschedules the difference (class doc, :11-18). The class doc's second paragraph (:19-25) adds the one exception to "replan everything": a session already inside the lead window gets its immediate reminder once, when it becomes tracked on this device, and never again on a later replan, unless the replan that should have issued it could not run, in which case the reminder stays owed until one can. The third paragraph (:26-29) states the concurrency rule: every read-mutate-write of the tracked set runs one at a time.
    • Depends on: ILocalNotificationService, IDevicePreferences, ISessionLookupService, ILiveEventUIService, SessionReminderPlanner, LocalNotificationRequest, LiveEventContext, SessionInfo, SessionReminder, LiveEventLookup. Externals: BCL TimeProvider (the clock, :36), SemaphoreSlim (the tracked-set gate, :54), IStringLocalizer<T>, ILogger<T> with a source-generated [LoggerMessage]. The class also implements IDisposable (:37, :320) solely to release that gate.
    • Concept introduced, best-effort derived state behind a capability gate. Two ideas meet here. First, [Rubric §19, State Management]: a scheduled local notification is derived state that only stays correct if it tracks the bookmark set, and the bookmark set changes from any page and any device. This class is the one place that derivation lives, and because a resync from a page load can overlap a bookmark toggle, the read-mutate-write cycle is serialized by _trackedGate (:54): MutateTrackedAsync (:117) and ApplySettingsAsync (:82) both WaitAsync on it and release in finally (:94-97, :138-141), so neither can overwrite the other's change. Second, [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]: reminders are a convenience and must never fail a bookmark operation, so every entry point is best-effort. Both wrap their work in catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException) and log a warning through LogReminderSyncFailed (:90-93, :134-137, defined :322-323), rather than propagating. Note the exception filter: a genuine cancellation is not swallowed. Third, and this is what makes the coupling cheap, every entry point begins with if (!notifications.IsSupported) return; (:77-80, :112-115), before touching the gate, so on a web head the whole class is a no-op that touches no storage and issues no calls. The [LoggerMessage] source generator is the framework's structured-logging default, [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: a failure here is invisible to the user by design, so a log entry is the only signal that reminders may be stale.
    • Walkthrough (constants, then the four entry points, then the private engines)
      • The preference keys and defaults are consts: EnabledKey (:40) and LeadMinutesKey (:43) and DefaultLeadMinutes = 15 (:51) are public, while the tracked-set key (:45) and the owed-immediate key OwedImmediateKey (:48) are private. IsSupported (:57) forwards the capability flag so a settings page can hide the section entirely.
      • NotifyBookmarkAddedAsync (:60-61) and NotifyBookmarkRemovedAsync (:64-65) are one-liners over MutateTrackedAsync, appending with Distinct() and filtering with the default equality comparer for the identifier alias respectively.
      • ResyncAsync (:71-72) replaces the tracked set outright with an authoritative bookmark map. Its doc (:67-70) names the reason it exists: a page that loads the user's bookmarks has the truth in hand, so this is the moment to heal drift caused by changes made on another device.
      • ApplySettingsAsync (:75-98) persists both settings then replans with an empty newly-tracked set (:88), which is also how disabling works: the replan cancels everything when enabled is false. The empty set means a settings change never newly issues an immediate reminder (it can still issue one that was already owed).
      • GetSettingsAsync (:101-106) reads the pair back for the device-settings UI, defaulting to enabled and 15 minutes. It takes no gate, since it only reads.
      • MutateTrackedAsync (:108-142) is the shared write path: take the gate, read the tracked array, apply the caller's mutation, compute newlyTracked = updated.Except(tracked) (:122), persist the new array (:123), cancel reminders for sessions that left the set (:125-130), then replan the rest passing newlyTracked along (:132). Cancelling before replanning is deliberate and the comment says so (:125). Because ResyncAsync runs through here too, a resync on every schedule load only counts the ids that were not already tracked as new.
      • ReplanAsync(tracked, newlyTracked, ...) (:155-167, doc :144-154) is a thin wrapper that owns the owed immediate bookkeeping. It reads the persisted owed ids, keeps only those still tracked, unions in newlyTracked (:160-163), runs TryReplanAsync, and persists the owed set back: emptied when the replan ran, kept as-is when it could not (:165-166). That is what stops an immediate reminder from being lost when its one chance to fire hit a denied permission, a missing live event or a failed catalog read.
      • TryReplanAsync(tracked, owed, ...) (:177-238, doc :169-176) is the heart of the class, returns bool, and reads as a sequence of early returns, each protecting the existing schedule: reminders switched off, or nothing tracked, cancels everything when off and returns true, a completed replan (:182-192); a denied OS permission returns false without scheduling, and the comment records that the prompt appears at most once and a denial leaves reminders silently off until the user grants them in system settings (:194-199); no live event returns false (:201-205); a catalog read the API refuses returns false, with the comment giving the reason, replanning against an empty catalog would cancel reminders that are still valid (:209-215). The live-event guard reads the LiveEvent member of the LiveEventLookup that ILiveEventUIService.GetCurrentEventAsync returns (:201; the interface doc at ILiveEventUIService.cs:9-14 names three states: the event, no published event, a failed read). The coordinator collapses the last two into one null and answers false for both, so a failed read and a genuinely absent event leave the schedule, and the owed set, exactly as they were. Note the shape of the catalog guard too: sessionLookup.GetAllAsync returns a Result and the code branches on TryGetValue (:212), so "the API said no" and "there are no sessions" are different outcomes.
      • Past the guards it calls PlanTrackedSessionsAsync (:217-218), then does the stale sweep (:227-234): the tracked ids minus the planned ids, cancelled. The comment there (:220-226) names the four ways a session can stay tracked yet drop out of the plan (deleted, its event ended, times cleared per BR-16, start moved into the past), notes that nothing upstream cancels those, and explains why the sweep sits after a plan was computed rather than beside the early returns: cancelling on a transient null live event would wipe reminders that are still valid. It then hands off to ScheduleAsync with the owed set and returns true (:236-237).
      • PlanTrackedSessionsAsync (:250-285, doc :240-249) does not narrow the plan to the live event. It builds a map of event id to LiveEventContext seeded with the live event and extended from liveEventService.GetPublishedEventsAsync (:263-267), drops sessions whose event's live window has closed (:277), groups the rest by their own event's IANA zone, falling back to the live event's zone when the event is not in the list (:278), and calls SessionReminderPlanner.Plan once per zone with the lead time and timeProvider.GetUtcNow() (:279-283, clock read at :257). The effect (A-21 in the doc): a bookmarked session of a later event keeps its reminder while another event is live, and a wrong fallback zone only shifts a reminder until the next replan replaces it by id (:259-262).
      • ScheduleAsync(plan, owed, ...) (:290-317) schedules each planned reminder as a LocalNotificationRequest, with one skip: a reminder whose IsImmediate is set and whose session is not in owed is passed over (:301-304). The comment (:297-300) gives the reasoning: re-issuing it would fire an already-delivered reminder again, and because its id is still in the plan the stale sweep above leaves any still-pending copy alone. The body text does not quote the configured lead: minutesUntilStart is the real gap between StartsAtUtc and DeliverAt, rounded up with a floor of 1 (:308), so a clamped reminder does not claim the full lead (:306-307). Title and body are localized, the body taking the session title and minutesUntilStart as format arguments (:311-312), so the wording is resource-driven rather than concatenated. [Rubric §27, i18n].
      • Dispose (:320) disposes the gate.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-042 puts device capabilities behind interfaces the web head can answer "unsupported" to, which is what lets this class be registered unconditionally (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:48, AddScoped<SessionReminderCoordinator>()) and injected into a service every head uses. Notification ids are derived deterministically from the session id (SessionReminderPlanner.GetNotificationId, SessionReminderPlanner.cs:47-48), which is what makes rescheduling replace instead of duplicate, and is why a replan-everything strategy is affordable. The two things a blind replan would get wrong are both handled by the owed set: re-firing a clamped immediate reminder on every resync (prevented because only owed ids pass the ScheduleAsync skip), and silently losing one whose replan could not run (prevented because ReplanAsync keeps the owed ids when TryReplanAsync answers false). Reading the clock through an injected TimeProvider (:36, used at :257) instead of DateTimeOffset.UtcNow puts the coordinator under the same fixed-clock testability as the planner; the Engagement UI wiring adds TimeProvider.System with TryAddSingleton, so the system clock that AddOfflineWriteQueue (and AddUIShared on the heads that call it) already registers is kept rather than duplicated (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:84-86).
    • Where it's used: injected as a concrete class by SessionBookmarkUIService (SessionBookmarkUIService.cs:39), which drives all three notify or resync members; by the offline replay handlers BookmarkCreateReplayHandler (BookmarkCreateReplayHandler.cs:27, calling NotifyBookmarkAddedAsync at :51) and BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler (BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler.cs:22, calling NotifyBookmarkRemovedAsync at :64), so a bookmark write queued offline updates reminders when it replays; and by the host's device-settings page (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/Pages/DeviceSettings.razor:7), which reads the settings (:62), writes them on change (:68, :74) and seeds its lead-time control from DefaultLeadMinutes (:58). [Rubric §14, Testability]: SessionReminderCoordinatorTests holds seventeen [Fact]/[Theory] methods covering the branches above (stale-sweep cases, no live event, an unsupported host, lookup failures never throwing out of the coordinator, a failed catalog read leaving the schedule alone, a resync not re-issuing an immediate reminder, and an immediate reminder naming the real remaining time).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: IsSupported (:57) has no consumer in the repo today, including the device-settings page its doc points at; the page relies on the internal no-ops instead. The class is registered scoped while the state it manages is device-global, so the _trackedGate serializes only calls made through one instance: correctness across instances rests on preferences being the single source of truth and on every mutation replanning from scratch. Whether a scheduled notification actually fires is the platform's business, outside this file.

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Lookups · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Lookups/AttendeeLookupService.cs:216 · Level 0 · record (private sealed, nested)

    • What it is: the wire shape of one row returned by the generic paged Identity users endpoint (users/paged, AttendeeLookupService.cs:25), declared privately inside AttendeeLookupService purely so System.Text.Json has something to bind to. It never leaves the service: every row is projected into the public AttendeeSummary before it reaches a caller.
    • Depends on: the UserIdentifierType alias (solution-wide global using, see primer §2). Externals: System.Text.Json binding at the call site, wrapped in PagedCollectionResult<T>.
    • Concept introduced, the private deserialization shape. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses how a consumer expresses the contract it reads. Two types for one payload looks redundant until you read what the private one is allowed to be: the doc comment (AttendeeLookupService.cs:211-215) records that this is the Identity roster row, whose identifier is id, that only the fields the check-in surfaces render are read, and that the lock state and live session count the row also carries are ignored, which is exactly the tolerant-reader posture. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] is the other half: Engagement redeclares five fields instead of referencing the Identity assembly for its list DTO (IAttendeeLookupService.cs:6-9 states that constraint for the public twin), so Identity can move, be versioned, or add columns without a compile-time edit here.
    • Walkthrough (AttendeeLookupService.cs:216-221): five positional members, Id, Email, FirstName, LastName, Role, structurally identical to AttendeeSummary minus its computed DisplayName (the identifier is Id here, matching the generic paged row, where the public twin calls it UserId). It is bound as PagedCollectionResult<AttendeeRow> (AttendeeLookupService.cs:71-72) so one read picks up both the page items and the pagination metadata, and converted one row at a time by the private ToSummary (:213-214), which maps row.Id onto UserId.
    • Why it's built this way: private sealed keeps the wire shape from becoming an accidental public contract. The projection point is the single place where a server rename would have to be absorbed, and the computed display fallback lives on the public record rather than on the row, so the transport type stays inert data.
    • Where it's used: only inside AttendeeLookupService, by SearchAsync (:54, :72-79) and, through it, by the roster snapshot LoadRosterAsync builds (:132-165).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: nothing at compile time keeps this shape aligned with what Identity actually serializes. A renamed server property binds to the member default rather than failing the build; only AttendeeLookupServiceTests round-tripping a JSON body catches it.

    AttendeeSearchField

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Lookups · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Lookups/IAttendeeLookupService.cs:41 · Level 0 · enum

    • What it is: which one of last name, first name or email the organizer's single search box applies to when looking an attendee up at the door.
    • Depends on: nothing (a bare enum).
    • Concept introduced, the enum that exists because of a server semantic. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether a client contract makes the server's actual behavior usable. The type doc states the reason outright (IAttendeeLookupService.cs:36-40): the Identity users endpoint ANDs its filters, so broadcasting one typed term across all three fields would match nobody. A UI that offered one box and no field picker would therefore be a UI that silently never finds anyone. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] covers the resulting shape: one box plus one explicit selector, so the organizer always knows which field the term is being matched against.
    • Walkthrough (IAttendeeLookupService.cs:41-51): three members with explicit values, LastName = 0 (:44), FirstName = 1 (:47), Email = 2 (:50). The explicit ordinals matter because the value is round-tripped as a string through the grid's filter state and parsed back with Enum.TryParse (AttendeeSearchPanel.razor.cs:49-51), which falls back to LastName when the stored value does not parse. LastName is also the field's initial value (AttendeeSearchPanel.razor.cs:36), which is the field an organizer reads off a badge first.
    • Why it's built this way: an enum rather than a raw string keeps the three-way mapping exhaustive and reviewable in one switch (AttendeeSearchPanel.razor.cs:116-122), which projects the selected member onto the matching AttendeeSummary property name and writes a single ("contains", term) filter (:120).
    • Where it's used: only by AttendeeSearchPanel, as the bound value of a MudSelect (AttendeeSearchPanel.razor:15-22) and as the discriminator in its filter builder; the resulting filter is what IAttendeeLookupService.SearchAsync receives as its email / firstName / lastName arguments (IAttendeeLookupService.cs:73-79).

    SessionInfo

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Lookups · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Lookups/ISessionLookupService.cs:10 · Level 0 · record

    • What it is: the lightweight projection of a Conference session carrying just what Engagement pages and the session reminders need to label a session: id, title, optional start and end times, the owning event id, and the Sessionize status the live layer gates on (ISessionLookupService.cs:5-9). It sits at the top of ISessionLookupService.cs because it is the shape that lookup contract returns.
    • Depends on: the SessionIdentifierType and EventIdentifierType aliases (Conference identifier aliases, solution-wide global using, see primer §2). No first-party service dependencies.
    • Concept introduced, the cross-module display projection. Engagement owns no session table (database-per-service, ADR-006), so it cannot join to a session title: it fetches the fields it needs over HTTP and holds them in this small record, a deliberately thinner shape than Conference's own SessionDTO. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses how a consumer models another service's data at its boundary; declaring six fields here means a change to unrelated SessionDTO members never ripples into Engagement. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] is the same decision seen from the extraction side, and it is the identical posture the neighbouring AttendeeSummary takes against Identity: the consumer redeclares the view it renders rather than depending on the producer's assembly.
    • Walkthrough (ISessionLookupService.cs:10-16): six positional members, (SessionIdentifierType Id, string Title, DateTime? StartsAt, DateTime? EndsAt, EventIdentifierType EventId, string? Status = null). StartsAt and EndsAt are nullable because a session imported from the schedule source may not yet have times assigned, so every consumer has to tolerate an unscheduled session. Status (:16) is the last member and the only one with a default, so a caller that only labels a session (a test fixture, for one) can omit it; the type doc ties it to BR-49 and Conference's SessionStatuses.IsEligible (:7-8), which is the check the live pages run on it. It is a plain public record, not sealed.
    • Why it's built this way: a compact record lets SessionLookupService build a whole-catalog dictionary cheaply, and value equality plus init-only members mean a page can hold, compare and sort the rows client-side without a second fetch per row.
    • Where it's used: returned by ISessionLookupService (a catalog keyed by id, or one row), constructed by SessionLookupService from SessionDTO payloads, Status included (SessionLookupService.cs:73-74, :63-64); consumed by CheckInScan as its session list (CheckInScan.razor.cs:55), by SessionReminderPlanner as the bookmarked-session input it schedules against (SessionReminderPlanner.cs:58), by SessionReminderCoordinator as the catalog it hands on (SessionReminderCoordinator.cs:252), and by the live-session pages, which hold one row (Pages/SessionLive/SessionLive.razor.cs:66, Pages/SessionLive/PresenterView.razor.cs:50) and refuse a session whose status is not eligible (SessionLive.razor.cs:155, PresenterView.razor.cs:127).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: nothing here constrains Title to non-empty or the times to a sane order; both come straight off the Conference payload, and the nullable times are the only shape signal that an unscheduled session exists. Status is a free string, not an enum: which values count as eligible, and how a null status is treated, is decided by Conference's SessionStatuses.IsEligible, not in this file.

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Lookups · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Lookups/AttendeeLookupService.cs:198 · Level 1 · record (private sealed, nested)

    • What it is: the wire shape of the POST users/search request body that AttendeeLookupService sends, the client's private copy of Identity's UserSearchRequest (doc, AttendeeLookupService.cs:197; server side MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.API/Controllers/UsersController.cs:41).

An organizer's search term is often an attendee's email address, and a query string is exactly what request telemetry and ingress logs keep; carrying the generic paged contract (filters with their operators, sort, paging) in a body is what keeps the term out of them (class doc, :9-12; the server endpoint's own doc, UsersController.cs:37-38, :255-256). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: the shape is the same filter, sort and paging contract GET users/paged takes, moved from the query string into JSON, so nothing about the caller's filters changes but their transport.
    • Walkthrough (:198-203): five positional members, Filters (a Dictionary<string, SearchFilter>), SortColumn and SortDirection (both string?), PageNumber and PageSize. BuildSearchBody (:171-195) fills Filters with an ordinal-comparer dictionary keyed by property name (:178), drops an entry with no operator (:181-184), and turns a blank sort column or direction into null (:189-194) so an unsorted request carries no sort.

The endpoint is [HttpPost("search")] gated on IdentityPermissions.UsersRead (UsersController.cs:261-262). AttendeeLookupServiceTests pin the body shape: filters posted verbatim (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Tests/Services/Lookups/AttendeeLookupServiceTests.cs:101), an email term kept out of the URL (:133), and a value-less operator sent without a value (:172).
