    • Concept: the dynamic feedback form (the answer state, the validation delegates, the required-answer gate, the UnsavedChangesGuard pairing and the StateHasChanged-before-navigate ordering) is taught on SessionFeedback and is the same shape here: both pages hold their questions, answers, saved ids and missing-required set in one FeedbackAnswers<TAnswerId>, here closed over EventQuestionAnswerIdentifierType (:65). The submit strategy matches the session page: SubmitFeedbackAsync calls FeedbackService.SubmitAnswersAsync once with the whole answered set (EventFeedback.razor.cs:218), so the server applies the batch atomically and there is nothing partial left to report. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] still applies: an unanswered required question, rating included, is caught locally before any request (:199-203), an empty submit on an all-optional form sends no batch (:216), and a failed submit leaves _isDirty set so the same Submit button retries. Two things carry over from the session page. First, the submit and delete awaits read LifetimeToken (:32, _cts.LifetimeToken()) instead of _cts.Token: reading Token off a disposed source throws ObjectDisposedException, whereas Dispose cancels before it disposes, so a handler resuming after navigation gets a cancelled token and exits through its OperationCanceledException path. Second, a refused submit goes through ReportSubmitFailure (:261-271): an ErrorType.Unexpected result (a 500, transport failure or timeout) keeps the generic Snackbar.SubmitFailed toast (:263-267), while any other refusal is stored in _submitResult (:80, :269) so ErrorSummary lists its field errors after the snackbar times out, and NotifyOnFailure toasts the server's own message (:270; ADR-027 Decision 9 carve-out per the method's doc comment). _submitResult is cleared at the start of each submit (:206).
    • Walkthrough of what differs from SessionFeedback
      • There is no precondition gate and no _preconditionMessage: an event either loads or it does not. OnInitialized (EventFeedback.razor.cs:85-97) builds both validation delegates, _validateAnswerText and _validateAnswerEmail, from one prototype FeedbackAnswerModel and one DataAnnotationsModelValidator(L) (:87-90), and also builds the breadcrumb trail (:91-96).
      • Loading is parameter-driven. OnParametersSetAsync (:99-108) compares EventId with _loadedEventId (:39); a feedback deep link to another event while this form is open reuses the routed instance with only a new EventId, so a new id starts LoadFormAsync (:110) and an unchanged id does nothing.
      • LoadFormAsync (:110-185) first calls _load.Begin() (:113), which supersedes and cancels the previous event's load, then resets everything that belonged to the previous form, _loadNotFound and _answerState = new() included (:116-122). It resolves the event name from EventLookup.GetAllAsync(token) (:127), setting a localized _loadError when the lookup itself fails (:131); when the id is absent from it, it also sets _loadNotFound (:141-142). That flag (:61) picks the markup's DetailLoadStateContent state (EventFeedback.razor:27): NotFound for an event that does not exist, otherwise Failed with a Retry wired to LoadFormAsync. Each await is followed by token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() (:128, :148, :160), so a superseded load stops rather than writing stale state. The rest (the "Event" questions handed to _answerState.SetQuestions at :156, the saved answers fetched at :159) matches the session page step for step. A cancelled load is swallowed (:173-176), and IsLoading is cleared only when _load.IsCurrent(generation) still holds (:177-184), so a superseded load leaves the flag to the load that replaced it.
      • The pre-fill applies the same cross-entity guard in the page: _answerState.PreFill receives only answers whose EventId matches the current event (:169-171, the filter at :170), because questions are shared across events.
      • SubmitFeedbackAsync (:187-253) validates the form, then runs _answerState.FlagMissingRequiredAnswers(), and returns with a Snackbar.RequiredFields warning if either fails (:189-203). It takes pending from _answerState.PendingAnswers() (:212); if it is non-empty it posts the whole set in one call to SubmitAnswersAsync(EventId, ...) (:216-218), and on failure calls ReportSubmitFailure and returns with _isDirty still set (:219-223). It then deletes every saved answer the attendee blanked, from _answerState.BlankedSavedAnswers(), through TryDeleteSavedAnswerAsync, stopping at the first failed delete with the form still dirty (:229-235), so a submit never reports success while an old answer survives. Only then does it clear _isDirty and toast Snackbar.FeedbackSubmitted with pending.Count (:237-238). The id is the typed parameter, so there is no parse step.
      • DeleteAnswerAsync (:273-288) and the submit's blanked-answer loop share TryDeleteSavedAnswerAsync (:296-312): it returns true when no saved id exists, calls FeedbackService.DeleteAnswerAsync(EventId, answerId, LifetimeToken) (:303), toasts Snackbar.ClearAnswerFailed and returns false on failure (:306-307), and otherwise calls _answerState.ClearSavedAnswer (:310). A cleared answer leaves _isDirty as it is (:277-278): the delete commits only that answer on the server, so unsaved edits to other answers keep the unsaved-changes guard armed.
      • NavigateBack (:314-315) returns to the Conference event detail route, formatting the id with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture. The disposable pattern (:317-340) cancels and disposes _cts and disposes _load (:328-330).
    • Why it's built this way: the page owns orchestration only, all I/O goes through injected UI service interfaces, which keeps it testable under bUnit and swappable per host. A single batch SubmitAnswersAsync call removes the partial-save case entirely: a refusal means nothing was written, so the retry story is a plain resend rather than a per-question accounting. Reloading from OnParametersSetAsync behind a LatestLoadGuard means a route change to a different event cannot leave the previous event's questions or answers on screen, or let a slow earlier load overwrite a newer one. Sharing the answer state with SessionFeedback through FeedbackAnswers<TAnswerId> rather than through a base page class keeps each page self-contained while the answer rules exist once.
    • Where it's used: rendered at /feedback/event/{EventId:int}, reached from the public event detail page's SubmitFeedback (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Public/Events/PublicEventDetail.razor.cs:196). The same route is also expressed as EngagementRoutePaths.EventFeedback(eventId) (EngagementRoutePaths.cs:17). Its dependencies are registered by the Engagement UI DependencyInjection. Component-tested by EventFeedbackTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the markup, the resource strings and UnsavedChangesGuard's own behavior live outside this file; this section covers the code-behind plus the bindings its members exist to serve.

    SessionFeedback

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Pages.Feedback · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Pages/Feedback/SessionFeedback.razor.cs:16 · Level 6 · class (partial)

    • What it is: the code-behind for the attendee session-feedback page (@page "/feedback/session/{SessionId:int}", SessionFeedback.razor:1). It checks three business preconditions before it will render the question form at all, then loads the dynamic question set, pre-fills any answers the attendee already submitted, posts the whole form back in one atomic call, and deletes any saved answer the attendee blanked. The question, answer and saved-id state sits in a FeedbackAnswers<TAnswerId> instance closed over SessionQuestionAnswerIdentifierType (:65), so this class holds the lifecycle, the preconditions and the I/O.
    • Depends on: IQuestionLookupService, ISessionFeedbackUIService, IEntityService<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (bound as IEntityService<SessionDTO, SessionIdentifierType>, SessionFeedback.razor.cs:20), IToastService, FeedbackAnswers<TAnswerId>, LatestLoadGuard, DetailLoadState (through the markup's DetailLoadStateContent, SessionFeedback.razor:27), SessionDTO, QuestionDTO, FeedbackAnswerModel, ModelValidation and DataAnnotationsModelValidator, SessionStatuses.IsEligible for the BR-49 check, plus the IsNotFound() result extension from MMCA.Common.UI.Common. Externals: Blazor NavigationManager, MudBlazor MudForm / BreadcrumbItem, and from the markup an injected IStringLocalizer<SessionFeedback> L (SessionFeedback.razor:8), the shared UnsavedChangesGuard component (SessionFeedback.razor:12) and ErrorSummary (SessionFeedback.razor:136). The failure path also uses the Result helpers HasErrorType / NotifyOnFailure with ErrorType.Unexpected (SessionFeedback.razor.cs:291, :298).
    • Concept introduced, the precondition-gated dynamic form. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture] assesses component/logic separation: the markup lives in SessionFeedback.razor, the behavior in this partial class, and the form's answer state in FeedbackAnswers<TAnswerId>, so the page's flow is reviewable apart from its layout and its state rules. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] is the load-bearing category here and it shows up four times. First, CheckPreconditions (SessionFeedback.razor.cs:191) refuses before rendering inputs, so when feedback is not permitted the attendee gets one sentence explaining why rather than a form that fails on submit. Second, validation is declarative and single-sourced: _validateAnswerText (:73) and _validateAnswerEmail (:77) are two delegates built from FeedbackAnswerModel's annotations (TextValue and EmailValue) and handed to the text and email fields respectively, so the 4000-character rule is never written twice and the email-format rule lives on the model rather than in the page. Third, a required check covers what MudForm cannot: a star rating is not a form input, so form validation never blocks an unanswered required rating, and the missing-required set on the answer state (FeedbackAnswers<TAnswerId>.MissingRequired, filled by FlagMissingRequiredAnswers, called at :227) does, for every question type, and drives the inline error on each question's field (SessionFeedback.razor:72, :86). Fourth, UnsavedChangesGuard IsDirty="_isDirty" wraps the page, so navigating away with unsaved edits prompts first. The dynamic part is the interesting one: the questions are data, not markup, so the render branches on the DTO's QuestionType. A RATING question gets the star control (SessionFeedback.razor:63); anything else goes through a switch over question.QuestionType?.ToUpperInvariant() (SessionFeedback.razor:88) that picks an email MudTextField bound to EmailValue and validated by _validateAnswerEmail (case "EMAIL", :90-93) or a three-line multiline MudTextField (:106), and each field's required flag and RequiredError come from the DTO rather than from the page. [Rubric §19, State Management] covers the answer state; [Rubric §27, i18n] covers the fact that every visible string, error messages included, is an L["..."] lookup.
    • Walkthrough (teaching order)
      • Injected services (SessionFeedback.razor.cs:18-22) and the [Parameter] SessionIdentifierType SessionId (:24) arrive from the route. The parameter is the typed id alias, and the route template carries the :int constraint (SessionFeedback.razor:1), so the router parses it and the page needs no parse step.
      • LifetimeToken (:31, _cts.LifetimeToken()) is the token the submit and delete awaits use. Reading Token off a disposed CancellationTokenSource throws ObjectDisposedException; Dispose cancels before it disposes, so a handler resuming after the attendee navigated away gets a cancelled token and stops through its OperationCanceledException path (:28-30).
      • IsLoading / IsSubmitting (:41-42) and SubmitButtonText (:44-55) drive the chrome: the button reads "Submitting" while a post is in flight, then "Update" or "Submit" depending on _answerState.HasExistingFeedback (:53). The private state fields hold the load error (:57), the _loadNotFound flag that says the error reports a session that does not exist rather than a failed load (:59-60), the precondition message (:61), the session title (:62), the _answerState (:65), the MudForm reference (:66), the _isDirty flag (:67), the two validation delegates (:73, :77) and _submitResult (:80), the last submit's refusal kept so ErrorSummary can list its field errors. MarkDirty (:82) is the one-line handler every input's @bind-...:after calls.
      • OnInitialized (:85-97) builds both delegates once, by handing a throwaway FeedbackAnswerModel prototype, the model => model.TextValue and model => model.EmailValue selectors and one DataAnnotationsModelValidator(L) to ModelValidation.ForProperty (:87-90), and builds the three-item breadcrumb trail (:91-96). The strongly-typed ForProperty overload (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Validation/ModelValidation.cs:69) is the right one here because these fields have no For expression and the value being validated has not been written to a model yet; the localizer resolves the ErrorMessage resource key (ADR-027).
      • Loading is parameter-driven. OnParametersSetAsync (:99-108) compares SessionId with _loadedSessionId (:38); a feedback deep link to another session while this form is open reuses the routed instance with only a new SessionId, so a new id starts LoadFormAsync (:110) and an unchanged id does nothing. LoadFormAsync begins with _load.Begin() (:113), which supersedes and cancels the previous session's load, and resets everything that belonged to the previous form, including _loadNotFound = false and _answerState = new() (:116-123).
      • It then loads the session through SessionService.GetByIdAsync(SessionId, false, token) (:128). The failure branch (:130-139) splits the two reasons apart: _loadNotFound = sessionResult.IsNotFound() (:134) picks the page's own "session not found" wording for a genuine 404 and the generic load failure for anything else (:135-137). The same flag drives the markup's DetailLoadStateContent (SessionFeedback.razor:27), which offers a Retry wired to LoadFormAsync for a failed load and none for a session that does not exist.
      • CheckPreconditions(session) runs next (call at :143), and a returned message stops the load before any questions are fetched (:144-148). Only then does it load the "Session" questions (:151), hand them to _answerState.SetQuestions (:160), fetch the attendee's saved answers (:163), and pre-fill with _answerState.PreFill over only the answers whose SessionId matches this session (:171-175, the filter at :174): questions are shared across sessions, so a foreign answer would otherwise match by question id. Each await is followed by token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() (:129, :152, :164); OperationCanceledException is swallowed as expected on disposal or supersession (:177-180), and in finally IsLoading is cleared only when _load.IsCurrent(generation) still holds (:181-188), so a superseded load leaves the flag to the load that replaced it.
      • CheckPreconditions (:191-213) encodes three rules, each returning a localized message. BR-91 rejects service sessions (session.IsServiceSession, :194). BR-49 rejects any session SessionStatuses.IsEligible does not allow, an unset Status or "Accepted" (case-insensitive) are the only eligible values (:200), the same shared allow-list Conference applies elsewhere. BR-16 rejects unscheduled sessions, where StartsAt or EndsAt is null (:207), because session feedback is a time-gated action. Returning null means feedback is allowed.
      • SubmitFeedbackAsync (:215) validates the form and toasts a warning if it is invalid (:222), then runs _answerState.FlagMissingRequiredAnswers() and toasts the same Snackbar.RequiredFields warning and returns when it reports a gap (:227-231), so an unanswered required rating, or an entirely empty submit on a form with a required question, never reaches the server. It then takes the answered questions as a pending list of (QuestionId, AnswerValue) tuples from _answerState.PendingAnswers() (:240), which drops blanks. An empty list (possible only when every question is optional) sends no batch, rather than a request the batch endpoint would refuse as empty (:242-244). Otherwise it makes one call, FeedbackService.SubmitAnswersAsync(SessionId, pending, LifetimeToken) (:246), which the interface documents as applied atomically server-side (IFeedbackUIService.cs:66-73). _submitResult is reset to null first (:234). A failure therefore wrote nothing: the page calls ReportSubmitFailure(result) (:249, defined :289-299) and returns with _isDirty still set, so the same Submit button retries. That method keeps the generic Snackbar.SubmitFailed toast for an ErrorType.Unexpected result (a 500, transport failure or timeout, :291-295, the ADR-027 Decision 9 carve-out), and otherwise stores the result in _submitResult (:297) so ErrorSummary (SessionFeedback.razor:136) lists the field errors after the snackbar times out, and NotifyOnFailure toasts the server's own stated message (:298). After the batch it deletes each saved answer the attendee has since blanked (_answerState.BlankedSavedAnswers()), through the same TryDeleteSavedAnswerAsync the Clear button uses, and returns with the form still dirty at the first failed delete (:254-263): the upsert has no delete semantics, so without this step the submit would report success while the old answer survived. On success it clears _isDirty (:265), toasts the count (:266), then calls StateHasChanged() before NavigateBack() (:269, :271); the inline comment (:267) and the BL0012 suppression note (:268) explain why: the flush lets UnsavedChangesGuard's IsDirty parameter update before NavigateTo fires the LocationChanging handler, otherwise the guard would prompt over changes that were just saved.
      • DeleteAnswerAsync (:301-316) clears one previously-saved answer through TryDeleteSavedAnswerAsync (:324-340) and toasts Snackbar.AnswerCleared when it succeeds. That helper returns true when there is no saved id (:326-329), calls FeedbackService.DeleteAnswerAsync(SessionId, answerId, LifetimeToken) (:331), toasts Snackbar.ClearAnswerFailed and returns false on failure (:332-336), and otherwise calls _answerState.ClearSavedAnswer(questionId) (:338), which removes the id and resets the model (TextValue and RatingValue; EmailValue follows TextValue). A clear leaves _isDirty as it is (:305-306): the delete commits only that answer on the server, so unsaved edits to other answers keep the unsaved-changes guard armed.
      • NavigateBack (:342-343) returns to the Conference session detail route through EngagementRoutePaths.SessionDetails(SessionId). The wire string for each answer comes from FeedbackAnswerModel.AnswerValue, which the answer state calls.
      • Dispose(bool) / Dispose() (:345-368) implement the standard disposable pattern, cancelling and disposing _cts and disposing _load (:356-358) so in-flight loads stop when the attendee leaves.
    • Why it's built this way: pushing the three business rules into one CheckPreconditions method keeps the render path binary (either a precondition message or the form) and makes each BR individually reviewable and individually testable. Keeping the answer state in FeedbackAnswers<TAnswerId> means the page replaces one object to discard a stale form, the pre-fill, required-gate, payload and blanked-answer rules can be read without the lifecycle code around them, and EventFeedback runs the identical rules. The single batch submit is the more consequential choice, and EventFeedback makes the same one: because the server applies a whole session form atomically, there is no partially-saved state to report to the attendee, so the failure path is a plain retry rather than a "3 of 5 saved" message. The cancellation-token discipline (the disposal-safe LifetimeToken on submit and delete, the superseding LatestLoadGuard token on load), the split between a stated refusal and an unexpected fault in ReportSubmitFailure, and the StateHasChanged-before-navigate ordering are correctness, not style.
    • Where it's used: rendered at /feedback/session/{SessionId:int}, reached from the public session detail page's SubmitFeedback (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Public/Sessions/PublicSessionDetail.razor.cs:318). The same route is also expressed as EngagementRoutePaths.SessionFeedback(sessionId) (EngagementRoutePaths.cs:18). Its dependencies are registered by the Engagement UI DependencyInjection. Component-tested by SessionFeedbackTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the markup, the resource strings and UnsavedChangesGuard's own behavior live outside this file. The BR numbers in the comments are the page's own claim about which business rule it implements; the authoritative statements live in the ADC specifications guide, not in this file.

    PointsAwarder

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Points.Services · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/Services/PointsAwarder.cs:30 · Level 10 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the only implementation of IPointsAwarder. It writes one award idempotently, or writes nothing when the rule is switched off or the account has been erased.
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork, PointsSettings via IOptions<T>, PointsEntry, ErasedUserGuard, IUniqueConstraintViolationDetector, Result; externals: IOptions<T>, ILogger<T> with [LoggerMessage].
    • Concept introduced, the configuration kill switch and the value snapshot. [Rubric §17, DevOps & Deployment] (assesses whether operational levers are configuration rather than code), [Rubric §8, Data Architecture], and [Rubric §11, Security] in its anti-abuse sense. Three ideas are stated once here so no earn rule has to restate them. (1) The stored Points value is a SNAPSHOT of the configured award at the moment it was earned (PointsAwarder.cs:14-17), so retuning the economy mid-conference changes what the NEXT award is worth and never rewrites history: a total is always explainable by what the rules said when it was earned. (2) The unique index on (UserId, ActivityType, SubjectKey) is the source of truth for both idempotency and anti-farming (:20-23), which is what makes a replayed broker message and a farmed scan both land exactly once. (3) A configured 0 is a per-rule kill switch that takes one earn rule out of service without a deploy.
    • Walkthrough: four constructor dependencies (PointsAwarder.cs:30-34), one method (:37-96).
      • Kill switch (:44-52): settings.Value.GetPointsFor(activity); when the value is <= 0 it logs at Debug and returns success without writing. GetPointsFor maps each of the six activities to its configured property and returns 0 only for an activity it does not map (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/Points/PointsSettings.cs:49-59). Every mapped property carries a non-zero default (PointsSettings.cs:19-38), so a missing configuration entry keeps its default award, and switching a rule off takes a deliberate 0, which is what the comment at :44-46 states. Writing nothing (rather than a zero-value row) keeps the ledger free of entries that would otherwise have to be filtered out of every read.
      • Erased-account guard (:54-61): ErasedUserGuard.EnsureNotErasedAsync checks the ErasedUser record for the user (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/ErasedUsers/ErasedUserGuard.cs:26-70). The guard itself returns a Forbidden failure, but here it is turned into a success no-op, logged at Debug, exactly like the disabled rule above, so the calling adapter does not log its award-rejected warning. Because every points adapter (the Conference feedback event included) comes through this method, the one check covers them all (:54-56).
      • Idempotency pre-check (:65-74): ExistsAsync on (UserId, ActivityType, SubjectKey). The comment (:65-66) enumerates what lands here: a repeat scan, a second answer to the same feedback form, and a broker redelivery. All three leave as a clean success.
      • Create (:76-78): PointsEntry.Create validates its own invariants and returns a Result (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/Points/PointsEntry.cs:76-104), unwrapped with TryGetValue(out var entry) so the entry is non-null on the success branch. A failure here is the one case that propagates as a failure, because it means the caller passed something invalid.
      • Save with a race backstop (:80-92): the same IsUniqueConstraintViolation filter as CreateBookmarkHandler, but the verdict is the opposite one. Here a lost race is a SUCCESS (:85-91), because "the award the caller wanted now exists" is exactly the outcome requested; a bookmark create, by contrast, is a user-visible action whose duplicate the user should be told about.
      • Five [LoggerMessage] partials (:98-111): rule disabled, erased account, already awarded, and lost race all log at Debug, while an actual award logs at Information, so the conference-day log volume tracks real awards rather than no-ops.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc is explicit that the pre-check "is not the rule" (:22-23). Reading the index as the authority and the pre-check as an optimization is what keeps the concurrent case correct rather than merely unlikely.
    • Where it's used: registered as IPointsAwarder (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:90) and called by the four award adapters listed under IPointsAwarder. Read back by PointsService and by the data-subject export, where the ledger and the check-in history are exported as separate collections (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Exports/UserEngagementExportService.cs:55-57,117).

    BookmarkCountsGrpcService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service.Grpc · MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Grpc/BookmarkCountsGrpcService.cs:30 · Level 9 · class (public sealed)

    • What it is: the server-side gRPC endpoint that publishes Engagement's in-process IBookmarkCountService over the wire. It is the counterpart of BookmarkCountServiceGrpcAdapter: the adapter runs inside Conference and speaks gRPC out, this service runs inside Engagement and answers.
    • Depends on: IBookmarkCountService (injected via primary constructor, :24), and the generated proto base BookmarkCountService.BookmarkCountServiceBase plus the four messages from bookmark_count.proto (namespace MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Contracts.V1, :2). Externals: Grpc.Core (ServerCallContext).
    • Concept, the server-side bridge. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness], [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]. This is the producer half of the pattern whose consumer half is taught in Group 13: the module keeps one C# interface, the proto generates an abstract server base, and this thin subclass forwards one to the other. Because the interface did not change when Engagement moved out of the monolith, neither Conference's call sites nor Engagement's BookmarkCountService had to change; only this bridge and its client twin were added. It mirrors, on the Engagement side, Conference's SessionBookmarksGrpcService, completing the bidirectional Conference-Engagement gRPC pair.
    • Concept, a documented unauthenticated trust boundary. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether every exposed surface has a stated authorization posture. This endpoint is mapped without .RequireAuthorization() (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:255, with the reasoning restated at the call site, :326-332), and the class doc (:11-22) argues why the requirement is not addable rather than merely absent: the Conference callers serve [AllowAnonymous] output-cached REST endpoints (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Speakers/SpeakerSessionsController.cs:71 and :87), so a cache-miss request from an anonymous visitor carries no bearer for JwtForwardingClientInterceptor to forward, and the public speaker pages would break. The exposure is bounded by the payload (aggregate counts per session id, no PII and no user ids on the wire) and by the network boundary: the Engagement container app's ingress is external: false (MMCA.ADC/infra/main.bicep:1921), so the endpoint stays on the internal service network and the Gateway never routes it. Contrast UserEngagementExportGrpcService, which is mapped .RequireAuthorization() (Program.cs:271) because it carries personal data.
    • Walkthrough
      • GetBookmarkCountForSession(request, context) (:28-40): null-guards both arguments with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull (:32-33), awaits inner.GetBookmarkCountForSessionAsync(request.SessionId, context.CancellationToken) (:35-37), threading the gRPC call's own cancellation token (and therefore the client's deadline) through to the database, then wraps the int in a response message (:39).
      • GetBookmarkCountsForSessions(request, context) (:43-61): the batch rpc. It materializes the repeated field with a collection expression, [.. request.SessionIds] (:51), calls the interface's batch method, then projects the returned dictionary into repeated SessionBookmarkCount messages via AddRange(... Select(...)) (:55-59).
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the wire endpoint a paper-thin forwarder means the real read logic (a COUNT under the soft-delete filter, over the SessionId index UserSessionBookmarkConfiguration declares) lives once and is reused identically in-process and over gRPC. The endpoint is published through AddGrpcServiceDefaults() (Program.cs:318), which also installs the GrpcResultExceptionInterceptor and gRPC reflection; for these methods the interceptor has nothing to translate, since the interface returns bare values rather than a Result.
    • Where it's used: mapped at MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:255, served over the service's Http2-only cleartext (h2c) endpoint (ADR-012). Its remote caller is Conference.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the class doc's own citations have drifted further. It names lines 385 and 405 of SpeakersController.cs (:15-16), a file that now has only 374 lines, and infra/main.bicep:1289-1295 (:20), but the anonymous bookmark-count actions it describes have since moved out of SpeakersController.cs entirely, to SpeakerSessionsController.cs:71 and :87, and the Engagement internal ingress is now at infra/main.bicep:1921. The argument still holds; only the citations are stale.

    ManualCheckInHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.CheckIns.UseCases.ManualCheckIn · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/CheckIns/UseCases/ManualCheckIn/ManualCheckInHandler.cs:19 · Level 12 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the organizer's manual fallback for when a badge will not scan. No credential is involved: the attendee is named in the request, and after an erased-user check everything is the same core the scan path runs.
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork, IEventLiveValidationService, ICurrentUserService, ErasedUserGuard, CheckInProcessor, CheckInResultDTO, ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult>; externals: TimeProvider, ILogger<T>.
    • Concept reinforced, the shared core with a per-entry-point difference. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] and [Rubric §11, Security]. Compared with CheckInAttendeeHandler, the credential extraction and badge lookup are simply absent; command.UserId goes into the processor as given. The doc comment carries the compensating control (ManualCheckInHandler.cs:14-18): an organizer-only endpoint backs it, which is what makes naming another user acceptable here and unacceptable on the attendee-facing flows in this unit. The payoff is stated in the same comment: a manual check-in and a scanned one produce identical rows and events, so nothing downstream needs to know which door the check-in came through. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance]: because the attendee id arrives in the request body, the handler first runs ErasedUserGuard.EnsureNotErasedAsync (:44, guard at MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/ErasedUsers/ErasedUserGuard.cs:26) and returns its failure unchanged (:45-48). The comment (:41-43) names the risk: an organizer working from a stale roster must not leave a check-in under an erased id that no erasure will ever revisit (ADR-005).
    • Walkthrough: five constructor dependencies (:19-24), one HandleAsync (:27-67). ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(command) (:31), the same RequireUserId("CheckIns.Forbidden") caller guard as the scan path (:33-37, the organizer id taken at :39), the erased-user guard on command.UserId (:44-48), the delegation to CheckInProcessor.ExecuteAsync (:50-59), and a success-only Information log, gated on the same result.TryGetValue(out var checkIn) unwrap as the scan path (:61-64), whose template differs from the scan path only by the word "manually" (:69-75), which is what lets an operator tell the two apart in the logs even though the rows are identical.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the fallback on exactly the same core avoids the classic drift where the rarely used path slowly stops enforcing a rule the main path gained. The erased-user check sits in front of that core because this is the entry point where the attendee id is typed in rather than resolved from a badge.
    • Where it's used: CheckInsController (injected at CheckInsController.cs:46, called from ManualCheckInAsync at :134).

    UserEngagementExportGrpcService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service.Grpc · MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Grpc/UserEngagementExportGrpcService.cs:27 · Level 12 · class (public sealed)

    • What it is: the server-side gRPC endpoint that publishes Engagement's in-process IUserEngagementExportService to the Identity service, so Identity can fold a user's Engagement-owned personal data into the aggregated data-subject export document. Same server-bridge shape as BookmarkCountsGrpcService, with two extra concerns: only the subject (or a privileged caller) may read the export, and timestamps and enums have to survive a proto3 wire crossing.
    • Depends on: IUserEngagementExportService (primary constructor, :27) and its DTOs from MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared.Exports (:4); the generated base UserEngagementExportService.UserEngagementExportServiceBase and the messages from user_engagement_export.proto (namespace MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Contracts.V1, :3); the framework's GrpcWireFormat from MMCA.Common.Grpc (:6); IsServiceCaller() from ServiceCallerClaimsPrincipalExtensions (MMCA.Common.Grpc.Authentication, :7), GetUserId() / HasRole from MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth (:8, see ClaimsPrincipalExtensions), and RoleNames.Organizer (:5). Externals: Grpc.Core (ServerCallContext, RpcException), System.Globalization (:1).
    • Concept, cross-service data-subject export as a purpose-built read contract. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance] assesses whether a real data-subject-access and portability path exists; [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses talking through explicit contracts. Identity owns the export document but not Engagement's data, so it depends only on the narrow interface; this class is the producer half over the wire, twin to the client-side UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapter. The class doc (:12-19) enumerates session bookmarks, submitted session questions, the points ledger, leaderboard participation, and check-in history; the method also forwards poll votes, question upvotes and ticket records, which the doc comment does not name (:96-125). Unlike the bookmark-count endpoint, this one is mapped .RequireAuthorization() (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:271, with the contrast drawn at :252), which is the posture difference personal data justifies.
    • Concept, the subject check behind a forwarded token. [Rubric §11, Security]. The edge forwards the end user's JWT, so an authenticated caller is not yet an authorized one: the method throws PermissionDenied unless the caller's own user id equals request.UserId, the caller is a service, or the caller holds RoleNames.Organizer, the export privilege Identity's export endpoint grants (:38-45). Without it any signed-in user could request another user's export by id.
    • Concept, proto3 has no nulls and no DateTime. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]. Three encoding decisions are made here and mirrored exactly on the client:
      • Timestamps: SQL Server hands back DateTimeKind.Unspecified values, and the round-trip "O" format omits the Z marker for that kind, so each value goes through GrpcWireFormat.FormatUtc (:62, :69, :78, :100, :105), which stamps DateTimeKind.Utc before formatting (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.Grpc/GrpcWireFormat.cs:42-43). The format is written once in the framework and called by both ends of the contract. The doc comment (:20-25) is careful about what this is: the stored values are already UTC, so this restores a marker rather than converting an instant. CheckedInOn is a DateTimeOffset, already carrying its offset, and is formatted as-is with "O" (:92-94); the ticket's InvitedOn and LinkedOn are also formatted directly with "O" (:119, :124).
      • Absent values: an absent leaderboard name travels as the empty string (:55-57), an absent SessionId/SponsorId as 0 (:87-90), and an absent ticket OrderEmail or InvitedOn as the empty string (:116-119), each with the comment naming the client-side inverse.
      • Enums: ActivityType (:73-75), Scope (:82-84) and the ticket's LinkMethod (:121-123) cross as their numeric values, justified in place: the points activity numbers are part of the idempotency key, the scope numbers are named literally in the SQL index filters (CheckInConfiguration, CheckInConfiguration.cs:25-27), and the link-method numbers are persisted, so none is ever renumbered.
    • Walkthrough: one overridden method, GetUserEngagementExport(request, context) (:31-128). It null-guards both arguments (:35-36), runs the subject check (:41-45), awaits inner.GetUserEngagementExportAsync(request.UserId, context.CancellationToken) (:47-49), then builds the response: the two scalar leaderboard fields in the initializer (:51-58), then seven AddRange(... Select(...)) projections filling the repeated fields: bookmarks (:59-63), submitted questions with their Text (:64-70), points entries (:71-79), check-ins (:80-95), poll votes (:96-101, LivePollId, OptionId and a FormatUtc CreatedOn), question upvotes (:102-106, QuestionId and a FormatUtc CreatedOn) and tickets (:107-125: event id, source event name, external ticket id, ticket type, attendee names, order email, invite and link timestamps, link method).
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the endpoint a thin forwarder leaves the real work (server-side projections that the soft-delete query filter already narrows to active rows) in UserEngagementExportService, reused identically in-process and over gRPC (ADR-012). Because the read returns a DTO rather than a Result, the GrpcResultExceptionInterceptor has no failure trailer to translate and a transport fault becomes a gRPC status the caller's resilience pipeline handles; the subject check is the one deliberate RpcException.
    • Where it's used: mapped at MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:271. Its remote caller is Identity's ExportUserDataHandler via UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapter. Covered by UserEngagementExportGrpcServiceTests, the integration UserEngagementExportGrpcTests, UserDataExportGrpcCallerTests and the posture checks in GrpcViewAsPostureTests.

    CurrentEventNotificationScopeProvider

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Notifications · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Notifications/CurrentEventNotificationScopeProvider.cs:30 · Level 3 · sealed partial class

    • What it is: ADC's implementation of the framework's notification scope hook. It answers "which conference event is in focus right now" as the opaque string event:{EventId}, so a notification sent for an event that has since ended stops surfacing once the next event becomes the current one.
    • Depends on: INotificationScopeProvider (the framework contract it implements), NotificationScopeKey (the canonical key formatter), ILiveEventUIService, LiveEventLookup and LiveEventContext (the resolution source). Externals: TimeProvider, System.Threading.Lock, ILogger<T> with source-generated [LoggerMessage] methods.
    • Concept introduced, the app-supplied scope over a framework-owned mechanism. [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assess whether a cross-cutting concern is expressed as a framework extension point the application fills in rather than as application logic baked into the framework. MMCA.Common knows notifications carry an optional scope key (ADR-024) and nothing more; the meaning of that string is ADC's business, and the type doc says so directly (CurrentEventNotificationScopeProvider.cs:11-12: to the framework it is just an opaque string).
    • Concept introduced, failing closed on a view filter. [Rubric §11, Security]. The framework contract is blunt about the direction of failure: implementations must never throw, and in an application whose notifications are all scoped they must fail closed, returning the last known key rather than null, because null on that contract means "unscoped" and silently widens the view to every notification (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/INotificationScopeProvider.cs:9-14). ADC is such an application, so this provider never answers null. The remarks block (:20-24) spells out the consequence: an instance that has never resolved an event answers with the UnresolvedScopeKey sentinel, event:0 (:39), a well-formed key (it satisfies NotificationScopeKey.Pattern, so the hub's channel-key guard accepts it) that no row carries, so the reader sees an empty inbox instead of everyone's.
    • Walkthrough:
      • The primary constructor (:30-33) takes the live-event service, a TimeProvider and a logger, and the class declares INotificationScopeProvider. UnresolvedScopeKey is composed from NotificationScopeKey.EventPrefix (:39, and MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Notifications/NotificationScopeKey.cs:23) so the sentinel cannot drift from the prefix the pattern at NotificationScopeKey.cs:32 accepts. CacheDuration is five minutes (:41).
      • The cache is two fields plus a Lock (:46-48). The comment above them (:43-45) is the concurrency reasoning worth reading: the lock guards the two fields only, the refresh runs outside it (a Lock cannot be held across an await), so two callers racing an expired cache both fetch. That is accepted deliberately, because the events read is idempotent and both callers converge on the same key, which beats serializing every poll behind a gate.
      • GetCurrentScopeKeyAsync(ct) (:51) takes the lock, returns the cached key while it is still fresh (:53-59), then resolves outside the lock: liveEventService.GetCurrentEventAsync(ct) now answers a three-state LiveEventLookup (failed, none, or found: MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/SessionLive/LiveEventLookup.cs:3-10), and the provider reads only its .LiveEvent (:64, property at LiveEventLookup.cs:25), so a failed read and "no published event" both arrive here as null. When an event comes back it builds the key through NotificationScopeKey.ForEvent (:67), which formats the identifier under CultureInfo.InvariantCulture (NotificationScopeKey.cs:44-45) so a culture with non-ASCII digits cannot produce a key the pattern rejects.
      • The two unresolved paths log and fall through, and both leave scopeKey null. A null LiveEvent logs at Information (:71, :139-140); because LiveEventService answers an unreadable events API with LiveEventLookup.Failed rather than throwing (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/SessionLive/LiveEventService.cs:23-28), an ordinary API outage lands on this path too. A lookup that still throws is caught and logged at Warning (:75-79, :136-137); the general catch carries a scoped CA1031 suppression whose justification states the contract, a failed lookup is logged and caches nothing, so the next call retries it (:74, :76).
      • The fail-closed answer (:81-86) returns LastResolvedOrSentinel() (:128-134), the last key this instance resolved or event:0. Nothing is cached on that path (:83-84) and the expiry is left alone (:125-126), so the very next call retries the lookup rather than serving a stale answer for a whole window.
      • The write-back (:88-92) caches only a successful resolution, stamping _cacheExpiresOn five minutes out from the injected clock.
      • GetCurrentScopeDisplayNameAsync(ct) (:107-121) is the optional half of the contract (a default interface method, INotificationScopeProvider.cs:41): it returns the current event's name, read off the same .LiveEvent, for a send surface to caption its target (:111-112), and fails closed the way that member defines it, by returning null so a missing caption hides information rather than stating the wrong audience (:118-119, logged at Debug via :142-143). Its catch carries the same scoped CA1031 suppression, justified as "the scope display name is cosmetic" (:114).
    • Why it's built this way: the caching is not premature. Both notification HTTP services ask for the scope on every call (NotificationInboxService.cs:180, PushNotificationService.cs:34) and NotificationBell polls the unread count on a PeriodicTimer whose default interval is 30 seconds (NotificationBell.razor.cs:127, MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/NotificationBellOptions.cs:23), so an uncached provider would put an events fetch behind every poll. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] and [Rubric §31, Cost/FinOps] both land on that arithmetic. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: the three [LoggerMessage] methods are source-generated and each message states what the operator loses, not just that something failed. The registration is the other deliberate detail: services.AddScoped<INotificationScopeProvider, CurrentEventNotificationScopeProvider>() (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:87) uses plain AddScoped so it overrides the NullNotificationScopeProvider that AddNotificationUI registers with TryAddScoped (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/DependencyInjection.cs:24), which keeps the two calls order-independent (DependencyInjection.cs:81-83); the line above it (:86) registers the clock with TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System), a TryAdd because AddOfflineWriteQueue earlier in the same method (and AddUIShared on the heads that call it) already registers the system clock (:84-85).
    • Where it's used: resolved by the framework's notification services listed above, and by the send page for its targeting caption (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Notifications/NotificationSend.razor.cs:78); never called directly by an ADC page. Covered by CurrentEventNotificationScopeProviderTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the cache is per instance and the registration is scoped, so on Blazor Server the window is per circuit, not per user or per process. How long a stale key can survive an event rollover is therefore bounded by the five-minute window, not by any invalidation signal.

    AttendeeCheckedIn

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared.CheckIns.IntegrationEvents · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/CheckIns/IntegrationEvents/AttendeeCheckedIn.cs:25 · Level 3 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the cross-module announcement that an attendee was checked in. One record carries every check-in shape: an organizer badge scan, the manual organizer fallback, a self-recorded sponsor booth visit, and a room check-in.
    • Depends on: BaseIntegrationEvent (the base it derives from, AttendeeCheckedIn.cs:33) and the module identifier aliases (UserIdentifierType, EventIdentifierType, SessionIdentifierType, SponsorIdentifierType). It names CheckInScopeNames only in its documentation, never as a type in its signature. It carries an explicit wire name through [EventName("Engagement.AttendeeCheckedIn.v1")] (:23), so the contract on the broker does not move when the CLR type is renamed or relocated. Externals: DateTimeOffset.
    • Concept introduced, the wire contract written for consumers you cannot redeploy. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether contracts are versionable rather than merely correct today, and this record makes three deliberate choices for that. First, Scope is a string (:26), not the CheckInScope enum: the doc comment (:11-14) states the reason, which is that adding a scope later stays an additive change for a consumer that has not been rebuilt, where an unknown enum member would deserialize into a value the consumer's own enum cannot name. Second, SponsorId is optional and last (:31), with the doc comment (:22) recording that placement so a consumer keeps deserializing payloads written before sponsor visits existed. Third, the v1 suffix in the event name (:23) makes the version part of the routed contract rather than an implicit property of the assembly. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] covers the delivery half: this is an integration event, not a domain event, so it does not merely dispatch in process. It is captured with the row that produced it and published by the outbox processor (ADR-003). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] applies because the payload is all scalars: nothing on it can only be resolved inside the Engagement process.
    • Walkthrough: seven positional members. UserId (:25) is the attendee. Scope (:26) is one of the CheckInScopeNames string constants. EventId (:27) is set for every scope, which is what lets a consumer bucket any check-in by conference without a lookup. SessionId (:28) is nullable and set only for a Session scope. CheckedInByUserId (:29) records who performed the check-in, an organizer for a scan and the attendee themselves for a self-recorded visit (:20), which is what keeps self-recorded rows distinguishable downstream. CheckedInOn (:30) is the recorded instant. SponsorId (:31) is the trailing optional member, defaulted to null.
    • Why it's built this way: the doc comment (:6-10) ties the event to the aggregate factory: it is added inside CheckIn.Create (CheckIn.cs:112-119) rather than in a handler, so the outbox captures it in the same transaction as the row. That gives the property the points economy depends on: a persisted check-in has published exactly one event, and a duplicate scan, which short-circuits before the factory, publishes none. Note the raise call is AddDomainEvent (CheckIn.cs:112): the framework's dual-dispatch treats an IIntegrationEvent added to an aggregate as outbox-bound, so an aggregate raises both kinds through one API. See ADR-072 for the surrounding badge-and-points decision.
    • Where it's used: raised by CheckIn (CheckIn.cs:112), consumed by AttendeeCheckedInPointsHandler. The Engagement service subscribes its own receive endpoint to this type (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/EngagementBrokerConsumers.cs:26), which the host's composition comment (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:207-214) calls out as ADC's first broker self-consumption: the message leaves this process through the broker and comes back to it, except under the InProcess test transport, where it is delivered in process so the integration tier exercises the same handler without a broker.

    LiveChannelPublishProcessor

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Live · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Live/LiveChannelPublishProcessor.cs:41 · Level 3 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the single background reader that drains LiveChannelPublishQueue and forwards each queued broadcast to ILiveChannelPublisher. It is the piece that keeps live-layer broadcasts (poll opened, results changed, question approved) off the command request path, and it drains what is still queued when the host stops.
    • Depends on: LiveChannelPublishQueue (the concrete queue, injected as itself for its Reader and Complete(), LiveChannelPublishProcessor.cs:42), ILiveChannelPublisher resolved per item (:131), and BestEffort (:125). Externals: BackgroundService from Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting, IServiceScopeFactory, and ILogger.
    • Concept introduced, the single-reader hosted drain. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses what work sits on the request path: a command handler here never awaits a broadcast, it enqueues, and this worker pays the network cost afterwards. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] is the reason the loop looks the way it does: the publish is best effort (BR-229, ADR-039), so no failure is allowed to escape the drain, and a down or hung Notification peer costs at most the adapter's own deadline per item and can never crash the host or fail a command (:15-20). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] covers the diagnostics: the swallow is delegated to BestEffort, so a peer that has quietly stopped accepting broadcasts is countable on the besteffort.dispatch.failed meter rather than being a Warning nobody alerts on (:21-28, and the meter itself at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Services/BestEffort.cs:109-112). The queue counts its own backpressure drops separately (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Live/LiveChannelPublishQueue.cs:68-77). [Rubric §29, Resilience, Reliability & Business Continuity] covers the lifetime mismatch this class exists to bridge: a BackgroundService is a singleton while the gRPC publisher adapter is registered scoped, so the worker opens one scope per item (:130-131). The same section covers the shutdown posture: a scale-in or revision swap stops a replica mid-session, so StopAsync drains the queue instead of dropping it, inside one fixed budget (:30-38, :50).
    • Walkthrough
      • The primary constructor (:41-44) takes the queue, an IServiceScopeFactory and a logger. The class is sealed partial since the shutdown warning is a source-generated [LoggerMessage] (:140-143); the per-item swallow still lives inside BestEffort.
      • PublishOperationPrefix (:47) is the constant "live-channel-publish:". It is completed per item with the work item's event name (:126) to form the best-effort operation name. The comment above the class (:21-28) explains the cardinality reasoning: the event name is a small fixed set of channel constants and is therefore safe as a metric tag, while the channel key is per session and is deliberately left out because fanning the tag out tells an operator nothing they can act on.
      • ExecuteAsync (:85) is a two-level loop: WaitToReadAsync(stoppingToken) (:89-90) waits for work, then an inner TryRead loop (:94-97) publishes each item. Both loops check stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested first (:89, :94), so an item is never dequeued after the stop: it would be published on the cancelled token and lost, and is left for the shutdown drain (:92-93). There is exactly one of these loops in the process, and the queue is created with SingleReader = true (LiveChannelPublishQueue.cs:37), which is what makes delivery FIFO and therefore per-session order preserving: successive poll.results-changed tallies cannot arrive out of order (LiveChannelPublishProcessor.cs:11-14).
      • PublishAsync (:124-138) is the shared per-item path, used by both the live loop and the drain. It hands the body to BestEffort.ExecuteAsync (:125) with the operation name, the logger, the publish lambda and the caller's token. Inside the lambda an async DI scope is created (:130), the publisher is resolved from it (:131), and PublishAsync is awaited with the work item's channel key, event name and pre-serialized payload plus the token the helper passes in (:132-136).
      • StopAsync (:53-82) is the shutdown drain. It first closes the queue with queue.Complete() (:57), so the drain sees a finite set of items, then creates one ShutdownDrainBudget of 5 seconds (:50) and links it to the host's token (:59-60). base.StopAsync(drain.Token) (:67) cancels the stopping token and waits, inside the budget, for ExecuteAsync to return. Only if the worker has let go of the reader (ExecuteTask is null || ExecuteTask.IsCompleted, :72) does DrainRemainingAsync (:109-122) publish the remainder in FIFO order on the drain token, which exists because the gRPC publisher fails a cancelled call immediately (:33-34). Whatever is left (queue.Reader.Count, :77) is logged by the generated LogShutdownDrainAbandoned warning (:80, :140-143) and abandoned.
      • Cancellation is separated from failure, and the split is shared rather than local: BestEffort rethrows the caller's own cancellation instead of recording it as a failure (BestEffort.cs:59-64), and both the live loop (:100-105) and the drain (:118-121) catch that rethrow when their own token is cancelled and return quietly.
    • Why it's built this way: the enqueue side cannot block and cannot fail, so backpressure has to be resolved somewhere. It is resolved in the queue, not here: the channel is bounded at 1024 items with BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest (LiveChannelPublishQueue.cs:18, :36), which chooses the freshest broadcast over the oldest when the drain falls behind, because live channel events are ephemeral. A DropOldest write always succeeds, so the queue registers an itemDropped callback (LiveChannelPublishQueue.cs:40, :61-65) as the only way a discard becomes observable. This worker's job is to be the one reader that gives that channel its ordering guarantee, to make its swallowed failures countable rather than merely logged, and to drain on stop. The drain is bounded on purpose: the whole stop shares one 5-second budget, well inside the 30-second Container Apps and host shutdown grace (:36-37), so a hung Notification peer cannot hold the host. The in-flight publish is NOT allowed to finish, because it runs on the stopping token and the cancellation aborts it (:34-35, :62-66), and the check-then-TryRead pair is two steps, so a stop landing between them can still lose one dequeued item (:62-66).
    • Where it's used: registered as a hosted service by the module's infrastructure registration (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:26), so it starts with any host that boots the Engagement module. Its producers are the live-layer handlers that hold ILiveChannelPublishQueue (for example MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/LivePolls/UseCases/Open/OpenLivePollHandler.cs:24 and .../SessionQuestions/UseCases/Submit/SubmitQuestionHandler.cs:29). In the deployed topology the publisher is the gRPC adapter targeting Notification's dedicated Http2 endpoint (ADR-012). Covered by LiveChannelPublishProcessorTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: whether a given deployment actually reaches a Notification peer is configuration and runtime, not source. Nothing in this file retries a failed publish; a dropped or failed broadcast is gone, which is the stated contract rather than an omission. The shutdown drain is best effort too: the in-flight item, any item lost to the dequeue race, and anything left when the 5-second budget expires are not delivered.

    UserSessionBookmarkCacheEvictionHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.UserSessionBookmarks.DomainEventHandlers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/UserSessionBookmarks/DomainEventHandlers/UserSessionBookmarkCacheEvictionHandler.cs:38 · Level 3 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the handler that requests an output-cache eviction on the Conference service every time a bookmark is created, reactivated or removed, so Conference's cached session reads stop serving a stale bookmark count. It only raises a flag; the broadcast itself belongs to BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessor.
    • Depends on: IDomainEventHandler<in TDomainEvent> implemented over UserSessionBookmarkChanged (:39), BookmarkCacheEvictionSignal, the coalescing flag injected through the primary constructor (:38), and ConferenceCacheTags, the Conference.Shared constant its tag aliases (:1, :47). The broadcast types, OutputCacheEvictionRequested and BestEffort, are used by the processor, not by this handler (BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessor.cs:7-8).
    • Concept introduced, evicting a cache you do not own. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether a cross-cutting concern is solved once at the right layer. ASP.NET Core's output cache is per host: IOutputCacheStore is a local store, so a write in the owning service leaves a stale cached response sitting in front of every other process until its TTL expires (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/IntegrationEvents/OutputCacheEvictionRequested.cs:10-13). Bookmark counts are the sharp case: they are owned by Engagement but served by Conference. The class comment (:12-18) names the symptom that motivated the class, a speaker watching their dashboard seeing a star land up to a minute later, and the previous answer, a short TTL, which is a floor rather than a fix. The fix is to make eviction an event like any other: the processor this handler feeds publishes OutputCacheEvictionRequested carrying one tag, and the Conference host's own eviction handler drops that tag on arrival (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:280, and the reasoning at :204-215). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] is why it has to be an event at all: under database-per-service (ADR-006) and process-per-service, Engagement has no handle on the other host's cache store, so the broker is the only reachable path. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] covers the failure posture: the publish runs through BestEffort inside the processor (BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessor.cs:26-29), so a failure becomes one Warning plus one metric and the stale entry expires on Conference's own TTL exactly as it did before this existed. The TTL stays deliberately, as the backstop for a dropped or delayed message (Program.cs:214-216).
    • Concept introduced, pacing a burst by raising a flag instead of publishing. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether per-event work scales with load. Publishing one eviction per star would keep Conference's session cache permanently cold when a changeover produces a burst of stars (:21-25). The handler therefore does no I/O: HandleAsync calls signal.Request() (:58), a TryWrite into the signal's single pending slot (BookmarkCacheEvictionSignal.cs:42). The single-reader hosted processor (BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessor.cs:35, registered at MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:27) broadcasts at once when idle, then waits one pacing window and sends ONE trailing broadcast for everything that arrived meanwhile (BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessor.cs:17-23). A burst costs one eviction per window per replica, not one per star.
    • Concept introduced, subscribing to the aggregate rather than to the use case. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses where a reaction is hooked. The obvious hook is the create command handler, but the delete path runs on the framework's generic DeleteEntityCommand<TEntity, TIdentifierType> and has no ADC handler at all to add a line to. UserSessionBookmarkChanged is raised by the aggregate itself on every path that moves a count (UserSessionBookmark.cs:57 on create, :73 on reactivate, :88 on delete), so subscribing to the domain event covers all three with one class and leaves the delete flow untouched (:28-32). It also inherits the dispatch guarantee: domain-event dispatch is deferred until after the transaction commits and dropped on rollback, so no eviction is ever requested for a bookmark that did not persist (:32-34).
    • Walkthrough
      • The primary constructor (:38) takes only the BookmarkCacheEvictionSignal (:37). It needs no scope factory or logger, because it never reaches the scoped event bus: that is the processor's job.
      • SessionsCacheTag (:47) is a public const alias of ConferenceCacheTags.Sessions, whose value is "conference:sessions" (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Shared/Caching/ConferenceCacheTags.cs:24). Its doc comment (:41-46) is the load-bearing part: the tag string IS the contract between the two hosts, so the handler takes it from the same constant Conference registers its cache policies with (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:192, :202, :216). Both sides reading one constant is the point of that type, whose own comment records that a policy and an eviction spelling a tag differently fail silently, the stale entry simply living out its TTL (ConferenceCacheTags.cs:6-7). The compiler now enforces the agreement, at the cost of an Application-layer reference to MMCA.ADC.Conference.Shared (:1).
      • HandleAsync (:50) is synchronous: it null-guards (:54), calls signal.Request() (:58) and returns Task.CompletedTask (:59). The publish through the event bus, with its outbox persistence (ADR-003), happens in BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessor.
      • The handler deliberately does not filter on domainEvent.State, and the comment says why (:56-57): every state the aggregate raises (Added on create and reactivate, Deleted on removal) moves the count Conference has cached.
    • Why it's built this way: the alternative shapes each fail on something concrete. Hooking the command handlers misses the generic delete. Calling EvictByTagAsync locally does nothing, because the cache entries are in another process. Publishing per star would keep Conference's cache cold under burst load. Raising a coalescing flag from the aggregate's own event, and letting a paced best-effort processor do the broadcast, covers every write path, crosses the process boundary, and cannot hurt the write it reacts to. The caching strategy this fits into is ADR-026, and the authenticated-read caching it evicts is ADR-040.
    • Where it's used: registered as a singleton by the convention scan (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:94, reaching MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:51-56). Its counterpart on the receiving side is OutputCacheEvictionHandler, registered on the Conference host. Covered by UserSessionBookmarkCacheEvictionHandlerTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the Conference host comment records that both halves are needed, the handler and the broker consumer, and that registering only one is a silent no-op (Program.cs:279); nothing in this file can detect that the other half is missing. Whether the broadcast actually reaches Conference is broker configuration and runtime, not source.

    IEventFeedbackUIService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Feedback · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Feedback/IFeedbackUIService.cs:23 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the UI contract for submitting and reading a user's own answers to event feedback questions.
    • Depends on: EventQuestionAnswerDTO, Result, and the EventIdentifierType / QuestionIdentifierType / EventQuestionAnswerIdentifierType aliases. Externals: BCL Task.
    • Concept introduced, POST-as-upsert (BR-107). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses how idempotent write semantics are expressed to clients. SubmitAnswerAsync (IFeedbackUIService.cs:26-30) is one method for both the first answer and every edit: the server upserts on (eventId, questionId) for the caller, so the UI never branches on create-versus-update and never has to know whether an answer already exists. That is what lets EventFeedback retry a partially failed submit by pressing the same button, since re-posting an already-saved answer is a no-op. The type doc names the rule outright (:19-22). This is the cross-module UI service abstraction of ISessionBookmarkUIService (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/UserSessionBookmarks/ISessionBookmarkUIService.cs:15) specialized to feedback, with the same "every member answers with a Result" contract (ISessionBookmarkUIService.cs:9-12).
    • Walkthrough (IFeedbackUIService.cs:23-51): SubmitAnswerAsync(eventId, questionId, answerValue, ct) returns Result<EventQuestionAnswerDTO>, the persisted answer (:26-30); SubmitAnswersAsync(eventId, answers, ct) creates or replaces the caller's answers to a whole event feedback form in one call, applied atomically so the result is all-or-nothing (:32-39); GetMyAnswersAsync(eventId, ct) returns the caller's answers for one event (:42-44), which is what the page pre-fills from (EventFeedback.razor.cs:117-118); DeleteAnswerAsync(eventId, answerId, ct) removes one by its server-assigned id (:47-50). Note the answer value crosses as a plain string: rating and text questions share one transport shape and the question type decides how it is read back.
    • Why it's built this way: it is kept as its own type rather than folded into one generic contract with its session twin ISessionFeedbackUIService, because the answer DTOs and the identifier aliases differ and a shared generic would buy nothing at three members apiece. Its batch member now mirrors ISessionFeedbackUIService's SubmitAnswersAsync, so the two twins stay parallel at both the single-answer and whole-form shape.
    • Where it's used: implemented by EventFeedbackService (EventFeedbackService.cs:15), registered scoped (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:52), consumed by EventFeedback (EventFeedback.razor.cs:20, submitting at :194).

    IPointsUIService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Points · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Points/IPointsUIService.cs:14 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the UI contract for the points game surfaces: the attendee's own ledger, the leaderboard and its opt-in switch, and the organizer rollup.
    • Depends on: MyPointsDTO, LeaderboardEntryDTO, PointsOverviewDTO, Result. Externals: BCL Task. The UI service abstraction itself is taught on ISessionBookmarkUIService (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/UserSessionBookmarks/ISessionBookmarkUIService.cs:15).
    • Concept introduced, the server-owned identity on a write. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether a client can influence data it should not own. SetLeaderboardParticipationAsync(participate, ct) (:41) takes a single boolean and nothing else, and the doc says why (:35-38): the published name is taken from the caller's token server-side, never from this call. A client that could pass its own display name could publish someone else's, so the parameter simply does not exist. The same discipline shapes GetMyPointsAsync (:23-26), which carries no user identifier at all: "mine" is whoever the bearer token says it is.
    • Concept, opt-in as the default privacy posture. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance] assesses how personal data reaches a public surface. Points accrue for every attendee, but the leaderboard shows only those who opted in, under the name they published at opt-in (:28-31), and the opt-in is an explicit write the attendee makes. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] covers the rest of the shape: like every service in this module, every member answers with a Result, so a refusal is data the page renders and only the caller's own cancellation still propagates (:9-12).
    • Walkthrough (IPointsUIService.cs:14-51):
      • GetMyPointsAsync(pageNumber = 1, pageSize = 20, ct) (:23-26) returns the running total, the opt-in state and one page of awarded entries, newest first, in a single MyPointsDTO. The three concerns travel together because the "my points" page renders them as one screen.
      • GetLeaderboardAsync(ct) (:33) returns the whole public leaderboard as one list, with no paging parameters: it is a short, capped list by nature.
      • SetLeaderboardParticipationAsync(participate, ct) (:41) joins or leaves, returning a bare Result because there is nothing to read back.
      • GetPointsOverviewAsync(recentCount = 20, ct) (:48-50) is the organizer rollup, with the recent-entry count as the only knob; organizer only (:43-45).
    • Why it's built this way: one interface for four related reads and one write keeps the whole points vocabulary and its single points resource (PointsService.cs:20) in one place, in the same shape as ICheckInUIService does for check-in (ADR-072 defines the check-in and points model together).
    • Where it's used: implemented by PointsService (PointsService.cs:15-17), registered scoped (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:61), and injected into two pages: MyPoints (MyPoints.razor.cs:28, reading at :75 and :85 and writing the opt-in at :117) and OrganizerPointsOverview (OrganizerPointsOverview.razor.cs:24, reading at :46).

    IQuestionLookupService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Feedback · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Feedback/IFeedbackUIService.cs:11 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: a small read contract that loads the feedback questions to render, filtered by whether they apply to an Event or a Session.
    • Depends on: QuestionDTO, a Conference-owned contract (IFeedbackUIService.cs:2), and Result. Externals: BCL Task.
    • Concept, the cross-module UI read. [Rubric §18, UI Architecture] and [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]. Feedback lives in Engagement but the questions are Conference-owned, so this contract lets the Engagement UI pull them through the same authenticated HTTP layer without a compile-time reference to Conference internals: only the shared QuestionDTO crosses the boundary. This is a different trade-off from the mirrored shape on NowNextSessionInfo, and the difference is worth noticing: a .Shared DTO is a published contract project both sides may reference, while a mirror is what you write when you do not want the reference at all.
    • Walkthrough (IFeedbackUIService.cs:11-17): one method, GetQuestionsAsync(questionEntity, ct), where questionEntity is the string discriminator ("Event" or "Session"), returning Result<IReadOnlyList<QuestionDTO>>. The discriminator is a bare string rather than an enum, so a typo at a call site is a runtime empty list, not a compile error; both call sites pass a literal (EventFeedback.razor.cs:104).
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the question read on its own interface rather than duplicating it on both feedback services means one implementation serves both pages, and the discriminator stays the only difference between the two calls.
    • Where it's used: implemented by QuestionLookupService (QuestionLookupService.cs:20), registered scoped (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:51), consumed by both EventFeedback (EventFeedback.razor.cs:19, :104-105) and SessionFeedback (SessionFeedback.razor.cs:18) to build their question lists.

    ISessionFeedbackUIService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Feedback · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Feedback/IFeedbackUIService.cs:57 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the UI-side contract for session feedback, four members covering the whole attendee-facing lifecycle of an answer: submit one, submit a whole form at once, read back what the caller already answered, and remove an answer (IFeedbackUIService.cs:57-85). It is the third of three interfaces declared in one file, beside IQuestionLookupService (:11) and IEventFeedbackUIService (:23).
    • Depends on: Result and Result<T> from MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions (:4), SessionQuestionAnswerDTO and QuestionDTO from the Conference contracts (:1-3), plus the SessionIdentifierType, QuestionIdentifierType and SessionQuestionAnswerIdentifierType aliases. No BCL dependency beyond Task and CancellationToken.
    • Concept introduced, the Result-typed client contract. Every member here answers with a Result rather than a nullable DTO or a bare Task, and the class doc states it outright (:46). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether a client abstraction preserves the distinctions the server makes: a nullable return collapses "no such answer", "you are not allowed" and "the network is down" into one null, while a Result keeps the server's own ErrorType and error code intact all the way to the page. [Rubric §24, Forms/Validation/UX Safety] is the front-end consequence: a feedback form can render the server's validation message for the field that failed instead of a generic banner. The pattern itself is taught in the primer and ADR-013; what is new at this layer is that the transport now speaks it too, through ProblemDetailsResultReader and HttpResultExecutor.
    • Walkthrough
      • SubmitAnswerAsync (:51-55) takes the session, the question and the answer string, and returns the persisted SessionQuestionAnswerDTO. It is a POST-as-upsert (BR-107, :46): the caller never has to know whether it is creating a first answer or replacing an existing one.
      • SubmitAnswersAsync (:61-64) is the batch form, taking IReadOnlyList<(QuestionIdentifierType QuestionId, string AnswerValue)> and returning every saved answer. Its doc comment carries the contract that matters most (:57-60): the server applies the form atomically, so the result is all-or-nothing. That is the difference between a form that half-saves on a flaky connection and one that does not.
      • GetMyAnswersAsync (:67-69) reads the caller's own answers for a session. No user identifier appears in the signature: the server scopes the read to the token holder.
      • DeleteAnswerAsync (:72-75) removes one answer by identifier, with the owning sessionId alongside it, and returns the valueless Result.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the contract in the UI layer over Shared DTOs only is what lets SessionFeedback be bUnit-tested against a mock with no HTTP in sight. [Rubric §1, SOLID]: the batch member exists as its own method rather than as an overload with an options flag, because it maps to a genuinely different endpoint with a different guarantee.
    • Where it's used: implemented by SessionFeedbackService and registered scoped (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:53); injected by SessionFeedback (SessionFeedback.razor.cs:19), which drives all four members (:122, :226, :259).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the interface says nothing about idempotency. That the batch submit carries an Idempotency-Key is an implementation decision, described at SessionFeedbackService.

    EventFeedbackSubmittedPointsHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Points.IntegrationEventHandlers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/IntegrationEventHandlers/EventFeedbackSubmittedPointsHandler.cs:27 · Level 4 · class (sealed partial)
