    • What it is: the award adapter that turns Conference's EventFeedbackSubmitted into an event-scoped points award. It is one of the handlers in this folder and the simplest of them.
    • Depends on: ScopedIntegrationEventHandlerBase<TIntegrationEvent> closed over EventFeedbackSubmitted (:30), which is the framework base that implements IIntegrationEventHandler<in TIntegrationEvent>; IPointsAwarder (resolved from the supplied scope, :38), PointsSubjectKeys (:40) and PointsActivityType (:44). Externals: IServiceScopeFactory and a source-generated [LoggerMessage] (:53-54), which is why the class is partial.
    • Concept introduced, the thin award adapter. [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] assesses where knowledge sits. The rule the module protects is stated on IPointsAwarder (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/Services/IPointsAwarder.cs:10-17): neither the awarder nor the ledger entity names an event, a session or a check-in, so an award is a user, an activity, an opaque subject key and a timestamp. All the conference vocabulary lives in adapters like this one, which is what would make lifting the ledger into MMCA.Common a move rather than a rewrite. [Rubric §1, SOLID] shows up twice: mapping lives here while idempotency and the per-rule kill switch live once in the awarder, and the two blocks every integration handler would otherwise repeat (the DI scope preamble and the log-and-rethrow envelope) live once in the base (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DomainEvents/ScopedIntegrationEventHandlerBase.cs:45-63). [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] covers the delivery posture: the base propagates exceptions rather than swallowing them, so delivery stays at-least-once and redelivery is normal (ScopedIntegrationEventHandlerBase.cs:26-33), which is why this handler is written to be safely repeatable rather than to guard against a second call.
    • Walkthrough: the class overrides HandleScopedAsync (:33-36) instead of HandleAsync. The base has already null-guarded the event and opened the per-delivery async scope, and hands in that scope's IServiceProvider (ScopedIntegrationEventHandlerBase.cs:47-55), so the body is only its own resolutions plus its own logic: resolve the scoped IPointsAwarder (:38), build the subject key with PointsSubjectKeys.ForEvent(integrationEvent.EventId) (:40), which delegates to NotificationScopeKey.ForEvent and therefore produces the invariant-culture event:{id} string (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/Points/PointsSubjectKeys.cs:19-20, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Notifications/NotificationScopeKey.cs:44-45), then award PointsActivityType.EventFeedback at the event's own SubmittedOnUtc (:42-47). A rejected award (the awarder returning a failure rather than throwing) is logged at Warning and not rethrown (:49-50), because the awarder only fails when the entry itself is invalid, which is a caller bug rather than a retryable condition (IPointsAwarder.cs:30-34). An exception takes the other path: the base logs it once and lets it propagate so the delivery is retried.
    • Why it's built this way: the class comment (:13-18) states the multiplicity fact that makes this handler safe to keep this simple. Event feedback writes one answer row per question (BR-107), so one submitted form arrives here as several events. Nothing counts them: they all resolve to the same event subject key, and the awarder's uniqueness rule collapses them into a single award. That same property is what makes a broker redelivery a no-op, so no dedupe logic is written twice.
    • Where it's used: registered by the convention scan (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:94), which reaches MMCA.Common's singleton registration for every IIntegrationEventHandler<> implementation (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:58-63); the singleton lifetime is exactly why the base opens a scope per delivery (:19-23). The Engagement service subscribes the matching consumer (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/EngagementBrokerConsumers.cs:28). Covered by EventFeedbackSubmittedPointsHandlerTests.

    SessionFeedbackSubmittedPointsHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Points.IntegrationEventHandlers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/IntegrationEventHandlers/SessionFeedbackSubmittedPointsHandler.cs:29 · Level 4 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the award adapter for session feedback, mapping Conference's SessionFeedbackSubmitted onto a session-scoped award. The structural twin of EventFeedbackSubmittedPointsHandler.
    • Depends on: the same set as its sibling, with SessionFeedbackSubmitted as the base's closed type (:32) and IPointsAwarder resolved from the scope the base supplies (:40).
    • Concept: the thin award adapter is taught on EventFeedbackSubmittedPointsHandler; the same reasoning applies unchanged. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] is worth naming here: the two files are near-identical and are deliberately kept separate rather than folded into one generic handler, because each is bound to a different event type at the DI boundary and, once ScopedIntegrationEventHandlerBase<TIntegrationEvent> absorbed the scope and error plumbing, what is left to share is five lines of mapping.
    • Walkthrough of what differs: only two lines. The subject key is built with PointsSubjectKeys.ForSession(integrationEvent.SessionId) (:42), producing session:{id} (PointsSubjectKeys.cs:25-26, NotificationScopeKey.cs:50-51), and the activity is PointsActivityType.SessionFeedback (:46). Everything else, the HandleScopedAsync override (:35-38), the awarder resolution (:40), the SubmittedOnUtc timestamp (:48) and the log-and-continue path for a rejected award (:51-52), matches the event handler line for line.

    • Where it's used: registered by the convention scan as a singleton (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:94, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:58-63); the consumer is wired at MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/EngagementBrokerConsumers.cs:27.     SessionQuestionSubmittedPointsHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Points.DomainEventHandlers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/DomainEventHandlers/SessionQuestionSubmittedPointsHandler.cs:53 · Level 4 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the award adapter for session Q and A. It awards PointsActivityType.QuestionAsked the first time an attendee asks a question in a session. It is the one award adapter in the module that rides a domain event rather than an integration event, which makes it the best place in this chapter to see the two delivery models side by side.
    • Depends on: IDomainEventHandler<in TDomainEvent> implemented over SessionQuestionChanged (:55), BestEffort wrapping the award (:81), IPointsAwarder resolved per event (:87), PointsActivityType (:93), PointsSubjectKeys (:94) and DomainEntityState (:65). Externals: IServiceScopeFactory, ILogger, and three source-generated [LoggerMessage] methods (:104-111), which is why the class is partial.
    • Concept introduced, choosing at-most-once on purpose. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses whether a delivery guarantee is a decision or an accident. Its siblings in Points/IntegrationEventHandlers all consume outbox-published integration events, which are at-least-once and survive a crash. This one subscribes to an in-process domain event, and the class comment (:30-39) argues the trade-off explicitly: dispatch happens after the question's transaction commits, so a crash in the window between the commit and this handler loses one small award and nothing else, no question is lost and no total is corrupted. The alternative (a second outbox contract, a broker round trip and inbox dedup for a handful of points) buys durability the feature does not need. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] is the same paragraph read from the operations side, and it names the exit: promoting the path later is a one-file change on each side, the aggregate raises an integration event instead and this class becomes an IIntegrationEventHandler. Contrast UserDeletedPointsHandler, which sits on the integration path and deliberately lets an exception propagate, because a missed erasure is not a missed nicety.
    • Concept introduced, taking everything off the event rather than reading it back. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether a class works with the data it is actually given. The comment at :22-29 records the trap this file is written around: SessionQuestionChanged is captured by value while the aggregate is still new, so on the Added path its QuestionId is zero (the identity is generated by the INSERT, which has not run when the event is raised, and the event is never re-stamped). The event contract states the same rule at its own source (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/SessionQuestions/DomainEvents/SessionQuestionChanged.cs:16-22) and carries UserId and SessionId precisely because they are set before the raise (:24-28). This handler therefore reads no row at all: the two fields it needs come off the event, so there is no read-back to get wrong.
    • Concept introduced, the subject key as the anti-farming rule. The subject key is the session, never the question (:94), so an attendee who asks five questions in one session earns once. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] is why that holds under concurrency: the limit is enforced by the ledger's unique index inside PointsAwarder rather than by counting here (:18-20), so two simultaneous submissions cannot both slip past a read-then-write check.
    • Walkthrough
      • The primary constructor (:53-55) takes an IServiceScopeFactory and a logger. Domain event handlers are registered as singletons by the framework's convention scan (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:51-56), which is why this class opens its own scope instead of injecting scoped services (:48).
      • HandleAsync (:61) null-guards the event (:63), then returns unless the state is DomainEntityState.Added (:65-69). SessionQuestionChanged is raised for moderation and deletion too (SessionQuestion.cs:147, :158, :190, :234), so this filter is what keeps a moderator approving a question from paying the asker a second time. The skip is logged at Debug (:67, :104-105).
      • The second guard rejects a defaulted UserId (:71-78). The comment (:73-75) is worth reading as a lesson in log-level choice: the path is unreachable through the aggregate, because the Create invariants reject a default user, so reaching it can only mean a new raise site forgot to pass the asker, and a silent skip there would award nobody without a trace. It is therefore a Warning (:76, :107-108), not a silent return.
      • The award runs inside a BestEffort.ExecuteAsync call (:81, comment :80) named by the OperationName const "session-question-points-award" (:58). Inside its delegate one async DI scope is opened (:86) and the scoped IPointsAwarder resolved (:87). AwardAsync is called with the event's UserId, PointsActivityType.QuestionAsked, PointsSubjectKeys.ForSession(domainEvent.SessionId), domainEvent.DateOccurred and the wrapper's own token (:91-96). The comment (:89-90) explains the timestamp choice: DateOccurred is stamped when the aggregate raised the event (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/DomainEvents/BaseDomainEvent.cs:28), which is when the attendee actually asked, so no clock has to be injected here.
      • A rejected award (the awarder returning a failure) logs at Warning (:98-99, :110-111).
      • There is no local try/catch. BestEffort.ExecuteAsync swallows a thrown award failure and rethrows only the caller's own cancellation, so the handler carries no CA1031 suppression and no bespoke failure log message: the failure is reported by the helper as one Warning plus one besteffort.dispatch.failed increment (class comment :43-45, ADR-096). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] covers the discipline around it: the swallow is never silent, and the class comment states the rule that every declining path says so at a level matching how surprising it is (:41-43).
    • Why it's built this way: both guards exist so the game can never damage the feature it decorates. The state filter keeps the ledger honest, the BestEffort wrapper keeps a points outage from becoming a Q and A outage, and taking the asker off the event removes the only lookup that could quietly award nobody. The swallow is also why this class implements IDomainEventHandler<in TDomainEvent> directly rather than deriving from the framework's SafeDomainEventHandler<TDomainEvent>: it wants the exception to stop here, not to be logged and rethrown. The points design as a whole is ADR-072.
    • Where it's used: discovered and registered as a singleton by ScanModuleApplicationServices<ClassReference>() (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:94), and invoked by the framework's domain event dispatcher after the Q and A write path's SaveChangesAsync. Its raise site is SessionQuestion.Create (SessionQuestion.cs:122). Covered by SessionQuestionSubmittedPointsHandlerTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: how many points QuestionAsked is worth, and whether the rule is switched off at all, is configuration read inside PointsAwarder, not here.

It POSTs { EventId, Answers } to eventquestionanswers/batch (:60-69) and reads back the saved list as a plain List<EventQuestionAnswerDTO>, mapped to IReadOnlyList<EventQuestionAnswerDTO> (:71-74).

The envelope is read as a PagedCollectionResult<T> and Mapped to a bare IReadOnlyList with a collection expression (:96), so the page never sees the paging wrapper.

The batch submit now matches its session-scoped twin's shape: same idempotency-key-before-retry pattern, same /batch route convention.

The server's EventQuestionAnswers controller now exposes a batch route (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventQuestionAnswersController.cs:301), so this service is no longer missing the batch shape its session-scoped twin has.

    • Concept: the authenticated-HTTP shape from BookmarkApiClient (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/BookmarkApiClient.cs:21), applied to a surface where authentication is doing four different jobs at once. The class doc (:11-14) enumerates them, and they are worth reading as a [Rubric §11, Security] exercise: the ledger read and the leaderboard opt-in are caller-scoped ("my points"), the leaderboard read is caller-agnostic but still requires a signed-in attendee (PointsController.cs:35), and the overview is role-gated on the server (PointsController.cs:122). The client enforces none of that and does not try to: it attaches the token and lets the server decide, which is why a 403 arrives as a Forbidden failure the page can render rather than as a page that guessed wrong about permissions.
    • Walkthrough (in interface order)
      • GetMyPointsAsync (:23-40) GETs points/me?pageNumber=&pageSize= with invariant formatting (:32) and returns MyPointsDTO. No user id is sent; the server reads the caller from the token (PointsController.cs:50).
      • GetLeaderboardAsync (:43-56) GETs points/leaderboard, reads a List<LeaderboardEntryDTO> (:53) and Maps it to the interface's IReadOnlyList (:54). The variance cast is the only transformation: the ordering and the ranks are the server's.
      • SetLeaderboardParticipationAsync (:59-78) PUTs a SetLeaderboardParticipationRequest carrying only the boolean (:67) to points/me/leaderboard-participation. The inline comment (:65-66) explains the shape of the round trip: the endpoint answers 204 with no body (PointsController.cs:100), so the method returns the valueless Result and the caller re-reads its own points to pick up the new opt-in state and display name.
      • GetPointsOverviewAsync (:81-97) GETs points/overview?recentCount= (:89) for the organizer rollup.
      • All four share the same three-step shape: HttpResultExecutor.ExecuteAsync on the outside, the retry policy with the cancellation-token overload in the middle, ProblemDetailsResultReader.ReadAsync on the response.
    • Why it's built this way: every number the game shows (totals, per-activity breakdowns, ranks) is computed server-side and arrives as a DTO, so there is no client-side scoring logic to keep in step with the earn rules. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance]: the leaderboard is opt-in, so publishing a name is an explicit act with its own endpoint rather than a side effect of earning points. See ADR-072 for the surrounding decision.

    SessionFeedbackService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Services.Feedback · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Feedback/SessionFeedbackService.cs:13 · Level 4 · sealed class

    • What it is: the HTTP implementation of ISessionFeedbackUIService, backed by the sessionquestionanswers resource (:18). The session-scoped counterpart of EventFeedbackService, same POST-as-upsert contract (BR-107, class doc :11-12), plus one call its event twin does not have.

    • Concept introduced, the client half of request idempotency. The auth, retry and Result-reading story is taught at BookmarkApiClient (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/BookmarkApiClient.cs:21) and the upsert contract at EventFeedbackService; neither is re-taught. What is new is SubmitAnswersAsync, and specifically where its idempotency key is minted. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether a retry can be taken safely, and the inline comment at :54-57 is the reason it can be: the key is generated once, outside the retried delegate. A key generated inside would differ per attempt, the server could not recognize the retry, and a timed-out submit would re-apply the whole form. Because the HttpClient is created per logical operation and serves every attempt, setting the key as a default request header (:58) makes it ride along unchanged through all three retries. The generator itself is inherited: NewIdempotencyKey() is a compact GUID (AuthenticatedServiceBase.cs:61), and its remarks (:36-41) say the same thing from the framework side. The server end is ADR-017, applied to this route by the [Idempotent] attribute (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Sessions/SessionQuestionAnswersController.cs:301-302).
    • Walkthrough
      • SubmitAnswerAsync (:21-40) POSTs the anonymous { SessionId, QuestionId, AnswerValue } object (:31) to the root resource and reads back the persisted SessionQuestionAnswerDTO (:38). Same shape as its event twin.
      • SubmitAnswersAsync (:43-76) is the batch form. It null-checks the answers list (:50), mints and attaches the idempotency key (:58), projects the tuples into an anonymous { SessionId, Answers = [{ QuestionId, AnswerValue }] } body (:60-64), POSTs to sessionquestionanswers/batch (:68), and Maps the returned List<T> to the interface's IReadOnlyList (:74). The server applies the form atomically, so one Result covers the whole submit.
      • GetMyAnswersAsync (:79-98) reads the caller's answers from the dedicated sessionquestionanswers/mine?sessionId={sessionId} route (:87; server side [HttpGet("mine")] at MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Sessions/SessionQuestionAnswersController.cs:216) and unwraps the envelope (:96).
      • DeleteAnswerAsync (:101-117) DELETEs by answer id with sessionId as a query parameter (:110).
      • All four calls use the retry overload that takes the CancellationToken (:33, :66, :89, :111).
    • Why it's built this way: a session feedback form is several answers a person filled in at once, and half-applying it on a flaky conference wifi connection would be worse than failing outright. The batch endpoint plus the replayed idempotency key is what turns "submit the form" into a single atomic, safely retryable operation.
    • Where it's used: registered scoped as ISessionFeedbackUIService (MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:53); injected by SessionFeedback (SessionFeedback.razor.cs:19), which reads existing answers (:122), submits the whole pending form through the batch call (:226) and deletes single answers (:259). [Rubric §14, Testability]: SessionFeedbackServiceTests covers eleven facts, including that the batch call sends the whole form in one request (:61) and that it carries an Idempotency-Key header (:91), that a domain-exception response becomes a failure carrying the server's own message (:43, :109, :191), that an empty envelope reads as an empty list (:162), and that an already-cancelled token aborts before a request is sent (:209).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: SubmitAnswerAsync (the single-answer form) sends no idempotency key, even though the server route carries [Idempotent] (SessionQuestionAnswersController.cs:274-275). A retried single-answer submit is therefore deduped by the upsert semantics rather than by replay. The read carries no pageSize, same as the event side.

    UserDeletedPointsHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Points.IntegrationEventHandlers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/IntegrationEventHandlers/UserDeletedPointsHandler.cs:38 · Level 8 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the erasure handler for the leaderboard. When Identity deletes an account, this takes the entry off the public board and overwrites the display name it published there. It is the one consumer in this folder that awards nothing.
    • Depends on: ScopedIntegrationEventHandlerBase<TIntegrationEvent> closed over Identity's UserDeleted (:40), IUnitOfWork (:50), the IRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType> it obtains for LeaderboardOptIn (:51) and that aggregate's own Delete() / EraseDisplayName() members (:69, :81). Externals: IServiceScopeFactory, source-generated [LoggerMessage] (:96-103).
    • Concept introduced, cross-database erasure by event. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance] assesses whether a deletion promise actually reaches every copy of the data. Under database-per-service (ADR-006) Identity cannot delete a row in the Engagement database, so an erasure has to travel as an event and be carried out by the owning service. The class comment (:13-21) names the exact scope: the leaderboard is the one place Engagement holds a name rather than a scalar id, LeaderboardOptIn.DisplayName is a snapshot the attendee published at opt-in, and without this handler that name would keep sitting in the table after the account was erased. It also names what is deliberately left alone: the points ledger, because a PointsEntry carries a scalar user id and an opaque subject key and names nobody, the same posture already applied to session bookmarks. That is the ADR-005 distinction between soft-delete for lifecycle and erasure for personal data, applied per column rather than per table. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] covers the retry posture stated at :26-27: exceptions are deliberately not caught, so a failure is logged once by the base and then propagates, and the outbox and the broker retry it rather than acking it away with a log line (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DomainEvents/ScopedIntegrationEventHandlerBase.cs:26-33). The award adapters share that exception posture, because they share the base; what differs is what they do with a rejected award, which they log and move past, whereas this handler has no such branch: a missed point is a nuisance, a missed erasure is a broken promise.
    • Walkthrough
      • HandleScopedAsync (:43-46) is the override; the base has null-guarded the event and opened the per-delivery scope. The body takes the user id (:48), then reaches the scoped IUnitOfWork (:50) and a tracked repository for LeaderboardOptIn (:51) out of the supplied provider.
      • The read (:56-61) is the subtle line. It passes asTracking: true (mutations follow) and ignoreQueryFilters: true, and the comment (:53-55) explains that the flag is load-bearing here for the opposite reason it is used on the join path: an attendee who left the board earlier still has a soft-deleted row carrying the published name, and a filtered read would walk straight past the very row that has to be erased.
      • The loop (:65-84) does two independent things per row. If the row is not already deleted it calls Delete() and, on failure, logs and moves to the next row rather than aborting the batch (:67-77). If the display name is not already erased it calls EraseDisplayName() (:79-83). Either action sets changed.
      • When nothing changed the handler logs and returns without a save (:86-90); otherwise it saves once for the whole batch and logs the row count (:92-93).
    • Why it's built this way: the two-flag loop is what makes the handler idempotent in both directions (:22-25): an account that never joined the board has no row and writes nothing, and an account already off the board with an erased name reaches the same end state and writes nothing again. At-least-once delivery makes redelivery normal, so that property is a requirement rather than a nicety.
    • Where it's used: registered as a singleton by the convention scan (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:94, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:58-63), with the consumer wired at MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/EngagementBrokerConsumers.cs:29; the host's composition comment (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:201-205) records that this is the one consumer here that earns nothing. Covered by UserDeletedPointsHandlerTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the privacy commitment the comment cites (PRIVACY.md section 5) lives in the ADC repo's private docs, not in this file. What EraseDisplayName() writes in place of the name is defined on LeaderboardOptIn.

    • Why it's built this way: this handler is where the module's most interesting delivery property lives. The event is published by the same service that consumes it, so the check-in write and the award are two separate transactions joined by the broker (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:207-214). That keeps the scan endpoint's latency independent of the points write and lets the award retry on its own. The same comment records the fallback if a deployment ever has trouble with the round trip (:215-217): the award could move to an in-module domain event handler on the same CheckIn creation, which is a one-file change because the module already awards session-question points that way, through SessionQuestionSubmittedPointsHandler.
    • Where it's used: registered as a singleton by the convention scan (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:94, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:58-63), which is why the base opens a scope per delivery (:23-27); the consumer is wired at MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/EngagementBrokerConsumers.cs:26. Covered by AttendeeCheckedInPointsHandlerTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: how many points each activity is worth, and whether a rule is switched off, is decided inside PointsAwarder from configuration, not here.

    MyPoints

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Pages.Points · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Pages/Points/MyPoints.razor.cs:16 · Level 5 · class (partial)

    • What it is: the code-behind for the attendee's own points page (@page "/points", MyPoints.razor:1, @attribute [Authorize], MyPoints.razor:2). It shows the running total, the ledger entries behind it, the leaderboard opt-in switch, and the public board.
    • Depends on: IPointsUIService (MyPoints.razor.cs:28), ViewerTimeZone (:29), Result (the load method's own return type, :95, and the parameter of SaveErrorMessage, :180), PointsEntryDTO (:48), LeaderboardEntryDTO (:49), MyPointsDTO (read at :97-105) and PointsActivityType (:192). Externals: Blazor ComponentBase, MudBlazor BreadcrumbItem / Icons / MudSwitch, and an injected IStringLocalizer<MyPoints> named L from the markup (MyPoints.razor:6).
    • Concept introduced, making a stateful child control follow the server. [Rubric §19, State Management] assesses who owns a visible piece of state. A MudSwitch keeps its own checked state, and Blazor re-parameterizes a child only when a parameter actually changes, so after a rejected write the control would keep showing what the attendee clicked while the page holds what the server accepted. The page solves it with a render key: _switchGeneration (:55) is bound as @key on the switch (MyPoints.razor:74) and incremented whenever the server's value disagrees with the requested one (:167-170), which re-mounts the control and forces it to drop its internal state. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] covers the second decision in the same method: a failed write and a failed read-back are reported differently (:133-136), because conflating them made a refresh blip force the switch back to the pre-write value and show the opposite of the server state. A third decision sits on the failed-write branch: SaveErrorMessage (:180-183) looks for the one refusal the attendee can fix, the error code Points.DisplayNameUnavailable (DisplayNameUnavailableCode, :26, raised for a caller with no display name on their token), and answers it with its own localized advice (Error.DisplayNameUnavailable); every other failure keeps the generic Error.SaveFailed, so the server's diagnostic text is never surfaced (:173-179). [Rubric §27, Internationalization] covers both the L["..."] resource lookups and the culture-aware timestamp rendering (ADR-027).
    • Concept introduced, a page that reads failures instead of catching them. [Rubric §1, SOLID] and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] both show in one detail: LoadAsync returns Result (:95) rather than throwing, and it composes the two service calls by propagating their errors (:98-101, :108-111). The only exception the page catches is OperationCanceledException on disposal (:81-84, :153-156), so the error state is driven by a value the UI service returned, not by an exception type the page has to recognize. SaveErrorMessage follows the same rule: it branches on the Code of the returned errors, not on an exception type.
    • Walkthrough (teaching order)
      • EntryPageSize (:19) fixes the activity feed at 20 entries per read; DisplayNameUnavailableCode (:26) names the one refusal code the page recognizes; the injected IPointsUIService (:28) and ViewerTimeZone (:29), a CancellationTokenSource (:31) and the breadcrumb list (:38) follow. LifetimeToken (:36) wraps _cts.LifetimeToken(): reading Token off a disposed source throws ObjectDisposedException, and Dispose cancels before it disposes, so a load or handler that resumes after the attendee navigated away gets a cancelled token and stops through its OperationCanceledException path (comment :33-35). Every service call below passes LifetimeToken rather than _cts.Token. IsLoading is protected with a private setter (:41) so component tests can observe the first load.
      • The private state (:43-49) is a load error, a save error, an in-flight save latch, the total, the opt-in flag, the entries and the board. _switchGeneration (:55) is the render key described above.
      • OnInitializedAsync (:57) is not async: it builds the two-item breadcrumb trail (:59-63) and returns the task of LoadPageAsync (:65).
      • LoadPageAsync (:69) is the whole load cycle and, per its doc comment (:68), also the Retry action: the markup's error alert binds it as OnRetry (MyPoints.razor:21). It sets IsLoading and clears the previous load error first (:71-72), so a retry starts from the loading state rather than leaving the old error on screen, then awaits LoadAsync and sets the localized load error when it comes back a failure (:76-79), swallows OperationCanceledException as expected on disposal (:81-84), and clears IsLoading in finally (:85-88).
      • LoadAsync (:95) makes two calls: the caller's ledger (:97) and the public board (:107). Each is unwrapped with TryGetValue and short-circuits into Result.Failure carrying the service's own errors (:98-101, :108-111). Both are re-read after an opt-in change, because joining adds a row to the board and leaving removes one (:91-94).
      • OnParticipationChangedAsync (:123) returns early when a save is already in flight (:125-128), latches _isSaving and clears the previous save error (:130-131), then writes through SetLeaderboardParticipationAsync (:139). A failed write sets the message chosen by SaveErrorMessage(write) (:140-143); a successful write followed by a failed refresh sets the refresh-failed message instead and adopts the requested value locally (:144-151) so the key guard below does not re-mount the switch back onto a stale reading.
      • SaveErrorMessage (:180-183) is an expression-bodied method that tests write.Errors.Any(...) for an error whose Code equals DisplayNameUnavailableCode under StringComparison.Ordinal, returning the display-name advice when it matches and the generic save message otherwise.
      • ActivityLabel (:192-202) maps each PointsActivityType member to a resource key by an explicit switch rather than by enum name, so a renamed member breaks the build instead of silently rendering a missing key (:185-191).
      • OnAfterRenderAsync (:209-215) calls ViewerTime.EnsureResolvedAsync(LifetimeToken) on the first render only, once JS is available, and calls StateHasChanged when the zone changed, so award times move from the UTC fallback to the viewer's clock.
      • FormatOccurredOn (:225-226) delegates to ViewerTime.Format. The comment (:217-222) gives the reason: ViewerTimeZone.Format reads an Unspecified value as UTC, so a serializer that drops the UTC marker cannot shift the reading, whereas DateTime.ToLocalTime would use the server's clock on Blazor Server and during prerender.
      • Dispose(bool) / Dispose() (:230-250) are the standard disposable pattern with a _disposed latch, cancelling and disposing _cts so an in-flight load stops when the attendee navigates away.
    • Why it's built this way: the page makes one promise, that the switch shows the server's state and not the click's, and both the key bump and the split error messages exist to keep it. Everything else is orchestration only: all I/O goes through IPointsUIService, which keeps the page testable under bUnit and swappable per host.
    • Where it's used: routed at /points, the value of EngagementRoutePaths.MyPoints (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/EngagementRoutePaths.cs:26). Component-tested by MyPointsTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the tables, the empty states and every visible string live in MyPoints.razor and the resource files. Whether the page is reachable at all depends on the Engagement.Points feature gate on PointsController, which is configuration. The refusal code is raised by SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler (named in the DisplayNameUnavailableCode comment, :23); the page only recognizes the code string.

    BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessor

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Caching · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Caching/BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessor.cs:35 · Level 4 · sealed class

    • What it is: a BackgroundService that turns "a bookmark changed" into at most one cross-service cache eviction every ten seconds per replica. It drains the capacity-one flag held by BookmarkCacheEvictionSignal and publishes an OutputCacheEvictionRequested for the Conference session tag, so Conference's cached session reads and batched star counts stop serving stale numbers.
    • Depends on: BookmarkCacheEvictionSignal (:36), UserSessionBookmarkCacheEvictionHandler for the SessionsCacheTag constant (:73), BestEffort (:62). Externals: BackgroundService, IServiceScopeFactory, TimeProvider, ILogger, IEventBus, OutputCacheEvictionRequested.
    • Concept introduced, coalescing with a flag and a pacing delay. [Rubric §10, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether a hot write path can hammer a shared cache. Two pieces cooperate. The signal is a Channel<bool> bounded at one with BoundedChannelFullMode.DropWrite (BookmarkCacheEvictionSignal.cs:27-33), so any number of Request() calls made while one is pending collapse into that one (:42). The processor then sleeps PacingWindow (ten seconds, :46) after each broadcast (:79). Together the pacing, not the bookmark rate, sets the eviction rate: at a session changeover hundreds of attendees star sessions in the same minute, and an eviction per star would keep the session cache permanently cold and send every read to Conference's database (the signal's remarks, BookmarkCacheEvictionSignal.cs:11-18). The pacing window is worst-case six evictions a minute per replica (doc comment :41-45).
    • Walkthrough
      • ExecuteAsync (:52) loops on signal.Reader.WaitToReadAsync and does a single TryRead to empty the flag (:60), so anything raised after that read is the next broadcast's business.
      • The publish runs inside BestEffort.ExecuteAsync (:62) under the operation name "bookmark-cache-evict-broadcast" (:49). It opens a fresh async scope (:67), resolves IEventBus (:68) and publishes OutputCacheEvictionRequested with Tags = [UserSessionBookmarkCacheEvictionHandler.SessionsCacheTag] (:70-75). A failed publish is a Warning plus a metric, never an exception out of the loop.
      • Task.Delay(PacingWindow, timeProvider, stoppingToken) (:79) takes the injected TimeProvider, so tests drive the pacing with a fake clock rather than waiting ten real seconds.
      • An OperationCanceledException raised while the host is stopping is caught and ends the loop (:82); a request still pending at that moment is covered by Conference's TTL backstop (comment :84).
    • Why it's built this way: the eviction is a convenience over a TTL, not a correctness mechanism, so it is best effort and never blocks or fails the bookmark command that raised it (the signal's Request never blocks or fails, BookmarkCacheEvictionSignal.cs:21-22). The processor is a long-lived singleton, so it opens a scope per publish rather than holding a scoped bus. The wider caching story is ADR-040, the helper is ADR-096 and the in-process work-queue shape is ADR-121.
    • Where it's used: raised through the signal by UserSessionBookmarkCacheEvictionHandler; the signal and processor are registered in the module's Application and Infrastructure DependencyInjection.cs, and the Conference service host references it (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs). Covered by BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessorTests (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Tests/Caching/BookmarkCacheEvictionProcessorTests.cs).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: one flag per replica, so with several Engagement replicas each broadcasts independently; the code does not dedupe across replicas. The Conference-side TTL value is not defined in this file.

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Tickets.UseCases.ExpireRosterImport · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Tickets/UseCases/ExpireRosterImport/ExpireTicketRosterImportInternalCommand.cs:14 · Level 4 · record (public sealed)

    • What it is: the delayed privacy backstop of one roster import run. A durable internal command whose whole payload is the run id (:14), handled by ExpireTicketRosterImportHandler.

The doc comment (:5-11) states the contract: the command is scheduled in the same transaction as the run and falls due TicketImportRun.AbandonAfter later, which is 30 minutes (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/Tickets/TicketImportRun.cs:37). The doc cites ADR-005 (erasure) and ADR-114 (the durable internal-command queue).

Named in MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/CommandValidatorCoverageTests.cs and exercised by ExpireTicketRosterImportHandlerTests and StartTicketRosterImportHandlerTests.

DryRunRosterAsync (:33) reports the counts the commit would produce and writes nothing (:22-24); StartRosterImportAsync (:48) then commits the reviewed file as a background run and answers the queued run, with a conflict when the event's previous run is still active (:39-42).     ProcessTicketRosterImportInternalCommand

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Tickets.UseCases.ProcessRosterImport · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Tickets/UseCases/ProcessRosterImport/ProcessTicketRosterImportInternalCommand.cs:21 · Level 4 · record (public sealed)

    • What it is: the durable trigger that applies one committed roster import run in batches (:6-11). Like its sibling ExpireTicketRosterImportInternalCommand, the payload is the run id only (:21).
    • Depends on: IInternalCommand and IHasTimeout (:1-2, :22); InternalCommandNameAttribute naming it Engagement.ProcessTicketRosterImport.v1 (:20).
    • Concept introduced, the markers a background command leaves off. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses how commands opt into pipeline behavior; here the omissions are the design, and the remarks (:12-18) justify each. It is neither IRequiresPermission nor IFeatureGated: the organizer's permission and the feature flag were checked when the run started, and a refusal at this point would retry into a dead letter with the staged roster still on the run. It is not ITransactional either: each batch commits on its own so the processed count other replicas read moves as the run goes (ADR-107). [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance]: the holder data stays on the run, where every ending of the run clears it, so the internal-command row, kept for the queue's retention window, never holds a name or an address (:7-10).
    • Walkthrough: the positional RunId (:21) and one member, Timeout => TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10) (:28), the per-attempt execution budget. Its doc (:24-27) ties it to the backstop: ten minutes sits well under TicketImportRun.AbandonAfter (30 minutes, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/Tickets/TicketImportRun.cs:37), so the expiry never fires on a run that is still applying batches.
    • Why it's built this way: the queue is ADR-114's durable internal-command store, so an upload survives a restart between the commit and the processing.
    • Where it's used: scheduled with no delay by StartTicketRosterImportHandler (StartTicketRosterImportHandler.cs:115-117) and handled by ProcessTicketRosterImportHandler. The host comments in MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:168-177 and MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Service/Program.cs:340 name it as the reason the verified-user lookup edge must accept a service token: the import runs with no HttpContext, so there is no organizer bearer to forward.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the retry count and back-off between attempts belong to the internal-command processor's configuration, not to this record.

Externals: IHttpClientFactory, MultipartFormDataContent, ReadOnlyMemoryContent, MediaTypeHeaderValue.

The remarks (:20-24) state the rule: the four writes the API marks [Idempotent] (roster upload, invites, link-existing, claim) carry one Idempotency-Key per logical operation, added to the client's default headers before RetryPolicy.ExecuteAsync runs (:77, :113, :132, :234), so every attempt states the same key and a retried send replays the first answer instead of running twice. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] covers the upload: retrying a multipart post is normally unsafe because a stream is consumed, but the bytes are already in memory (at most TicketRosterLimits.MaxFileBytes, checked by the page), so each attempt builds a fresh form over them (:79-81, :87-94).

The comment (:85-86) records why the names matter: they bind to the controller's IFormFile parameter and two [FromForm] arguments, and a renamed part binds to its default and fails validation.

The in-process BookmarkCountService and this remote adapter implement the same interface, so a consumer swaps transport by swapping one DI registration and never edits a call site (ADR-007, ADR-008). Watch the name overlap: the generated proto service type is also called BookmarkCountService (in ...Contracts.V1), and this adapter's primary constructor takes its nested BookmarkCountServiceClient (:14-15); that generated type is distinct from the Application-layer class of the same name.

CallDeadline is a static TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5) (:20) applied to both calls (:32, :48), and the comment (:17-19) explains the reasoning: the shared resilience pipeline's 30s attempt / 90s total budget answers a refused peer well, but a hung peer would otherwise stall a caller's request, and bookmark counts sit inline in speaker-dashboard responses. A deadline turns "hung" into a fast DeadlineExceeded status the caller's Polly pipeline can act on.

      • GetBookmarkCountForSessionAsync(sessionId, cancellationToken) (:23-36): builds a GetBookmarkCountForSessionRequest { SessionId = sessionId } (:28-31), passes deadline: DateTime.UtcNow.Add(CallDeadline) plus the caller's token (:32-33), and returns response.Count (:35). The interface returns a plain int, not a Result<int>, so there is no failure trailer to parse: a transport fault surfaces as an RpcException.
      • GetBookmarkCountsForSessionsAsync(sessionIds, cancellationToken) (:39-52): the batch form. It fills the repeated SessionIds field with AddRange (:43-44), sends the same deadline (:48), and rebuilds a dictionary from the repeated response pairs with response.Counts.ToDictionary(c => c.SessionId, c => c.Count) (:51). This is the N+1 avoidance for a speaker dashboard listing many sessions: one round trip instead of one per session.

    ProcessTicketRosterImportHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Tickets.UseCases.ProcessRosterImport · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Tickets/UseCases/ProcessRosterImport/ProcessTicketRosterImportHandler.cs:29 · Level 11 · class (public sealed partial)

    • What it is: the handler for ProcessTicketRosterImportInternalCommand. It applies a committed run's staged roster to the event's tickets in batches, voids the tickets the file no longer lists, links tickets to existing confirmed accounts, and completes the run; any fault ends the run as failed.
    • Depends on: ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> (:34), IUnitOfWork (:30), IVerifiedUserLookupService (:32), TicketImportRun, Ticket, TicketRosterStaging, TicketRosterApplier, TicketRosterCounts, ExistingAccountLinker, TicketRosterImportErrorCodes and Result. Externals: IServiceScopeFactory, TimeProvider, ILogger<T> with [LoggerMessage].
    • Concept introduced, resumable batches with committed progress. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether long work survives a crash midway. Each pass of the loop takes roster.Entries.Skip(run.Processed).Take(BatchSize) (:116), applies it, then records the batch on the run and saves (:122-123), so the run's Processed count and the tickets it describes commit together. An OperationCanceledException (host shutdown or the attempt's timeout) is rethrown (:74-78) and the retry resumes at the committed progress. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture]: barcodes the file moves between its own tickets are parked first, in their own save, so no batch ever holds one barcode twice whichever batches the two tickets fall in (:107-111). The load reads every ticket of the event with ignoreQueryFilters: true (:99-104), so filtered rows are in the set the applier compares against.
    • Concept introduced, failing the run on a clean context. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]. The catch-all (:80) carries a scoped CA1031 suppression whose justification is on the pragma itself (:79): any fault fails the run in a fresh scope, is logged, and the handler returns success so the queue does not retry a run already marked failed. FailInFreshScopeAsync (:145-159) creates a new scope (:147), reloads the run there, fails it and saves, because the original context may still hold the change set that faulted (doc :144). A failed Result from ApplyAsync takes the same path with its first error code (:68-72). [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance]: a redelivery after the run ended applies nothing, but if a staged roster is somehow still present it is anonymized and saved anyway (:53-64), so the guarantee that a finished run holds no file data is unconditional.
    • Walkthrough
      • BatchSize = 100 (:37) and FailedCode = TicketRosterImportErrorCodes.Failed (:40) are public constants.
      • HandleAsync (:43-88) loads the run tracked (:49-52), handles the ended-run redelivery (:53-64), then runs ApplyAsync inside the try (:66-85).
      • ApplyAsync (:90-142) deserializes the staged roster and fails with Ticket.Import.StagingUnreadable when it cannot (:92-96), builds a TicketRosterApplier over the loaded tickets (:105), parks swapped barcodes (:109-111), loops the batches with addNew: true (:114-124), saves the voids from VoidMissing (:126-127), calls ExistingAccountLinker.LinkEventAsync (:129-135), and completes the run with the voided count and the linked count, which is 0 when the link step failed (:137-138). A lookup failure therefore never fails the upload, matching the host comment at MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:168-177.
      • Three [LoggerMessage] methods (:161-168): Information on completion with the counts, Error with the exception on a fault, Warning when a run ends as failed.
    • Why it's built this way: the command is deliberately not transactional (see its section), so this handler owns its commit points; the durable queue is ADR-114 and the per-handler transaction contract is ADR-107.
    • Where it's used: dispatched by InternalCommandProcessor for the row StartTicketRosterImportHandler schedules (StartTicketRosterImportHandler.cs:115-117). Its progress is what GetTicketRosterImportHandler answers and TicketRosterUpload polls through TicketService.GetRosterImportAsync. Covered by ProcessTicketRosterImportHandlerTests.

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Contracts · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Contracts · MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Contracts/UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapter.cs:20 · Level 12 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the client-side gRPC adapter for the data-subject export, the remote twin of the in-process UserEngagementExportService. It implements IUserEngagementExportService on top of the generated export client and is what Identity resolves.
    • Depends on: IUserEngagementExportService and its DTOs from MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared.Exports (including UserEngagementTicketExportDTO), plus CheckInScope, PointsActivityType and TicketLinkMethod from the module's Shared project (:3-6); the generated UserEngagementExportService.UserEngagementExportServiceClient and its messages (:2); the framework's GrpcWireFormat (:7). Externals: System.Globalization (:1), the Grpc.Net client factory.
    • Concept, the same-interface transport swap plus wire rehydration. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness], [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]. This is the export sibling of BookmarkCountServiceGrpcAdapter: the same interface as the in-process implementation, so consumers swap one DI registration (ADR-007). It also owns the inverse of every encoding decision the server made, and each inverse is written next to the decision it undoes.
    • Concept, parsing defensively across a rolling deploy. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]. The five DateTime fields are read with GrpcWireFormat.ParseUtc (:46, :53, :62, :80, :85), which parses with DateTimeStyles.AssumeUniversal | DateTimeStyles.AdjustToUniversal (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.Grpc/GrpcWireFormat.cs:37, :61-62) so that a peer replica still emitting the marker-less form (new Identity code running against an old Engagement replica during a rolling deploy) does not yield Kind=Unspecified, and AssumeUniversal alone would yield Kind=Local. The comment there (GrpcWireFormat.cs:32-36) also records why RoundtripKind is deliberately absent: DateTime.Parse rejects it alongside either Assume* or AdjustToUniversal with an ArgumentException, and its purpose (preserving a non-UTC kind) is the opposite of what this contract wants. The one parser in this file, ParseRoundtripOffset (:119-123), keeps the offset the server emitted rather than folding it into UTC, with AssumeUniversal covering an offset-less value from an old peer (:116-118). It reads the three DateTimeOffset fields: CheckedInOn (:74) and the ticket's InvitedOn and LinkedOn (:98, :103).
    • Walkthrough
      • CallDeadline (:26), a 5-second static, applied at :38. The comment (:23-25) gives the same reasoning as the bookmark adapter with an export-specific twist: the aggregation is best-effort per section, so a hung peer should degrade its section quickly rather than stall the export request.
      • GetUserEngagementExportAsync(userId, cancellationToken) (:29-114): sends a GetUserEngagementExportRequest { UserId = userId } with the deadline and the caller's token (:33-39), then rebuilds UserEngagementExportDTO from the seven repeated fields with collection expressions: bookmarks (:43-47), submitted questions (:48-54, including the question Text at :52), points entries (:55-63, casting the numeric ActivityType back to its enum at :59), check-ins (:64-75, casting Scope back at :68, mapping a 0 SessionId/SponsorId back to null at :72-73, and parsing CheckedInOn as a DateTimeOffset at :74), poll votes (:76-81, into UserEngagementPollVoteExportDTO), question upvotes (:82-86, into UserEngagementQuestionUpvoteExportDTO) and tickets (:87-104, into UserEngagementTicketExportDTO). The ticket mapping copies six string fields (:89-94), maps an empty OrderEmail and an empty InvitedOn back to null (:97-98, comment :96), and casts the numeric LinkMethod back to TicketLinkMethod (:102), lossless because those values are persisted and never renumbered (:100-101). Finally IsOnLeaderboard (:105) and the empty-string-to-null mapping for LeaderboardDisplayName (:110-112), whose comment (:107-109) notes the same mapping also covers an old peer that never sets the field at all.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc (:11-19) states the resilience posture, transport failures propagate to the caller (Identity's ExportUserDataHandler), which degrades the Engagement section to Available = false rather than failing the whole export. Best-effort cross-service aggregation: a peer outage never sinks an entire data-subject export. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance].
    • Where it's used: registered by DependencyInjection.AddEngagementUserExportClient(), called from MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Service/Program.cs:304. Covered by MMCA.ADC/Tests/Services/MMCA.ADC.Services.Tests/Exports/UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapterTests.cs.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the comment above ParseRoundtripOffset (:116-117) still calls check-in timestamps "the one DateTimeOffset on this contract", while the ticket fields at :98 and :103 now go through the same parser; the code is consistent, only that comment is narrower than the usage.

    DependencyInjection

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Contracts · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Contracts · MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Contracts/DependencyInjection.cs:19 · Level 13 · class (public static)

    • What it is: the Engagement *.Contracts DI facade (one of several DependencyInjection classes in this module; this is the extraction-wiring one). Three C# extension(IServiceCollection) members a consuming host calls to swap Engagement's in-process cross-module registrations for their gRPC-backed adapters: bookmark counts for Conference, and the data-subject export and the pending ticket invitation lookup for Identity (class doc :12-18).

    • Depends on: the generated BookmarkCountServiceClient / UserEngagementExportServiceClient / TicketInvitationServiceClient (:3), BookmarkCountServiceGrpcAdapter, UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapter, TicketInvitationServiceGrpcAdapter, IBookmarkCountService, IUserEngagementExportService, IPendingTicketInvitationService (:4-6), AddTypedGrpcClient<TClient> from MMCA.Common.Grpc (:7, defined at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.Grpc/DependencyInjection.cs:99) and WithServiceToken() from MMCA.Common.Grpc.Authentication (:8, defined at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.Grpc/Authentication/ServiceTokenHttpClientBuilderExtensions.cs:28). Externals: Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection and its ServiceCollectionDescriptorExtensions.Replace (:1-2).

    • Concept, the adapter-swap wiring lives in the contracts package. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness], [Rubric §17, DevOps & Deployment], [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]. ADR-007 requires each extracted service to publish a *.Contracts project holding the proto definitions and the DI wiring, so a consumer depends on that thin package rather than on the full module. The C# extension(IServiceCollection services) block (:21) adds the methods directly onto the collection (see primer §4).

    • Concept, Replace rather than TryAdd. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns]. Every method does the same two things: register a typed client, then replace one interface binding.

      Method File:Line What it swaps
      AddEngagementBookmarkCountClient(serviceName = "engagement") DependencyInjection.cs:46-55 registers BookmarkCountServiceClient (:48), then services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IBookmarkCountService, BookmarkCountServiceGrpcAdapter>()) (:52)
      AddEngagementUserExportClient(serviceName = "engagement") DependencyInjection.cs:79-88 registers UserEngagementExportServiceClient (:81), then services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IUserEngagementExportService, UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapter>()) (:85)
      AddEngagementTicketInvitationClient(serviceName = "engagement") DependencyInjection.cs:108-117 registers TicketInvitationServiceClient with .WithServiceToken() (:110), then services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IPendingTicketInvitationService, TicketInvitationServiceGrpcAdapter>()) (:114)

      At the moment of the call the container already holds some binding for the interface: either the real in-process implementation (when the Engagement module is enabled in that host) or the disabled stub (DisabledBookmarkCountService / DisabledUserEngagementExportService / DisabledPendingTicketInvitationService, registered by EngagementModule.RegisterDisabledStubs, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/EngagementModule.cs:31-35). TryAdd would silently lose to it; Replace guarantees the gRPC adapter wins either way, which the inline comments state at :50-51, :83-84 and :112-113.

    • Concept, one client that presents its own identity. [Rubric §11, Security]. The first two clients forward the caller's bearer; the ticket-invitation client cannot, because the Identity request it serves is anonymous. Its doc (:95-100) says the server maps the edge under the service-only ServiceCaller policy, so the client opts in to the service token with WithServiceToken(), and the calling host must register AddServiceTokenClient.

    • Walkthrough: AddTypedGrpcClient<T> is what makes each method two lines instead of twenty, it wires the client to Aspire service discovery (http://{serviceName}), the JwtForwardingClientInterceptor and the Polly resilience handler, all from MMCA.Common.Grpc (documented at :26-28 and :60-62). All three methods return IServiceCollection for chaining (:54, :87, :116).

    • Why it's built this way: the default serviceName = "engagement" matches the AppHost resource name, so the common call site is argument-free. [Rubric §33, Developer Experience]. The XML docs on all three methods (:38-42, :70-75, :101-104) spell out the one ordering requirement: call them after ModuleLoader.DiscoverAndRegister(...), so the in-process or stub registration is already in the container for Replace to find. That is an ordering constraint the compiler cannot enforce, which is why every method repeats it. The hosts meet it by registering each client in their ConfigurePipeline after .Register(moduleHost.RegisterModules).

    • Where it's used: MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:359 registers AddEngagementBookmarkCountClient() (after the module step at :358); MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Service/Program.cs:304 and :307 register AddEngagementUserExportClient() and AddEngagementTicketInvitationClient() (after :303), with the service-token rationale in the comment at :281-287. The AppHost documents the edges of the resulting topology, including why the Conference-to-Engagement reverse edge gets no reciprocal WaitFor (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosting/MMCA.ADC.AppHost/Program.cs:274-276, against the Engagement-to-Conference edge at :269), and the Identity-to-Engagement edge at :285-294.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: no method sets a per-call deadline; the 5-second budgets live in the three adapters themselves (BookmarkCountServiceGrpcAdapter.cs:20, UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapter.cs:26, TicketInvitationServiceGrpcAdapter.cs:20), so a host that registered a different implementation of the same interfaces would not inherit them.

[Rubric §4, DDD] assesses whether invariants are stated where the model can enforce them: keeping them in a static class that the factory composes means each rule is individually named, individually testable, and reusable by any future mutator on the same aggregate.
    • Walkthrough: one method. EnsureUserIdIsValid(userId, source) (:15-16) delegates to CommonInvariants.EnsureIdIsNotDefault with the stable error code "AttendeeBadge.UserId.Invalid", the message, the calling member name for attribution, and nameof(userId) as the target.     CheckInInvariants

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain.CheckIns · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/CheckIns/CheckInInvariants.cs:10 · Level 6 · class (static)

    • What it is: the five invariant rules for CheckIn. Four are simple id and enum checks; the fifth encodes the rule that makes one aggregate able to carry three different check-in shapes.
    • Depends on: CommonInvariants (EnsureIdIsNotDefault at CheckInInvariants.cs:17, :24, :31, and EnsureEnumIsDefined at :102), Result and Error (Error.Invariant at :88 and :93), plus CheckInScope (:45) and the UserIdentifierType / EventIdentifierType / SessionIdentifierType / SponsorIdentifierType aliases (solution-wide global using, see primer §2). No externals beyond the BCL.
    • Concept introduced, the discriminated-shape invariant. [Rubric §4, Domain-Driven Design] assesses whether the model can express an illegal state. This aggregate is a polymorphic row: a Session check-in must name a session and must not name a sponsor, a Sponsor visit is the mirror image, and an Event check-in names neither. EnsureTargetMatchesScope states that rule once, in the domain, so no handler and no controller can persist a row that belongs to two shapes at once (:33-38). [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] is the reason it matters beyond tidiness: the storage layer builds three filtered unique indexes on the same table, one per scope (CheckInConfiguration, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/CheckIns/CheckInConfiguration.cs:49-63), and a row with two targets set would be visible to two of them. The invariant and the index filters are two statements of one rule, which the doc comment names explicitly (:34-36).
    • Walkthrough (teaching order)
      • EnsureUserIdIsValid (:16-17), EnsureEventIdIsValid (:23-24) and EnsureCheckedInByUserIdIsValid (:30-31) are three CommonInvariants.EnsureIdIsNotDefault delegations with stable codes ("CheckIn.UserId.Invalid", "CheckIn.EventId.Invalid", "CheckIn.CheckedInByUserId.Invalid"). The event id is required for every scope (:19), which is what lets the attendance rollup bucket any row by conference. The recorder is whoever wrote the row: an organizer for a scan or manual check-in, the attendee for a self-recorded visit (:27).
      • EnsureTargetMatchesScope (:44-71) runs the session check first (:50-58) and returns it when it fails (:60-61), otherwise runs the sponsor check (:62-70), so the caller gets the first specific failure rather than a merged pair.
      • EnsureTargetPresence (:75-95) is the private rule stated once. isOwningScope decides the direction: the owning scope requires the id and treats null or default as missing (:85-90), and every other scope forbids it outright (:92-94). The comment above it (:73-74) records why one method serves both targets: both are int aliases, so the parameter is typed int?.
      • EnsureScopeIsDefined (:101-102) delegates to CommonInvariants.EnsureEnumIsDefined with the code "CheckIn.Scope.Invalid", which matters because a scope can arrive from a deserialized request rather than from C# code.
    • Why it's built this way: pushing the shape rule into the domain rather than into each use case means the three write paths (organizer scan, sponsor visit, room check-in) cannot drift apart, and the separate error codes make a failure legible at the API boundary without a message-parse.
    • Where it's used: composed with Result.Combine inside CheckIn.Create (CheckIn.cs:98-103); that factory is the only caller.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: EnsureTargetPresence treats a supplied-but-default id as missing only for the owning scope (:87); a non-owning scope rejects any non-null value, default included (:92).

    ErasedUser

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain.ErasedUsers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/ErasedUsers/ErasedUser.cs:20 · Level 6 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the aggregate root that records one erased account in the Engagement database: the erased user's id and when Identity erased it (ErasedUser.cs:23, :26). It holds no personal data, only the fact of erasure, so write handlers can ask "has this account been erased?" without reaching across a service boundary.
    • Depends on: AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> (bound to ErasedUserIdentifierType, :20), UserIdentifierType, CommonInvariants.EnsureIdIsNotDefault (:43-44) and Result. Externals: only System.DateTimeOffset.
    • Concept introduced, a tombstone that closes the erasure gap. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance] assesses whether erasure actually holds. An access token outlives the account it was issued for, and the per-feature erasure handlers only reach rows that exist when they run, so a question, vote, bookmark, badge, room check-in or sponsor visit written afterwards would carry an erased user id that no erasure revisits. The ErasedUser row is the answer: the erasure writes it once (UserDeletedSessionQuestionsHandler.cs:101-108, a no-op when a row for that user already exists) and every Engagement write handler keyed to the caller checks it through ErasedUserGuard (ErasedUserGuard.cs:26-43), which refuses with a Forbidden error coded Engagement.AccountErased (ErasedUserGuard.cs:18). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] is the other half: Identity owns the account, so Engagement keeps its own scalar copy of the id rather than a cross-database reference (ADR-005).
    • Walkthrough
      • UserId (:23) and ErasedOn (:26): private set scalars; ErasedOn is the time Identity erased the account, taken from the UserDeleted event, not the time Engagement processed it (:39).
      • Two constructors, an EF-only parameterless one (:29) and a private assigning one (:31-35). Construction always runs through the factory.
      • Create(userId, erasedOn) (:41-49): validates the id with CommonInvariants.EnsureIdIsNotDefault under the code Engagement.ErasedUser.UserIdInvalid (:43-44), re-wraps a failure as Result.Failure<ErasedUser> (:45-46), and otherwise builds the entity with Id = default (:48) so the database generates the key. No domain event is raised: nothing downstream subscribes to an erasure record being written.
    • Why it's built this way: the persistence side pins uniqueness, one row per erased account, with a unique index on UserId (ErasedUserConfiguration.cs:29-30, ErasedUserConfiguration), so a redelivered UserDeleted event cannot create a second record. The identifier alias follows the module convention (ADR-085).
    • Where it's used: created by UserDeletedSessionQuestionsHandler (UserDeletedSessionQuestionsHandler.cs:108); read by ErasedUserGuard; persisted by ErasedUserConfiguration and the AddErasedUsers migration (20261020142915_AddErasedUsers.cs); mapped into the Engagement database through the shared per-engine SQLServerDbContext, since ErasedUserConfiguration derives from EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<ErasedUser, ErasedUserIdentifierType> (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/ErasedUsers/ErasedUserConfiguration.cs:15-16). Unit-tested by ErasedUserTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: which handlers run the guard is spread across the write handlers and is not enumerated here; the class comment on ErasedUserGuard (:7-14) lists the write kinds it covers. The L207 marker in those comments is a backlog reference whose text is not in this source.

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API.Controllers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/Controllers/PointsController.cs:37 · Level 6 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the REST surface for the points game: the caller's own ledger, the public leaderboard, joining or leaving that leaderboard, and the organizer rollup.

Externals: ASP.NET Core MVC, Asp.Versioning, [FeatureGate], and [Range] from System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.
    • Concept introduced, the surface with no ownership argument. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how ownership is enforced per endpoint. Contrast this controller with BookmarksController, which has to bind a body field, a query argument and a stored row to the caller in three different ways. Here the class comment (:25-28) states the design instead: nothing on this surface takes a user id. The three attendee endpoints resolve the caller from the token inside their handlers, so there is no argument a caller could change, and the one endpoint that reads across every attendee returns no attendee identity at all. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance] is the other half: the leaderboard serves only the display-name snapshot an attendee published at opt-in (:71-74), so rendering the board makes no call into Identity and exposes nothing an attendee did not choose to publish, and the organizer overview carries activity, points and timestamps only (:118-119). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] covers the paging arguments: pageNumber/pageSize (:55-56) and recentCount (:127) are [Range]-validated and select how much comes back, never whose data it is (:46-48).
    • Walkthrough (endpoints in file order)
      • GetMyPointsAsync (:54), GET me: dispatches GetMyPointsQuery with the paging pair defaulting to page 1 of 20 (:55-56, :60), returning the running total, the caller's leaderboard status and a page of ledger entries.
      • GetLeaderboardAsync (:79), GET leaderboard: dispatches a parameterless GetLeaderboardQuery (:83). The board length is fixed by configuration (Points:LeaderboardSize), not by the caller (:73-74).
      • SetLeaderboardParticipationAsync (:104), PUT me/leaderboard-participation: the one write. The request carries only a boolean because the published display name is taken from the caller's token server-side and never from the body (:94-95), and it answers 204 (:101, :112).
      • GetPointsOverviewAsync (:126), GET overview: the only endpoint with a permission, [HasPermission(EngagementPermissions.PointsViewOverview)] (:122).
      • The whole controller is behind [FeatureGate(EngagementFeatures.Points)] (:34) with a bare [Authorize] (:35) as the floor, and [RefuseMachineClients] (:36) keeps a client-credentials caller off an attendee surface (ADR-140).
    • Why it's built this way: designing the routes so no endpoint accepts an identity is a cheaper guarantee than checking one. There is no filter to forget and no claim comparison to invert, which is the failure mode the ownership checks on BookmarksController exist to prevent. See ADR-072 for the points design and ADR-033 for the ownership axis this surface sidesteps.
    • Where it's used: mounted at /points by [Route("[controller]")] (:32) behind the Gateway; consumed by MyPoints and OrganizerPointsOverview through IPointsUIService. Covered by PointsControllerTests, and checked for the machine-client attribute by MachineClientParticipationTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: Points:LeaderboardSize and the per-activity point values are configuration, read by the handlers rather than by this controller. Note also that the one write here carries no [Idempotent], unlike the four POSTs on CheckInsController: setting participation is a PUT of an absolute value, so a replay lands on the same state without help.

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API.Controllers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/Controllers/TicketRosterImportController.cs:36 · Level 6 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the REST surface for the TicketLeap roster upload (BR-268, UC-48): a dry run that reports counts, a commit that queues a durable background import run, and a read of that run's status (TicketRosterImportController.cs:24-30).

Externals: ASP.NET Core MVC (IFormFile, [RequestSizeLimit], [FromForm]), Asp.Versioning, [FeatureGate].
    • Concept introduced, a long write answered as a queued run. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether the contract tells a client what happened. One route, POST roster, has two outcomes by design: a dry run answers 200 with the counts, and a commit answers 202 Accepted with the queued run (:61-62), because a whole roster is applied in batches by a background run whose progress GET roster/import reports (:42-45). A second commit while the event's run is active answers 409 (:44-45, :66). [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] is the reason for the split: the request returns as soon as the run is queued instead of holding a connection open for the whole apply, and the body is capped twice, by [RequestSizeLimit(TicketRosterLimits.MaxRequestBytes)] (:59) on the request and by TicketRosterLimits.MaxFileBytes on the file buffer (:77-78).
    • Concept, parse once at the edge. The upload is read into one buffer of exactly the declared length and parsed as CSV before any handler runs (:73-84): a missing, empty, oversize or truncated file answers Ticket.Roster.FileRequired (:80), text that is not CSV answers the reader's own code, and a file made only of white space answers CsvReader's EmptyCode from the controller itself (:88-97), because the reader would read a line of spaces as a one-cell header (:89-90). The raw bytes then go unchanged to whichever command runs (:100).
    • Walkthrough (members in file order)
      • ImportRosterAsync (:67), POST roster: binds the IFormFile, a [FromForm] eventId and dryRun defaulting to false (:68-71). After the edge checks it dispatches ImportTicketRosterCommand and answers Ok for a dry run (:102-108), otherwise dispatches StartTicketRosterImportCommand and answers Accepted (:111-115). It carries [Idempotent] (:58): the remarks (:52-56) explain that a replay spares a second upload on a dropped response and, for a commit, answers the run the first request started instead of a 409 against it (ADR-017).
      • GetImportAsync (:129), GET roster/import?eventId= (UC-48): dispatches GetTicketRosterImportQuery for the event's latest run (:134); an event with no run answers 404 (:118-120).
      • IsBlank (:141-143): true when every header and every field is white space.
    • Why it's built this way: the class comment (:24-30) places this controller as a sibling of TicketsController under the same /tickets prefix ([Route("Tickets")], :32) with the same posture: authenticated (:35), [HasPermission(EngagementPermissions.TicketsManage)] on every action (:60, :125), and behind [FeatureGate(EngagementFeatures.Tickets)] (:34), so with the flag off every route answers 404 (ADR-031).
    • Where it's used: fronted by the YARP Gateway on the /tickets prefix. Covered by TicketRosterImportControllerTests; the upload helper it calls is covered by FormFileCsvUploadTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: unlike TicketsController it carries no [RefuseMachineClients]. It is on the allow-list in MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Api/MachineClientParticipationTests.cs:69-70, with the reason that every action needs tickets:manage (ADR-140). The byte limits are constants on TicketRosterLimits; their values are not restated here.

Externals: ASP.NET Core MVC, Asp.Versioning, [FeatureGate].
    • Concept introduced, two audiences on one surface. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether each endpoint carries the weakest authorization that is still correct. Seven of the nine actions are organizer actions with [HasPermission(EngagementPermissions.TicketsManage)] (:65, :94, :170, :193, :217, :243, :294); the attendee pair, claim and mine, carries none, because both take the attendee from the token rather than the request (:114, :148-149; BR-269 in the class comment, :32-33). The claim endpoint adds enumeration resistance: an unknown barcode, a ticket linked to another account and a voided ticket all answer the same 404, so the endpoint does not confirm which barcodes exist, and each signed-in account has an attempt budget that answers 429 when spent (:115-118, :136). The comment records why there is no per-address limit: attendees at the venue share one address, and server-rendered calls share the UI host's (:118-119).
    • Concept, privacy by aggregation. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance]: the two insights reads are aggregate only (BR-278). The roster report carries no name, email address or account id and withholds a count of 1 or 2 in the email-domain mix (:186-188); the engagement report withholds every count of 1 or 2 on the server (:209-211). The CSV export writes a withheld count as "fewer than 3" and never the number behind it (:233-237).
