    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.ErasedUsers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/ErasedUsers/ErasedUserGuard.cs:15 · Level 8 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the one-call refusal of a write from an account that has been erased. Every Engagement write handler that a still-valid token could reach calls EnsureNotErasedAsync first and gets back a Result: success for a live account, an Error.Forbidden for an erased one. A second member, GetErasedUserIdsAsync, is the batch form for a write that acts for many accounts at once.
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork (parameter, :26-30, :54-57), the ErasedUser tombstone read through the unit of work's read repository (:32, :62, the batch read typed as IEntityQuerier<TEntity, TIdentifierType>), Result and Error. The user key is the module's UserIdentifierType alias.
    • Concept, erasure is checked at write time, not by token revocation. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance]. Erasure (see ADR-005) removes the user's rows, but a deleted account's token can stay valid for a while. Without a gate, a late request could re-create rows for an account that no longer exists. The guard asks the tombstone table whether the user was erased and refuses the write if so.
    • Walkthrough
      • AccountErasedCode (:18): the constant "Engagement.AccountErased", the error code callers and tests can match on.
      • EnsureNotErasedAsync(unitOfWork, userId, source, cancellationToken) (:26-43): obtains the read-side repository for ErasedUser (:32, typed as IEntityReader, so no tracking and no write surface), runs ExistsAsync(erased => erased.UserId == userId) (:33-35), then returns Error.Forbidden with AccountErasedCode, the message "This account has been deleted." and the caller-supplied source for attribution (:37-41), or Result.Success() (:42).
      • GetErasedUserIdsAsync(unitOfWork, userIds, cancellationToken) (:54-69): the batch form (doc :45-53, which names its use: linking an event's roster to existing accounts, BR-277). An empty input returns an empty set without touching the database (:59-60); otherwise one GetProjectedAsync projects UserId from the tombstones whose id is in userIds (:62-66) and returns the erased subset as an IReadOnlySet<UserIdentifierType> (:68). It returns data rather than a Result because the caller decides per account what to skip, rather than refusing the whole write.
    • Why it's built this way: a static helper rather than a decorator or a service, because the check needs the handler's own unit of work (one scope, one connection) and the source string so the error names the handler that refused. Forbidden rather than NotFound tells the client the request was understood and denied. The sibling handler SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler applies the same message and Forbidden type to its own erased-opt-in case under code Points.AccountErased.
    • Where it's used: EnsureNotErasedAsync is called from CreateBookmarkHandler (CreateBookmarkHandler.cs:32), GetOrCreateMyBadgeHandler (GetOrCreateMyBadgeHandler.cs:40), ManualCheckInHandler (ManualCheckInHandler.cs:44), RecordRoomCheckInHandler (RecordRoomCheckInHandler.cs:67), RecordSponsorVisitHandler (RecordSponsorVisitHandler.cs:58), PointsAwarder (PointsAwarder.cs:57), SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler (SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler.cs:71), TicketLinker (TicketLinker.cs:56), ClaimTicketHandler (ClaimTicketHandler.cs:56), plus the CastVoteHandler (:36), SubmitQuestionHandler (:66) and ToggleUpvoteHandler (:33) use cases. GetErasedUserIdsAsync has one caller, ExistingAccountLinker (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Tickets/Services/ExistingAccountLinker.cs:75). All sites are under MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the guard is internal, so it is unreachable from the API or UI projects, and each handler must remember to call it; no fitness test enforcing that is visible in this unit's source.

    UserDeletedTicketHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Tickets.IntegrationEventHandlers · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Tickets/IntegrationEventHandlers/UserDeletedTicketHandler.cs:28 · Level 8 · class (public sealed partial)

    • What it is: the erasure handler for roster tickets. When Identity deletes an account, every Ticket linked to that account has its holder fields anonymized and its link cleared (class doc, :10-15, BR-274), the same anonymize-then-unlink shape as the speaker erasure.
    • Depends on: ScopedIntegrationEventHandlerBase<TIntegrationEvent> closed over Identity's UserDeleted integration event (:31, imported at :4), IUnitOfWork (:40), the IRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType> it obtains for Ticket (:41), and that aggregate's Anonymize() and Unlink() (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/Tickets/Ticket.cs:337, :314). Externals: IServiceScopeFactory, ILogger<T> and the source-generated [LoggerMessage] (:67-68, which is why the class is partial).
    • Concept, erasure that must reach soft-deleted rows too. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance]. Under database-per-service (ADR-006) the ticket rows live in the Engagement database, so the owning service performs the erasure on receipt of the event, as the sibling UserDeletedBadgeHandler does. Unlike that sibling, this read bypasses the soft-delete filter (ignoreQueryFilters: true, :47): deleting a roster after the event only soft-deletes its tickets, and a deleted row must not keep naming the erased person either (:13-15). Anonymization follows ADR-005 (:12).
    • Walkthrough
      • HandleScopedAsync(integrationEvent, services, cancellationToken) (:34-65): takes the user id (:39), resolves the unit of work and the ticket repository (:40-41), then reads every ticket with LinkedUserId == userId, tracked and with query filters ignored (:43-48).
      • The loop (:51-58) calls ticket.Anonymize() first, then ticket.Unlink(), counting a ticket only when Unlink reports it changed something (:55-57). The comment (:53-54) explains the order: the holder fields must not survive a ticket this erasure touched, and Anonymize only assigns placeholders, so its Result is not inspected.
      • Zero unlinks returns without a save (:60-61); otherwise one SaveChangesAsync covers both changes for the batch (:63) and LogErased records the count at Information (:64, :67-68).
    • Why it's built this way: both changes land in one pass and one save because the link is the only way to find the tickets: an unlink committed without the anonymization would hide them from every later delivery (:17-18). Reading linked rows only makes a redelivered event find nothing and write nothing, and exceptions propagate so a failed erasure is retried rather than acked away (:21-23). [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity].
    • Where it's used: registered by the Application convention scan (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:94) and driven by the single UserDeleted consumer that EngagementBrokerConsumers registers (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/EngagementBrokerConsumers.cs:29), which runs every erasure handler for the type (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:193-196). Covered by UserDeletedTicketHandlerTests (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Tests/Tickets/IntegrationEventHandlers/UserDeletedTicketHandlerTests.cs) and exercised from ProcessTicketRosterImportHandlerTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: a ticket whose Unlink reports no change is anonymized in memory but not counted, and if no ticket in the batch unlinks, nothing is saved, so that anonymization is dropped. Whether that combination (a linked ticket that Unlink declines) can occur is not determinable from this file.

    SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Points.UseCases.SetLeaderboardParticipation · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/UseCases/SetLeaderboardParticipation/SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler.cs:33 · Level 9 · class (public sealed partial)

    • What it is: the command handler behind "put me on the leaderboard" and "take me off". One boolean in, a Result out, with all the interesting work in how it resolves the published name and how it reconciles with a soft-deleted prior opt-in.
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork, ICurrentUserService and its CurrentUserServiceExtensions.RequireUserId member (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Extensions/CurrentUserServiceExtensions.cs:35), IUniqueConstraintViolationDetector, IConcurrencyConflictDetector, LeaderboardOptIn, SetLeaderboardParticipationRequest, ErasedUserGuard (using MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.ErasedUsers, :3), and the framework contracts ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult>, Result and Error. Externals: System.Security.Claims, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging and its [LoggerMessage] source generator (which is why the class is partial, :241-245).
    • Concept, server-side identity for a public surface. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether trust decisions read from the token rather than the request body. SetLeaderboardParticipationRequest carries a single bool Participate and nothing else; the display name comes from the caller's claims (:76, :199-230). The class doc (:17-20) states the threat directly: a name in the body would let any caller publish a name they do not own, on a surface whose whole purpose is showing names to other people.
    • Concept, create-or-reactivate against a filtered unique index. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture], [Rubric §4, DDD]. Because the unique index declared in LeaderboardOptInConfiguration is filtered on the soft-delete flag, a soft-deleted opt-in still occupies the UserId slot for a filtered read but not for the constraint. JoinAsync therefore reads through FindIncludingDeletedAsync, which returns the active and the deleted matches as a tuple (:83-86), and the comment (:80-82) states the consequence of not doing so: every rejoin would insert a fresh row and collide with the index. State transitions stay in the aggregate (deleted.Reactivate(displayName) at :108, LeaderboardOptIn.Create(...) at :114), each returning a Result the handler propagates; the create result is unwrapped with TryGetValue(out var optIn) (:115) rather than a null-forgiving .Value!.
    • Concept, an erased account cannot join, two layers deep. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance]. Account erasure leaves a deleted account's token valid for a while, so the join path refuses that caller twice. First, before anything else, JoinAsync calls ErasedUserGuard.EnsureNotErasedAsync(unitOfWork, userId, nameof(SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler), ...) and returns its failure as-is (:71-74); the comment (:68-70) explains why only the join is guarded: leaving is the erasure's own direction. This closes the case of an erased account with no opt-in row at all, which would otherwise insert a fresh one carrying the token's display name. Second, the reactivate path keeps its own check: erasure (UserDeletedPointsHandler) leaves an existing row soft-deleted with an erasure marker in place of the name, so before reactivating, JoinAsync checks deleted.IsDisplayNameErased and returns Error.Forbidden with code Points.AccountErased instead of bringing the row back under a fresh public name (:100-106); the comment (:97-99) draws the line against an ordinary opt-out, which keeps its real name and still rejoins.
    • Concept, classifying both lost join races through injected detectors. [Rubric §1, SOLID], [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]. The save is wrapped in a try whose exception filter is when (IsLostJoinRace(exception)) (:125), and IsLostJoinRace (:144-146) is an OR of two injected abstractions. IUniqueConstraintViolationDetector covers the insert path: two first-time joins collide on the unique index on UserId. IConcurrencyConflictDetector covers the reactivate path: a rejoin after an opt-out has both requests updating the same soft-deleted row, and the loser fails the concurrency check rather than the index (comment :127-131). Both are abstractions rather than inline message matches, so the provider-specific knowledge of what each failure looks like lives once in the infrastructure layer (for the duplicate-key case, SqlServerUniqueConstraintViolationDetector) and this handler stays provider-agnostic. PointsAwarder leans on the unique-constraint collaborator too (PointsAwarder.cs:85).
    • Walkthrough
      • HandleAsync(command, cancellationToken) (:41-57): null-guards the command (:45), calls currentUserService.RequireUserId("Points.Forbidden") and returns its failure when there is no caller (:47-49), resolves the typed repository (:52), then dispatches on command.Participate to JoinAsync or LeaveAsync (:54-56).
      • JoinAsync (:63-136): refuse an erased account through ErasedUserGuard (:71-74); resolve the name and bail on failure, unwrapping it with TryGetValue(out var displayName) (:76-78); read both the active and the soft-deleted opt-ins for the user, tracked (:83-86); if any is active, return success without writing (:90-91), because re-publishing the name on every call would let a name change ride in on a no-op request (:88-89); otherwise, for a soft-deleted row, refuse an erased one with Points.AccountErased (:100-106) and reactivate any other (:108-110), or create the first one (:112-119); then save inside the race-filtered try (:121-133), which converts either lost join race (insert or reactivate) into the same success the already-on-board path returns, logging at Debug (:132). The comment (:127-131) frames it as intent satisfaction: being on the board is what was asked for.
      • IsLostJoinRace(exception) (:144-146): a private predicate, IsUniqueConstraintViolation(exception) || IsConcurrencyConflict(exception), so the exception filter on the catch stays one readable call.
      • LeaveAsync (:152-181): note the parameter type, IEntityQuerier<TEntity, TIdentifierType> rather than the full IRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType> (:153), because this branch only reads and then mutates the aggregate it already holds. A filtered, tracked read (:157-160), success without writing when there is nothing active (:161-162), otherwise active.Delete() (:164) and save inside a try (:168-178) whose filter is concurrencyConflictDetector.IsConcurrencyConflict(exception) only (:172): a concurrent opt-out soft-deleted the same row first, this save lost the rowversion check, and being off the board is what was asked for, so it logs at Debug through LogConcurrentLeave (:177, :244-245) and succeeds. No erasure guard runs here, by design (:68-70). Soft-delete, not erasure, which is what leaves the row available for the next reactivate. Unlike JoinAsync, the filter has no unique-index half, since leaving never inserts.
      • ResolveDisplayName(user) (:199-230): tries ClaimTypes.Name, then the raw name, then unique_name (:201-203), because inbound claim mapping is not uniform across the hosts that serve this module (:187-190). An empty result is an Error.Validation("Points.DisplayNameUnavailable", ...) (:206-213) rather than a placeholder, since "Attendee" or an email fragment would be meaningless or would leak something the attendee never chose to publish (:192-194). Over-long names are cut at LeaderboardOptIn.DisplayNameMaxLength (:215-229), backing off one index when the cut would split a surrogate pair (:223-227); the comment (:220-222) names the visible symptom it prevents, a U+FFFD in the public leaderboard response.
      • FindClaimValue(user, claimType) (:238-239): a null-tolerant one-liner over ClaimsPrincipal.
    • Why it's built this way: every branch that finds the world already in the requested state returns Result.Success() without writing, so the command is idempotent from the client's point of view and safe to retry. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven]. Note what the handler does not do: it carries no transactional marker, so the CQRS decorator pipeline opens no transaction around it, which is consistent with each branch performing at most one save. Both branches now absorb their lost race as success, so a retry or a double-tap never surfaces a conflict to the user.
    • Where it's used: injected into PointsController as ICommandHandler<SetLeaderboardParticipationRequest, Result> (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/Controllers/PointsController.cs:40, action at :103-104); reached from the UI through PointsService.SetLeaderboardParticipationAsync (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Points/PointsService.cs:58) off the MyPoints page (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Pages/Points/MyPoints.razor.cs:139). Covered by SetLeaderboardParticipationHandlerTests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the display-name cap is applied by truncation, not rejection, so a caller with a very long token name silently publishes a shortened one; nothing surfaces that to the user. Whether the resulting name is unique on the board is not enforced anywhere: the unique index is on UserId, not on DisplayName, so two attendees with the same token name appear identically.

    LiveEventListener

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Components · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Components/LiveEventListener.razor.cs:26 · Level 10 · class (public partial component)

    • What it is: the module's invisible layout component. It renders no markup; on the first render, and again on every authentication-state change, it decides the circuit's membership in the event-wide live channel: a signed-in user joins while the current event is inside its live window (so a poll opening reaches the attendee on whatever page they happen to be on), a signed-out user releases what was held. When the shell opens before the window, it arms a timer and joins when the window opens. The .razor half is only a comment wrapped in CascadingAuthenticationState / AuthorizeView / Authorized (LiveEventListener.razor:4-10); all the behavior lives in the code-behind, which does its own authentication check rather than relying on that wrapper.
    • Depends on: ILiveEventUIService, the LiveEventLookup its GetCurrentEventAsync returns (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/SessionLive/ILiveEventUIService.cs:14) and the LiveEventContext inside it, NotificationHubService (injected as the concrete sealed class, there is no interface in front of it), IToastService and ToastSeverity, LivePollChannel and LivePollOpenedPayload from MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared, IBatteryStatusService and IAccessibilityAnnouncer from MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Capabilities, and EngagementRoutePaths. Externals: Blazor's NavigationManager, AuthenticationStateProvider (injected at :42 for the auth-change subscription) and the cascading Task<AuthenticationState>, IStringLocalizer<LiveEventListener> (injected in the markup, LiveEventListener.razor:2), System.Text.Json, TimeProvider (injected at :41 for the live-window clock and the window timer), and the [LoggerMessage] source generator (:358-359).
    • Concept, the ambient listener that must never throw. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether a non-essential capability degrades instead of taking the user's session down with it. This component is contributed as a layout component and so is live on every page, and the shell's ErrorBoundary wraps only the page body, which the class remarks state directly (:19-25): an exception escaping its render lifecycle tears down the Blazor circuit and forces a full page reload wherever the user happens to be. Every evaluation (the first render and each auth change) therefore runs through EvaluateGuardedAsync, guarded end to end: OperationCanceledException is swallowed as the expected disposal signal (:126-129), and everything else is logged and absorbed behind an inline CA1031 suppression whose justification is written into the pragma itself (:130). Every join that runs outside an evaluation (the energy-saver toast action and the live-window timer tick) goes through JoinChannelGuardedAsync, which repeats the same two catches. The remarks add that the guard stays even though the live-event read already turns transport, timeout and resilience-pipeline faults into a failed lookup (:22-24).
    • Concept, a join that follows the auth state inside one shell. [Rubric §19, State Management]. The shell persists across an in-circuit sign-in on MAUI and WebAssembly (comment :59-60), so evaluating only on the first render would leave a user who signs in later without the channel. The component subscribes to AuthenticationStateChanged on the first render (:75-76) and re-evaluates on each change. A monotonically bumped _evaluation counter (:63-66, :108) makes an older evaluation stand down when a newer one started while it was awaiting (:111-116, :154), so a stale signed-out pass cannot release the join a newer sign-in made.
    • Concept, two concurrent holders of one channel. [Rubric §19, State Management] assesses how a shared per-circuit resource is owned when more than one component holds it at once. This listener joins LivePollChannel.ForEvent(liveEvent.EventId) (:163, :173, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/LivePolls/LivePollChannel.cs:24-25), and the Happening Now page joins the identical key for the same event. Membership therefore cannot be a set: it is reference-counted per key inside NotificationHubService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/NotificationHubService.cs:25-28, :186-189, :217-219), so navigating away from Happening Now releases one join and leaves this listener still receiving events on event:{id}. The flip side is that this listener must never leave a channel it did not join, or it would drop the other holder's reference: _joinedChannelKey (:50-52) records the join actually taken, kept distinct from _channelKey, which is also set while only the window timer is armed or the energy-saver opt-in is pending.
    • Concept, capability-aware live UX. [Rubric §21, Accessibility] and [Rubric §27, Internationalization]. Every user-visible string is a resource key resolved through the injected localizer (LiveEventListener.razor:2, ADR-027), and each poll-opened toast is mirrored to the platform's assistive channel through IAccessibilityAnnouncer (:328) so a screen-reader user gets the same event a sighted user sees.
    • Walkthrough
      • PayloadJsonOptions (:28): a static JsonSerializerOptions.Web, so payloads are read with the same web (camelCase) conventions the publisher serialized them with.
      • MaxWindowTimerStep (:32): a static one-day TimeSpan. The comment (:30-31) gives the reason: a timer delay above about 49.7 days (uint.MaxValue - 1 ms) throws, and the next published event can be months away, so the wait runs in steps of at most one day.
      • Nine [Inject] properties (:34-42): the live-event service, the hub service, the toast service, NavigationManager, the battery-status and accessibility-announcer capabilities, the typed logger, TimeProvider, and AuthenticationStateProvider. The [CascadingParameter] Task<AuthenticationState>? AuthState (:44-45) is nullable because the component can be rendered outside a CascadingAuthenticationState.
      • The mutable state: _subscription and _channelKey (:47-48), _joinedChannelKey (:52), _windowTimer and _disposed (:56-57), _authSubscribed (:61) and _evaluation (:66). The timer is armed when the shell opens before the live window, a tab or MAUI shell left open from the evening before (comment :54-55), so the join happens when the window opens instead of never.
      • OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender) (:68-79): a non-async method. Past the first render it returns Task.CompletedTask (:70-73); on the first it subscribes to AuthStateProvider.AuthenticationStateChanged and sets _authSubscribed (:75-76), then returns EvaluateGuardedAsync(AuthState) when a cascading auth state exists (:78).
      • OnAuthenticationStateChanged(authStateTask) (:84-85) and ReevaluateAsync(authStateTask) (:87-97): the event-handler signature discards the task explicitly rather than using async void (comment :81-83, VSTHRD100); ReevaluateAsync marshals onto the renderer with InvokeAsync(() => EvaluateGuardedAsync(authStateTask)) (:91) and swallows only ObjectDisposedException, the renderer torn down between the event and the dispatch (:93-96).
      • EvaluateGuardedAsync(authStateTask) (:104-138): bumps _evaluation and awaits the state (:108-109), stands down if a newer evaluation started meanwhile (:113-116), calls ReleaseAsync for an unauthenticated principal (:118-122), and otherwise awaits EvaluateSignedInAsync(evaluation) (:124). The two catches follow (:126-137); the catch-all logs through LogLiveChannelSetupFailed and stays silent in the UI, since this component renders nothing and has no place to show a message (:134-136).
      • EvaluateSignedInAsync(evaluation) (:146-175): a no-op once disposed or once a _channelKey is held (:148-151), because a token refresh also raises the auth event (doc :141-142). It reads (await LiveEventService.GetCurrentEventAsync()).LiveEvent (:153) and stands down on no event, on disposal, or on a newer evaluation (:154-157). It then reads "now" once from the injected TimeProvider (:159) and branches three ways. Before liveEvent.LiveWindowStartUtc it sets _channelKey and calls ArmLiveWindowTimer instead of joining (:160-166); after the window (per IsLiveAt, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/SessionLive/LiveEventContext.cs:22-23 for the half-open window it tests) it returns (:168-171); inside it, it sets _channelKey (:173) and awaits TryJoinAsync(JoinChannelAsync) (:174), the unguarded join, since it already runs inside the evaluation guard. Reading the clock through the injected TimeProvider rather than DateTime.UtcNow lets a test pin "now": the resilience tests register TimeProvider.System (LiveEventListenerResilienceTests.cs:49), and LiveEventListenerTests drives the window from a controlled clock (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Tests/Components/LiveEventListenerTests.cs:68, :100).
      • TryJoinAsync(join) (:182-200): the energy-saver check shared by the evaluation and the window timer. When Battery.IsEnergySaverOn (:187), the auto-join is skipped and an Info toast offers a "join anyway" action whose callback is JoinChannelGuardedAsync (:191-195), returning Task.CompletedTask (:196). The inline comment (:184-186) is explicit that only the lossy live channel is deferred and the core notification connection is untouched (ADR-042 Wave 3). Otherwise it returns the supplied join() (:199): unguarded from the evaluation path, guarded from the timer (:181).
      • ArmLiveWindowTimer(liveEvent, utcNow) (:206-215): computes the time until the window starts (:208), disposes any previous timer (:209), and creates a one-shot TimeProvider.CreateTimer whose due time is the smaller of that gap and MaxWindowTimerStep, with an infinite period (:210-214). The callback marshals onto the renderer with InvokeAsync(() => OnLiveWindowTimerAsync(liveEvent)) (:211).
      • OnLiveWindowTimerAsync(liveEvent) (:221-236): does nothing once _disposed is set or _channelKey has been cleared, which covers a tick queued before a sign-out released the channel (:223-226, comment :217-220); re-reads the clock and re-arms when the tick was a capped step that still lands before the window (:228-233); otherwise joins through TryJoinAsync(JoinChannelGuardedAsync) when the window is live, and joins nothing when it has already closed (:235).
      • JoinChannelGuardedAsync() (:242-258): the same two catches again, because the toast action and the timer tick fire outside the evaluation and inherit none of its guarding (doc :238-241, :189-190). IToastService.ShowAction documents the same rule from the other side: exceptions are the caller's to handle (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Interfaces/IToastService.cs:96-101).
      • JoinChannelAsync() (:260-276): a non-async method returning Task. A guard first (_disposed || _channelKey is null || _subscription is not null, returning Task.CompletedTask, :265-268), so a toast-triggered join after an auto-join cannot double-subscribe and a join that resumes after disposal takes nothing nobody would release (:262-264). Then HubService.OnChannelEvent(_channelKey, HandleChannelEventAsync) (:270), _joinedChannelKey recorded before the hub call because the hub counts the reference synchronously (:272-274), and HubService.JoinChannelAsync(_channelKey) returned directly, un-awaited (:275), so the caller's await observes the hub join and no extra state machine is allocated. Subscribing does not join the server-side group, and joining does not register a handler, so both calls are required.
      • ReleaseAsync() (:284-302): shared by disposal and a sign-out (doc :278-283). It disposes the window timer (:286-290), disposes the subscription and clears _channelKey (:292-294), and calls HubService.LeaveChannelAsync only when _joinedChannelKey is set, clearing it first (:296-301).
      • HandleChannelEventAsync(eventName, payloadJson) (:304-342): filters to LivePollChannel.PollOpened (the literal poll.opened, LivePollChannel.cs:14) with an ordinal comparison (:306-309), deserializes a LivePollOpenedPayload and returns silently on a JsonException or a null result (:311-324), announces the poll with the question text (:328), then marshals back to the renderer with InvokeAsync to raise the toast (:332-341). That call passes ToastSeverity.Info and requireInteraction: true (:340-341), so the toast is pinned open rather than expiring on the host timer, and it carries an action that navigates to EngagementRoutePaths.HappeningNow, that is /happening-now (:337, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/EngagementRoutePaths.cs:11).
      • DisposeAsync() (:345-356): sets _disposed first (:347), so a tick already queued on the renderer finds the flag and joins nothing; unsubscribes from AuthenticationStateChanged when subscribed (:348-352); awaits ReleaseAsync() (:354); and calls GC.SuppressFinalize(this) (:355).

    • Why it's built this way: the live layer is best-effort by design, so every failure on this path degrades to "no live channel" rather than surfacing to the user, and the authoritative data is always one page load away. The energy-saver deferral and the screen-reader announcement are the two device-capability touch points, both reached through interfaces whose web fallbacks are no-ops, so the same component runs unchanged on Blazor Server, WebAssembly, and the MAUI hybrid head.
    • Where it's used: contributed by EngagementUIModule as its single LayoutComponentTypes entry (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/EngagementUIModule.cs:45) and rendered by the shared MainLayout on every page; regression-tested by LiveEventListenerResilienceTests (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI.Tests/Components/LiveEventListenerResilienceTests.cs, for example the energy-saver and failing-join cases at :128, :154), with the live window and the auth-state behavior pinned by LiveEventListenerTests: a render sixty days before the window that must arm without throwing (LiveEventListenerTests.cs:100), a later in-shell sign-in that joins (:135), a sign-out that releases (:151), a stale signed-out evaluation that must not release a newer join (:167), and disposal cases that must leave another holder's channel joined or never join afterwards (:191, :207).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the battery state is read only at the moment of a join attempt (:187, on an evaluation or on the window-timer tick), and the component never subscribes to an energy-saver-changed notification, so turning energy saver off later does not auto-join; the toast action is the only way in for that session. Once a _channelKey is held, a later signed-in evaluation is a no-op (:148-151), so an event rescheduled after the timer was armed is not picked up until the next sign-in cycle or page load. The leave call in ReleaseAsync carries no try/catch of its own: on disposal it relies on the hub service handling its own failures, and on a sign-out a throw lands in the evaluation guard. The localizer L is declared only in the markup (LiveEventListener.razor:2), so it is invisible in the code-behind despite being used throughout it.

    UserEngagementExportService

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Exports · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Exports/UserEngagementExportService.cs:21 · Level 11 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the in-process implementation of IUserEngagementExportService. It gathers everything the Engagement module holds about one user (bookmarks, submitted questions, points ledger, check-in history, poll votes, question upvotes, linked roster tickets, leaderboard participation) into a single UserEngagementExportDTO for the cross-service data-subject export (PRIVACY.md section 12, class doc :12-20).
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork and the repositories it hands out; the aggregates UserSessionBookmark, SessionQuestion, PointsEntry, CheckIn, LivePollVote, SessionQuestionUpvote, Ticket and LeaderboardOptIn; the contract IUserEngagementExportService plus its DTO family from MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared.Exports (UserEngagementExportDTO, UserEngagementBookmarkExportDTO, UserEngagementSubmittedQuestionExportDTO, UserEngagementPointsEntryExportDTO, UserEngagementCheckInExportDTO, UserEngagementPollVoteExportDTO, UserEngagementQuestionUpvoteExportDTO, UserEngagementTicketExportDTO).
    • Concept, the data-subject export as eight server-side projections. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance] assesses whether there is a real, exercised access and portability path for personal data rather than a policy page; this class is the Engagement half of one. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether reads are shaped for the database: every collection is fetched with GetProjectedAsync, whose select expression is translated to SQL (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Persistence/IRepository.cs:105-110), so the server returns only the columns the export publishes and no aggregate is ever materialized. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]: Identity owns the export document but not Engagement's data, so it depends only on the interface, satisfied in-process here and over the wire by UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapter. Same shape as BookmarkCountService.
    • Concept, the soft-delete filter is part of the privacy semantics. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture]. None of the eight reads passes ignoreQueryFilters, so the EF global soft-delete filter stays in force and only active personal data is exported (UserEngagementExportService.cs:18-19). That is a deliberate definition of "your data", not an oversight: it is why an opt-in the user has since left reports as not on the leaderboard rather than as a historical membership, and why a retracted poll vote or a removed question upvote is absent (comment :68-69). A ticket's own status is a different matter: a voided linked ticket is still exported, because its imported fields are data held about the user whatever the status (comment :82-84).
    • Walkthrough (UserEngagementExportService.cs:21-125)
      • The primary constructor injects IUnitOfWork (:21), the only collaborator. Each read then resolves its own typed repository from it (:28, :34, :40, :55, :70, :76, :85, :106) rather than injecting IRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType> directly, which is the framework rule for staying on one unit of work per request.
      • Bookmarks (:28-32): projects to UserEngagementBookmarkExportDTO { SessionId, CreatedOn } filtered to b.UserId == userId.
      • Submitted questions (:34-38): projects to UserEngagementSubmittedQuestionExportDTO { QuestionId = q.Id, SessionId, Text, CreatedOn }, again filtered by user. Only the questions this user authored are read, so the only text that enters the document is the user's own, as stored: an erased question carries its placeholder (class doc :17-18).
      • Points ledger (:40-50): projects to UserEngagementPointsEntryExportDTO { ActivityType, Points, SubjectKey, CreatedOn }. Points travels as the value awarded at the time (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/Exports/UserEngagementPointsEntryExportDTO.cs:14-15), so a later change to the configured points-per-activity does not retroactively rewrite the subject's history.
      • Check-ins (:55-66): projects to UserEngagementCheckInExportDTO { Scope, EventId, SessionId, SponsorId, CheckedInOn }. The inline comment (:52-54) states why this is a separate read rather than something derived from the ledger, and the code it points at backs it up: PointsAwarder writes nothing when a rule's configured value is <= 0 (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/Services/PointsAwarder.cs:43-51) and returns a clean no-op on a repeat (:55-64), so the ledger is no proxy for the attendance record the data subject is entitled to.
      • Poll votes (:70-74): projects LivePollVote rows to UserEngagementPollVoteExportDTO { LivePollId, OptionId, CreatedOn } filtered to v.UserId == userId. The comment (:68-69) notes a retracted vote and a removed upvote are soft-deleted, so the export reports the user's active votes and upvotes.
      • Question upvotes (:76-80): projects SessionQuestionUpvote rows to UserEngagementQuestionUpvoteExportDTO { QuestionId = u.SessionQuestionId, CreatedOn }. Only the upvoted question's id travels, never its text, which keeps another attendee's content out of this subject's document.
      • Roster tickets (:85-101): projects Ticket rows with LinkedUserId == userId (:100) to UserEngagementTicketExportDTO carrying EventId, SourceEventName, ExternalTicketId, TicketTypeName, the attendee first and last name, OrderEmail, InvitedOn, LinkMethod and LinkedOn (:87-99). LinkMethod and LinkedOn are unwrapped with !.Value (:97-98), which the link filter makes safe. The comment (:82-84, BR-274) records the scope: an unlinked ticket is not attributable to an account, so it is never part of anyone's export.
      • Leaderboard participation (:106-110): projects to the bare string DisplayName rather than to a DTO, because the export carries only a boolean plus a name. The comment (:103-105) records the invariant that makes the check safe: a user holds at most one active opt-in, since rejoining reactivates the soft-deleted row (BR-135, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/Points/LeaderboardOptIn.cs:87) instead of inserting a second one.
      • Assembly (:112-123): one UserEngagementExportDTO built with collection expressions ([.. bookmarks] and friends, including PollVotes at :118, QuestionUpvotes at :119 and Tickets at :120), IsOnLeaderboard = leaderboardNames.Count > 0 (:121) and LeaderboardDisplayName = leaderboardNames.FirstOrDefault() (:122), which is null when the collection is empty.
      • The eight reads are sequential awaits on one unit of work, not a Task.WhenAll: a single EF context is not thread-safe for concurrent queries, so this is the correct shape, and the cost is eight round trips on a request that runs once per data-subject request.
    • Why it's built this way: projecting server-side to ids, enums, dates and the few text fields the user owns (their own question text, their ticket's imported fields) keeps the export cheap to build and cheap to ship across a service boundary, and it structurally prevents content authored by other users from leaking into one subject's document (UserEngagementExportDTO states that rule explicitly, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/Exports/UserEngagementExportDTO.cs:3-10). Returning a plain Task<T> rather than a Result<T> is what lets the aggregating side degrade: there is no business failure to model here, so an unreachable peer surfaces as an exception the caller turns into a missing section (ADR-007).
    • Where it's used: registered by the Engagement Application DI (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:49, TryAddScoped); exposed over the wire by UserEngagementExportGrpcService, which wraps this in-process instance (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Grpc/UserEngagementExportGrpcService.cs:27). The consumer is Identity's EngagementUserDataExportSection (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/EngagementUserDataExportSection.cs:20), which reaches it through UserEngagementExportServiceGrpcAdapter and re-projects the DTO into the Identity export document, rendering ActivityType and Scope as their readable names (EngagementUserDataExportSection.cs:53, :60), behind ExportUserDataHandler. When the module is switched off in a host, DisabledUserEngagementExportService stands in (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/EngagementModule.cs:34).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: erasure is not this class's job and is not visible here, it only reads. Whether the export is additionally rate-limited or audited when it runs in production is not determinable from this file.

    AttendeeBadgeConfiguration

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Persistence.EntityConfiguration.CheckIns · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/CheckIns/AttendeeBadgeConfiguration.cs:15 · Level 8 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the EF Core mapping for the AttendeeBadge aggregate: two required columns and two unique indexes, one per identity the badge is looked up by (the attendee, and the scannable credential).
    • Depends on: the engine shim base EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType> and AttendeeBadge. Externals: EF Core's EntityTypeBuilder<T>.
    • Concept introduced, the module entity configuration over the engine shim. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses whether the schema is designed for the queries and constraints the application actually needs rather than inherited from conventions; [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] assesses whether persistence concerns stay out of the domain. Every Engagement configuration in this file group follows one shape: extend EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, call base.Configure(builder) first (AttendeeBadgeConfiguration.cs:21), then declare only what is specific to this entity. The base applies the framework conventions once (table and schema resolution, the soft-delete global query filter, audit columns, the concurrency token); the full hierarchy is taught in Group 07. The engine is the choice of base class, so re-pointing an entity at the Cosmos or SQLite shim is a base-class swap with no body edits (ADR-018); every Engagement entity uses the SQL Server shim today. The domain entity itself carries no EF attributes, which is what keeps MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain free of a persistence dependency.
    • Concept introduced, unique index as a race backstop. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] and [Rubric §11, Security]. Both indexes here are unique and unfiltered in the source: HasIndex(b => b.UserId).IsUnique() (:31-32) and HasIndex(b => b.Credential).IsUnique() (:35-36). The first is the concurrency guarantee the get-or-create path leans on (the inline comment at :29-30 says so), the second makes a scan a single seek on a Guid column (AttendeeBadge.Credential, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/Badges/AttendeeBadge.cs:24) and forbids two badges sharing a credential. Note what is NOT written here: neither index declares HasSoftDeleteFilter(), because SoftDeleteUniqueIndexConvention already stamps IsDeleted = 0 onto every unique index of a soft-deletable entity at model finalizing (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Conventions/SoftDeleteUniqueIndexConvention.cs:61-71) and leaves an index that already carries the predicate untouched (:73-76).
    • Walkthrough (AttendeeBadgeConfiguration.cs:19-37): base.Configure(builder) (:21); UserId required (:23-24); Credential required (:26-27); the unique UserId index (:31-32); the unique Credential index (:35-36). That is the whole file: five statements, each with a comment naming the behavior it protects.
    • Why it's built this way: the remarks (:11-14) state the cross-module rule the whole module obeys, UserId is a scalar reference into the Identity database and never a cross-database FK, because Engagement cannot see the Identity model (database-per-service, ADR-006). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness].
    • Where it's used: discovered by assembly scanning and applied when the Engagement SQLServerDbContext builds its model; the unique UserId index is what GetOrCreateMyBadgeHandler classifies through IUniqueConstraintViolationDetector when two requests race (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/CheckIns/UseCases/GetOrCreateMyBadge/GetOrCreateMyBadgeHandler.cs:62).

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Persistence.EntityConfiguration.CheckIns · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/CheckIns/CheckInConfiguration.cs:20 · Level 11 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the EF Core mapping for CheckIn, the one aggregate that carries all three check-in scopes (event arrival, session attendance, sponsor booth visit). It is the most constraint-dense configuration in the module: three scope-partitioned unique indexes plus two read indexes.
    • Depends on: EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, CheckIn, CheckInScope (by value, not by reference, see below), and IndexBuilderExtensions. Externals: EF Core's EntityTypeBuilder<T>.
    • Concept introduced, partitioning one table by a discriminator through filtered indexes. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture], [Rubric §4, DDD]. One aggregate covers every scope because the row shape, the idempotency rule and the attendance query are identical and only the required target differs (CheckInScope documents this, and CheckInInvariants enforces it). The cost is that a single unique index cannot express "one per attendee per event, and separately one per attendee per session": the three uniqueness rules must not collide with each other. Each index therefore carries its own scope predicate through HasSoftDeleteFilter(additionalFilter: ...) (CheckInConfiguration.cs:52, :56, :62), and the extension ANDs that predicate in front of the soft-delete one (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Configuration/IndexBuilderExtensions.cs:63-65). The three scope literals are hoisted into private const string fields (:24-26) with a comment explaining why they are literals at all (:22-23): an index filter is SQL, so it cannot read the C# enum. That is also why the enum's numeric values are documented as load-bearing and never renumbered.
    • Concept, the database as the concurrency backstop behind an application-level check. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity], [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven]. The remarks (:11-18) describe the two layers together: CheckInProcessor makes a repeat scan a no-op by looking for the existing row first (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/CheckIns/Services/CheckInProcessor.cs:73-77), and these indexes make a concurrent double scan a DbUpdateException instead of two rows, so the broker retry that follows lands on the no-op path.

    • Why it's built this way: sponsor visits are self-recorded by the attendee from a printed QR, so the cap has to be structural rather than procedural. Keeping the identifiers scalar (:16-17) is the same database-per-service rule the rest of the module follows (ADR-006).
    • Where it's used: applied to the Engagement model by assembly scanning. Its indexes are the contract every check-in writer is written against: all four handlers route through CheckInProcessor, the organizer paths CheckInAttendeeHandler (CheckInAttendeeHandler.cs:60) and ManualCheckInHandler (ManualCheckInHandler.cs:50) through ExecuteAsync (CheckInProcessor.cs:129), and the self-service paths RecordRoomCheckInHandler (RecordRoomCheckInHandler.cs:108) and RecordSponsorVisitHandler (RecordSponsorVisitHandler.cs:77) through RecordAsync (CheckInProcessor.cs:60). The unique index is declared .IsUnique().HasSoftDeleteFilter() (LeaderboardOptInConfiguration.cs:33-35). That extension member (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Configuration/IndexBuilderExtensions.cs:52-66) builds the predicate from the model rather than from a hand-typed "[IsDeleted] = 0", so the column name follows a rename and the quoting comes from the engine; it takes an engine parameter defaulting to DataSource.SQLServer and an optional additionalFilter that is ANDed in front of the soft-delete predicate (IndexBuilderExtensions.cs:63-65). On a unique index the call is belt-and-braces (the convention would have added the same predicate), and it is idempotent in effect because the convention skips any index that already declares the predicate; on a non-unique index it is the only way to get the filter at all.

Storing DisplayName here at all is deliberate denormalization: the name is the snapshot the attendee published, so the leaderboard query never has to reach into Identity, which is a cross-database read this topology does not allow.     • Where it's used: applied to the Engagement model by assembly scanning; the snapshot column is read by GetLeaderboardHandler (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/UseCases/GetLeaderboard/GetLeaderboardHandler.cs:41), and the unique index is the constraint SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler both navigates and catches (SetLeaderboardParticipationHandler.cs:123-129).

    LivePollVoteConfiguration

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Persistence.EntityConfiguration.LivePolls · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/LivePolls/LivePollVoteConfiguration.cs:17 · Level 8 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the EF Core mapping for the LivePollVote aggregate root, whose centerpiece is the filtered unique index guaranteeing one active vote per user per poll (BR-225).
    • Depends on: EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType> (the shared base that maps audit fields, soft-delete and RowVersion), LivePollVote, and IndexBuilderExtensions for HasSoftDeleteFilter(). Externals: EF Core's EntityTypeBuilder<T>.
    • Concept introduced, the filtered unique index as the backstop for a soft-delete aggregate. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses whether uniqueness and concurrency are enforced at the storage layer rather than hoped for in application code. Because a vote toggles via soft-delete rather than hard-delete, a naive unique index would permanently block a user from re-voting: the deleted row keeps occupying its unique slot. Scoping the index to active rows is what makes the handler's create-or-reactivate dance race-safe (the remark at LivePollVoteConfiguration.cs:12-16 says exactly that). Note how the scoping is expressed: .HasSoftDeleteFilter() (:37), the framework extension member at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Configuration/IndexBuilderExtensions.cs:52-66, rather than a hand-typed HasFilter("[IsDeleted] = 0"). The extension builds the predicate from the model, so a renamed soft-delete column or a different engine follows automatically. On a unique index the call is belt and braces: SoftDeleteUniqueIndexConvention already stamps the same predicate onto every unfiltered unique index of a soft-deletable entity at model finalizing (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Conventions/SoftDeleteUniqueIndexConvention.cs:57, :60-70) and recognizes the predicate it finds rather than doubling it (:74-75). Writing it explicitly keeps BR-225 legible in the file that owns it. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] applies in that the database constraint and the domain Reactivate method are two halves of one idempotent-write pattern; the identical shape guards SessionQuestionUpvote through SessionQuestionUpvoteConfiguration.
    • Walkthrough (LivePollVoteConfiguration.cs:21-41): Configure (:21) calls base.Configure (:23), then requires LivePollId (:25-26), OptionId (:28-29) and UserId (:31-32); note there are no navigations, because a vote is a separate aggregate by design and so carries scalar FKs only. The filtered unique index on { LivePollId, UserId } (:35-37) is BR-225, one active vote per poll and user, with the soft-delete predicate applied through HasSoftDeleteFilter() and the rule named in the comment above it (:34). The second, non-unique index on { LivePollId, OptionId } (:40) supports the grouped COUNT per option that the tally issues (:39).
    • Why it's built this way: the filter is what lets soft-delete and uniqueness coexist, routing it through the shared extension keeps every filtered index in the codebase producing byte-identical SQL, and the second index matches the tally query shape exactly, so results are computed from an index rather than by scanning the vote table.
    • Where it's used: applied by the Engagement SQLServerDbContext at model build; CastVoteHandler relies on the unique index as the final arbiter when two concurrent votes race, and LivePollResultsBuilder is the reader the second index serves. Covered by EngagementEntityConfigurationTests (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Tests/Persistence/EngagementEntityConfigurationTests.cs).

    PointsEntryConfiguration

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Persistence.EntityConfiguration.Points · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/Points/PointsEntryConfiguration.cs:21 · Level 8 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the EF Core mapping for PointsEntry, one row per awarded activity. Its composite unique index is not an optimization: it is the enforcement point for two separate rules at once.
    • Depends on: EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, PointsEntry, PointsSubjectKeys (for the key length), and IndexBuilderExtensions. Externals: EF Core's EntityTypeBuilder<T>.
    • Concept introduced, one index carrying two business rules. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] and [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven]. The unique index on (UserId, ActivityType, SubjectKey) (PointsEntryConfiguration.cs:46-48) is simultaneously the idempotency key for an at-least-once award (a replayed integration event collides with the row it already wrote) and the anti-farming rule (N questions or N answers for one session collapse onto one subject key, so they award once). The remarks (:12-20) spell out the two-layer interplay: PointsAwarder pre-checks with an ExistsAsync on exactly those three columns so the ordinary duplicate is a clean no-op (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/Points/Services/PointsAwarder.cs:65-74), and a concurrent race that gets past the pre-check surfaces here as a provider exception the awarder classifies as already-awarded rather than as a failure (PointsAwarder.cs:85). The database is the arbiter of last resort, not the first line.
    • Walkthrough (PointsEntryConfiguration.cs:25-53): base.Configure(builder) (:27); UserId (:29-30), ActivityType (:32-33) and Points (:35-36) required; SubjectKey required with HasMaxLength(PointsSubjectKeys.MaxLength) (:38-40), that is 64 characters (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/Points/PointsSubjectKeys.cs:14), a bounded key being what makes it indexable at all; OccurredOnUtc required (:42-43); then the filtered unique triple (:46-48) and a second, non-unique UserId index also carrying HasSoftDeleteFilter() (:51-52) so the "my points" ledger read is a seek. That second index is the case the convention does not cover: it is not unique, so without the explicit call it would carry no filter.
    • Why it's built this way: pushing idempotency into a unique constraint means correctness does not depend on the broker delivering exactly once, which it does not. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]. As everywhere in this module, UserId stays a scalar column, never a cross-database FK (:18-19).
    • Where it's used: applied by assembly scanning; the index is the contract PointsAwarder is written against, and the ledger it protects is read by GetLeaderboardHandler and the my-points queries, and exported by UserEngagementExportService (UserEngagementExportService.cs:40-50).

[Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness], [Rubric §8, Data Architecture]. See AttendeeBadgeConfiguration for the shared base-class story.

    TicketConfiguration

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Persistence.EntityConfiguration.Tickets · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/Tickets/TicketConfiguration.cs:19 · Level 11 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the EF Core mapping for Ticket, one imported TicketLeap ticket on an event's roster. Same base shape as the siblings in this part; what sets it apart is that it carries two filtered unique indexes at once, plus two non-unique filtered lookup indexes.
    • Depends on: EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, Ticket, TicketInvariants for every column width, and IndexBuilderExtensions for HasSoftDeleteFilter(). Externals: EF Core's EntityTypeBuilder<T>.
    • Concept reinforced, the database as the import's backstop. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture]. The remarks (TicketConfiguration.cs:11-18) name the rules each index enforces: one ticket per TicketLeap ticket ID per event (BR-268) and one ticket per barcode per event, the barcode claim's lookup (BR-273). The import checks for both itself; the indexes are what hold when that check is raced. Both are filtered to active rows, so a deleted roster never blocks a fresh upload for the same event, the same soft-delete-plus-unique interplay UserSessionBookmarkConfiguration uses for bookmarks.
    • Walkthrough (TicketConfiguration.cs:23-74): base.Configure(builder) (:25); EventId required (:27-28); then seven string columns, each width sourced from TicketInvariants: SourceEventName required, 200 (:30-32, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Domain/Tickets/TicketInvariants.cs:15); ExternalTicketId required, 100 (:34-36, TicketInvariants.cs:18); Barcode required (:38-40), its width forwarding to ClaimTicketRequest.BarcodeMaxLength (TicketInvariants.cs:21), that is 100 (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/Tickets/ClaimTicketRequest.cs:14), so the claim request and the column cannot disagree; TicketTypeName required, 200 (:42-44, TicketInvariants.cs:24); AttendeeFirstName and AttendeeLastName required, 100 each (:46-52, TicketInvariants.cs:30); OrderEmail bounded but optional (:54-55), its width forwarding to EmailInvariants.MaxLength (TicketInvariants.cs:33). Status required (:57-58). The indexes: unique { EventId, ExternalTicketId } (:60-62) and unique { EventId, Barcode } (:64-66), both with HasSoftDeleteFilter(); non-unique OrderEmail (:68-69) for the account-linking lookup (BR-272, which runs on every verified address per the remarks); non-unique LinkedUserId (:72-73), because "my tickets" and the erasure unlink both read by the linked account (:71). The two non-unique indexes need the explicit filter: the convention stamps only unique ones.
    • Why it's built this way: idempotent re-imports and concurrent claims are guaranteed by constraints rather than by timing, and the two lookup indexes match the hot reads. Cross-module identifiers (EventId, LinkedUserId) stay scalar columns, never cross-database FKs (:16-17). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness].
    • Where it's used: applied to the Engagement model by assembly scanning; it is internal. Covered by TicketConfigurationTests (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Tests/Persistence/TicketConfigurationTests.cs:38, :48, :64, :73), which pin the filtered unique index per event key, the order-email index, the string bounds and the optional order email.

    TicketImportRunConfiguration

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Persistence.EntityConfiguration.Tickets · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/Tickets/TicketImportRunConfiguration.cs:18 · Level 11 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the EF Core mapping for TicketImportRun, the row that tracks one queued or running roster import and holds its staged data. Its one index is the "one active import per event" rule.
    • Depends on: EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, TicketImportRun, TicketRosterImportStatus (whose numeric values the filter names), and IndexBuilderExtensions. Externals: EF Core's EntityTypeBuilder<T>.
    • Concept introduced, HasSoftDeleteFilter() with an additionalFilter. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture]. Every other unique index in this part filters on soft-delete alone; this one narrows further to active runs: .IsUnique().HasSoftDeleteFilter(additionalFilter: "[Status] IN (0, 1)") with the explicit name IX_TicketImportRun_EventId_Active (TicketImportRunConfiguration.cs:40-43). 0 and 1 are Queued and Running (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/Tickets/Imports/TicketRosterImportStatus.cs:10, :13), so finished and failed runs drop out of the index and any number of them may exist per event, while a second active run cannot. The remarks (:12-17) call it the backstop behind StartTicketRosterImportHandler's own check: two commits racing past that check cannot both start. The trade-off is that the predicate is a SQL literal over enum ordinals, so renumbering the enum would silently change the rule.
    • Walkthrough (TicketImportRunConfiguration.cs:25-44): a private ErrorCodeMaxLength = 100 (:22), since the ticket error codes are short dotted identifiers (:21); base.Configure(builder) (:27); EventId required (:29-30); Status required (:32-33); ErrorCode bounded and optional (:35-36); StagedRoster mapped with no length (:38), unbounded text holding the file's whitelisted fields only while the run is active (remarks :15-16); then the filtered unique index (:40-43).
    • Why it's built this way: the staged holder data lives on the run row so the internal-command payload carries only the run id, and the narrowed index lets the history of completed runs accumulate without loosening the single-active-run guarantee. EventId is a scalar column, never a cross-database FK (:16). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness].
    • Where it's used: applied to the Engagement model by assembly scanning; it is internal, and the brief records no reference outside the defining file.

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Persistence.EntityConfiguration.UserSessionBookmarks · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/UserSessionBookmarks/UserSessionBookmarkConfiguration.cs:16 · Level 8 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the EF Core mapping for UserSessionBookmark, the module's founding aggregate. Same base shape as the siblings above; it enforces BR-21 (one active bookmark per user per session) and adds the index the conference-day count path depends on.
    • Depends on: EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, UserSessionBookmark, IndexBuilderExtensions. Externals: EF Core's EntityTypeBuilder<T>.
    • Concept, indexing for the hot read, not just for the constraint. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]. The second index (UserSessionBookmarkConfiguration.cs:37-38) exists because BookmarkCountService counts by SessionId alone, and a leading-UserId composite cannot seek on that predicate; the comment (:36-37) says exactly this. It is non-unique, so HasSoftDeleteFilter() is required rather than optional: the convention only stamps unique indexes (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Conventions/SoftDeleteUniqueIndexConvention.cs:63-64), and the count query carries the soft-delete predicate, so an unfiltered index would not match it.
    • Walkthrough (UserSessionBookmarkConfiguration.cs:20-39): base.Configure(builder) (:23); UserId required (:25-26); SessionId required (:28-29); the filtered unique index on (UserId, SessionId) (:32-34); the filtered SessionId index (:38-39).
    • Why it's built this way: filtering the unique index on IsDeleted = 0 lets a user remove and re-add the same bookmark any number of times while guaranteeing only one is active, which is precisely why the bookmark write path reactivates rather than inserts. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture].
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the remarks (:12-16) note the FK relationship to Conference.Session is configured at the shared DbContext level (where both entity types are visible) rather than here, to avoid a cross-module Infrastructure-to-Domain dependency that would break module isolation. In the extracted topology those two entities live in different databases anyway, where CrossDataSourceDegradeConvention drops the constraint.

    LivePollConfiguration

    MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure · MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Persistence.EntityConfiguration.LivePolls · MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure/Persistence/EntityConfiguration/LivePolls/LivePollConfiguration.cs:16 · Level 9 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the EF Core mapping for the LivePoll aggregate root: column requirements, the question length limit, the two query indexes, and the access mode EF uses to materialize the encapsulated options collection.
    • Depends on: EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer<TEntity, TIdentifierType> (the shared base that maps audit fields, soft-delete and RowVersion), LivePoll, and LivePollInvariants for QuestionMaxLength. Externals: EF Core's EntityTypeBuilder<T> and PropertyAccessMode.
    • Concept introduced, the no-cross-database foreign key rule. The base class itself is taught in Group 07; what this file makes concrete is the remark at LivePollConfiguration.cs:11-15: EventId and SessionId point at Conference-owned rows in a different database, so they stay plain indexed scalar columns and consistency flows through the Conference gRPC validation boundary, never through an FK constraint. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses schema independence between services, which is exactly what the scalar-reference choice buys. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses the persistence contract (nullability, lengths, indexes) and the database-per-service discipline (ADR-006); all of it is visible in a dozen lines here, and it is the same rule AttendeeBadgeConfiguration states for UserId.
    • Concept introduced, pinning EF's access mode for an encapsulated collection. [Rubric §4, DDD] assesses whether the aggregate keeps its collections closed to outside mutation. LivePoll exposes Options as a getter over a private List returned through AsReadOnly(), which means EF must read and write the backing field, never the property, or materialization silently produces nothing. EF's convention already infers field access for this shape; :49-50 states it anyway with builder.Navigation(p => p.Options).UsePropertyAccessMode(PropertyAccessMode.Field). The comment at :43-48 gives the reason: stating it makes the mapping independent of that inference, so a later change to the property (a different projection, a computed wrapper) cannot silently turn materialization into a no-op. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses exactly this kind of fail-loudly-later choice. It is an access mode only, no schema change: the relationship itself stays configured from the child side in LivePollOptionConfiguration.
    • Walkthrough (LivePollConfiguration.cs:20-51): Configure (:20) calls base.Configure(builder) first (:22) so the common conventions land before any override; EventId required (:24-25); Question required with HasMaxLength(LivePollInvariants.QuestionMaxLength) (:27-29), sourcing the length from the domain constant so schema and invariant can never disagree; Status required (:31-32). Then HasIndex(p => p.EventId) (:35), non-unique, because the Happening Now page and the organizer manage view both query polls by event (:34); and HasIndex(p => new { p.SessionId, p.Status }) (:41), the composite added for GetOpenPollsHandler. Its comment (:37-40) is the performance record: that query filters on (SessionId, Status), runs once per attendee per session and again on every structural poll event, and only EventId was indexed, so it scanned. It deliberately mirrors SessionQuestionConfiguration, which already indexes the same pair. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether indexes match the real query shapes of the hot path. The file closes with the Navigation(...).UsePropertyAccessMode(PropertyAccessMode.Field) call described above (:49-50).
    • Why it's built this way: one length constant sourced from the domain, scalar cross-service references per ADR-006, indexes derived from the two live-layer read shapes rather than guessed, and an explicitly stated access mode so the aggregate's encapsulation and EF's materialization cannot drift apart.
    • Where it's used: discovered and applied at model-build time by the Engagement SQLServerDbContext through EF Core's configuration scanning; it is internal, so nothing else can reach it. Covered by EngagementEntityConfigurationTests (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Infrastructure.Tests/Persistence/EngagementEntityConfigurationTests.cs).
